items.title: Trump, Xi and Putin meet as global alliances hang in the balance
paragraphs: President Donald Trump, right, Chinese President Xi Jinping, center, and Russian President Vladimir Putin arrive for a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa Nov. 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China. Win McNamee/Pool photo via AP hide caption

SHENZHEN, China and MOSCOW, Russia — President Trump joined Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China on Thursday – capping two days of talks characterized by high-minded tributes to the role of great powers in maintaining peace, even as the men who led them had a role in starting some of the most intractable conflicts around the globe.
"History tells us when great powers are at peace, the world is secure," said Xi in opening remarks before cameras. "When great powers clash, the world is in chaos."
Putin noted their nations could make a "significant contribution to strengthening security and stability in the world."
"In that sense and I think in lots of other ways, we are making history," said Trump, who called it a "special responsibility" for the three countries to work together.
Yet, they offered few solutions toward peace, with the leaders offering divergent agendas going in:

Trump wanted to talk about reducing nuclear weapons and his mission to keep Iran from obtaining them; Putin was looking to push for an end to the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow; Xi was signaling he hoped to avoid wading too deep into either topic — preferring to showcase China's growing global clout with more general statements promoting peace and economic stability.
There were also topics to avoid: Trump refused to engage with journalists' questions over China's alleged role in an espionage plot to steal high end Nvidia chips.

In the end, the summit's key deliverable was arguably the image itself: the president of the United States gathering with authoritarian leaders from China and Russia for the first time in American history.

Despite being billed as a summit of "groundbreaking significance" by the Chinese hosts, sit-down talks between Trump, Xi, and Putin were relatively brief — with some of that time taken up by interpreters delivering simultaneous translation.
Trump's meeting with Putin lasted 42 minutes. His talks with Xi went about an hour. The trilateral group session went on for an hour and a half.
Still, it was enough time for familiar Trump bonhomie to emerge.
"Who's he? He's my friend," said a smiling Trump upon seeing Putin ahead of their bilateral meeting.
"We've known each other for a long time," added Trump after he and the Russian leader warmly shook hands. "And I think a lot of wonderful things can come of this. Or at least start."
Similarly, Trump told Xi "as long as you and I are in charge of things, we're never going to have a problem."

Both statements were tacit admissions the clock is ticking on Trump's remaining two years in office — with change coming even sooner to Washington when Democrats take control of Congress come January.

The China gathering was first proposed by Putin during an October phone call with Trump — an offer to meet together with President Xi when China hosted the Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference in China that November.

For Putin in particular, the meeting was always going to be a coup: the latest sign that — with Trump and Xi's help — he has effectively chipped away at Western attempts to isolate him politically over his invasion of Ukraine.

Back in Moscow, state media showed footage of the three leaders huddled together seemingly on loop — proof that Russia had regained what the Kremlin sees as its rightful place among global superpowers.
Ignored by Kremlin-friendly media were hints at more subtle power dynamics at play.

Xi greeted Trump on the tarmac personally — returning a gesture Trump had given the Chinese leader during his recent visit in Washington — while Putin received a more scaled down delegation upon arrival to Shenzhen.
Similarly, Trump was offered the top spot next to Xi during the APEC group photo and sat next to Xi during the APEC dinner reception — with Putin positioned at a separate table.
Was it a slight to Putin? A calculated attempt to flatter Trump? A reflection of Russia's vastly weaker economy? Whatever the answer, Xi wasn't ignoring his Russian guest entirely.
The two gathered privately for two hours on Wednesday — a sit-down China-Russia watchers estimated to be their 50th meeting all told.

Xi and Putin also echoed each other in their public speeches— both touching on familiar themes of the dawn of a new "multipolar world" and criticizing the use of sanctions as a sign of Western influence on the wane.
From the outset, critics of the summit voiced concern that Trump, Xi, and Putin would seek to carve the world into each country's perceived sphere of influence.

In Russia, the event was billed as a potential "new Yalta" — a reference to a moment in 1945 when the leaders of the U.S., Soviet Union, and United Kingdom hastily agreed to a post-World War II order for Europe.
Instead, the Shenzhen summit reflected the far more fragmented priorities of its participants.

Trump made no secret he hoped to include China in arms control talks — what Trump calls "denuclearization" — at a moment when key landmark nuclear treaties between Russia and the U.S. have all expired.
The catch: his Chinese hosts had little interest in the issue.
Beijing has repeatedly rebuffed U.S. attempts to include it in negotiations with Russia — noting that its arsenal remains far below those of Cold War-era rivals Moscow and Washington.

Differences also extended to the war in Ukraine, where Putin had hoped to press for U.S. and Chinese support for a settlement tilted in Moscow's favor — including a redrawn security map for Europe that would amount to a rollback of NATO from Eastern Europe.

Xi has insisted Europe have a seat at the table in any negotiated settlement. Trump has largely relied on his trusted envoys — real estate developer Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner — to hash out the complexities of any peace deal.
Following Trump's meeting with Putin, a Kremlin aide would only say that Ukraine had been the focus of the discussions — adding the Kremlin leader had left "in an excellent mood."

Just hours earlier, Ukraine carried out a missile strike on the lone bridge linking mainland Russia to the annexed Crimean peninsula for the third time this week — effectively disabling the structure for months to come.
The bridge is widely considered the Russian leader's pet project — a symbol of Russia's claim to territory illegally seized from Ukraine in 2014 rendered in steel.

items.title: Survivors of Uganda's deadly landslide seek justice at the UN
paragraphs: ByOndiro Oganga and Swaibu IbrahimBBC AfricaReporting fromKampala
Survivors of a 2019 landslide in eastern Uganda that killed more than 50 people have taken their fight for relocation and compensation to the United Nations.
The 48 complainants accuse the government of violating Uganda's constitution by failing to put effective disaster management measures in Bududa, a mountainous district prone to landslides.
Their case comes as heavy rains raise the risk of further landslides. They say the government relocation programme ignores their safety, land rights and livelihoods.
The UN Human Rights Committee is considering what is believed to be the first case seeking climate adaptation measures, one that could set a global precedent.
At least 33 of the 53 people who died in the 2019 landslide were children. Years later, survivors say every spell of heavy rain brings back fears of another tragedy.
William Tsama, one of the claimants, lost four members of his family.
"Victims in such situations, ignored by governments, can take them to court to compel them to help their citizens."
Uganda introduced a resettlement plan for landslide-prone areas in 2011, but progress has been limited, with relatively few people relocated.
Last month, it launched a new resettlement programme offering affected households 18m Ugandan shillings ($4,300; £3,300) to help them move to safer areas.
But some survivors have questioned whether the amount is enough to cover the cost of relocating and rebuilding their lives.

Under the programme, families can choose between receiving two acres of land, valued at 8m shillings, plus 10m shillings towards building a house, or taking the equivalent land allowance in cash, alongside the same housing grant.
The scheme is expected to benefit 1,410 households identified as living in high-risk areas.
The government has now given residents of designated high-risk areas two months, from November to December, to leave or face forced eviction.

The threat extends beyond landslides. The complainants say changing rainfall patterns and declining soil fertility have also affected farming, leaving many families struggling to secure their livelihoods.
"I want to get a new good place for my people, so even if I die, they will be okay. I am an old man, but I am doing it for my children," Tsama said.
The survivors first launched legal action in 2020 in Uganda, and received support from Ugandan environmental organisation Greenwatch three years later.
They are seeking compensation for lost family members and livelihoods, as well as emergency measures, including accessible early-warning systems in high-risk areas.
Greenwatch Executive Director Samantha Atukunda Kakuru Mwesigwa said the case is about changing how governments prepare and respond to climate-related disasters.

"Justice for claimants is not just about winning in court. It is about forcing government policy to keep pace with a changing climate, and ensuring loss and damage is no longer an afterthought in disaster management," she said.
The threat of climate-related disasters extends across East Africa.
In Kenya, floods and landslides killed at least 181 people between March and May 2024, according to the Kenya Red Cross. In Rwanda, floods and landslides killed 135 people in May 2023.

The dangers are also being felt further afield. In October 2026, a flash flood swept through Nepal's Gorkha district after a landslide blocked a river, washing away homes and infrastructure, and killing over 1,500 people.

"Disasters like the one in Bududa are only getting worse because of climate change – and they are happening all around the world, as we've seen recently and tragically in Nepal," ClientEarth lawyer Vesselina Newman said.
She said poorer countries, which have contributed relatively little to global emissions, are bearing some of the heaviest consequences of climate change and need greater financial support.
"High income countries must provide financial assistance and ensure that sufficient money goes directly to countries like Uganda, so they can roll out life-saving adaptation measures," she said.
The complainants say relocation must involve more than moving people out of danger.
They want the government to protect their livelihoods, respect their land rights, and take account of individual needs.
The case is now before the United Nations Human Rights Committee, which will ask the Ugandan government to respond within six months.

items.title: Westside Cowboy named BBC Introducing Artist of the Year 2026
paragraphs: Westside Cowboy have been announced as BBC Introducing Artist of the Year 2026.
Jimmy Bradbury, Reuben Haycocks, Aoife Anson O'Connell and Paddy Murphy formed the band in Manchester in 2023 and have since rocketed from the pub circuit to some of the UK's biggest festivals.

The award is presented to an up-and-coming artist or band who has, with the support of BBC Introducing, made a significant impact and has previously been won by Olivia Dean, Myles Smith and Tom Grennan.
Murphy, from Longridge in Lancashire, said the win put them in "good company", with Bradbury, from Shropshire, adding that it was "very flattering".

BBC Introducing supports new musical talent across the UK, providing a platform to propel new artists on to the local and national stage through 30 Introducing shows, three national radio shows and six shows across BBC Radio 1, Radio 1Xtra, Radio 2, 6Music, Radio 3 and Asian Network.
About 72,000 tracks from emerging UK artists supported by BBC Introducing make it on to the airwaves each year.

Westside Cowboy uploaded their debut single I've Never Met Anyone I Thought I Could Really Love (Until I Met You) to the Introducing platform in November 2024 and had their first play on radio within hours.

items.title: Waugh Thistleton Architects set to transform derelict bathing pavilion into Tracey Emin-backed studios and sauna
paragraphs: UK studio Waugh Thistleton Architects is set to transform the Edwardian Westbrook Pavilion in Margate, UK, into an arts centre for British artist Tracey Emin with a cafe, public sauna and changing rooms.
“The project will bring a much-loved seafront building back into use, combining its original purpose with new spaces for art, culture and the local community,” said Waugh Thistleton Architects.
The studio recently won planning permission from the local council to convert the abandoned building, which Emin purchased in 2023, into a facility run by the Tracey Emin Foundation.
The project aims to return the building to its former use as a changing room for swimmers and as a tea room, when it originally opened in 1914.
“Originally opened in 1914, the building provided public changing facilities for sea-bathing and a tea room,” said the studio.
“Following storm damage in the Great North Sea Storm of 1953, subsequent alterations detracted from its original Edwardian character,” it continued.

“The renovated pavilion will accommodate artist studios, an art gallery, clubroom, cafe, sea-bathing changing facilities, a new sauna and refurbished public toilets, restoring its original role as a place for bathing and socialising by the sea.”

Along with making the pavilion a building used by the public again, the studio aims to return the building’s core to its Edwardian look by removing later additions. It will also add glazed facades to the wings on either side of the central pavilion.
The building will be topped by a rooftop terrace, while a public toilet on the site will be renovated.

“The design draws on the proportions and character of the original building, removing later additions and reinstating lost features such as the historic belvederes which top the central tower structures,” said the studio.
“The beachfront facade will see a new glazing system and colonnade to each of the building’s wings, with a new sheltered archway forming a new seating terrace at the building’s heart,” it continued.
“The design seeks to reference the original architecture while providing contemporary needs of a public building. Where original features are references, these are distinguishable architecturally.”
Emin is one of the UK’s best-known living artists. We recently produced a video of a landmark exhibition of her work at Tate Modern.
Recent projects by Waugh Thistleton Architects include plans for the “tallest mass timber office building in the US”.
Images courtesy of Waugh Thistleton Architects

items.title: This artist's space goblins blend magical realism with classical portraiture
paragraphs: Lisa Lennon was born on the Isle of Man, a place steeped in myth and folklore. That perhaps shows in her art style, which defines as magical realism with a focus on classical portraiture. She works with watercolours, building up many layers while adding details.
Below, Lisa introduces four examples of her work. If you're inspired and need supplies for your own art, see our guides to the best watercolour paints and the best watercolour pencils.

“This science fiction piece was dreamed up while walking by the sea. Her headpiece is inspired by the pebbles there. I love wide open spaces; they give me a lot of scope to play with atmospheric scenes.”
“This is where fantasy meets science fiction. I was working with local folklore and became obsessed with goblins and elves. I developed a collection called ‘Space Goblins’.”
“Another in the ‘Space Goblins’ series. How did Tudor clothes end up in outer space? We can only speculate, but I do love a good riff, and it’s always a large technical challenge to get it right.”

“One of my classic goblins. I so enjoy painting these rather cantankerous, sassy personalities. My focus here – technique-wise – was to have a vintage look to the colour and quality, all while retaining a contemporary, whimsical feel. I love this one.”
You can see more of Lisa's work on her website.

items.title: The Specsavers GTA 6 campaign is hilariously on brand
paragraphs: GTA VI trendjacking was already everywhere, even before today's release of the most- anticipated video game in history (see our GTA VI review for our Digital Art Editor's experience playing it). A lot of the attempts to jump on the bandwagon have been lazy and half-hearted, with brands merely using AI image generators to give product shots a vaporwave makeover.
The optical chain Specsavers has turned out to be an unlikely exception. Its unusual GTA VI campaign might actually be the best brand collaboration of the year.
That's right, Specsavers has entered into its "biggest partnership of all time’. It's sponsoring GTA... just not that GTA.

The teaser post above might have raised eyebrows among gamers given that GTA VI developer and publisher Rockstar Games has very limited collaborations. There's it's deal with the Miami Heat (and with Oakley for the GTA VI Collector's Edition), but there are only parody fake brands in GTA VI itself.

But Specsavers isn't sponsoring the video game that everyone's talking about. It's hooked up with GTA Transport Ltd, a British road haulage company based in Leicester. Which sounds a bit like Leonida, right?

“It might not be the GTA partnership I originally had in mind but a deal’s a deal. I'm pleased to offer every driver at GTA Transport a free eye test,” the company's brand partnerships and sponsorships lead Neil Liddle said.

Bugz Singh from GTA Transport Ltd said: “We were surprised when Specsavers got in touch, but we’re delighted to be the GTA they’ve teamed up with. Our drivers spend all day on the road, so they’re looking forward to their eye tests.”

Specsavers' stunt rises above most of the GTA VI trendjacking that we've seen. It's funny, and it's a lot more creative and memorable than simply throwing Vice City hues onto brand imagery. Best of all, it shows that Specsavers really knows its brand and its public, maintaining consistency with the message it's been using for over 20 years.

Specsavers has been telling the same joke since 2002, and it still works. In fact, it's become even more effective. The line 'Should've gone to Specsavers', coined by then in-house creative director Graham Daldry, is now so ingrained in the public consciousness that it no longer needs to be appended onto the campaign. It's already implied.

Having already sold close to 16 million copies before today's release, GTA VI is a cultural phenomenon with a reach that extends well beyond that of most games. An AI-generated vaporwave graphic can't make an unrelated brand a part of that, but Specsavers has shown that on-brand creative thinking can forge a memorable connection to the entertainment event of the year.

items.title: How Premier League's big six keep getting richer
paragraphs: Companies put their money where supporters are prepared to spend it. It is a simple fact of business in every country, a reality of football's food chain.
In England, Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester United traditionally dominated viewing figures, column inches, shirt sales and sponsorship.
Over the past 20 years they have been joined by Chelsea, Manchester City and Tottenham.
This group of clubs now generate so much money it is hard to imagine how they can fail in the long term - even factoring in short-term performance issues.
We will use Everton, the only club not in the big six to be in the Premier League since its inception in 1992.
This tells a tale of how even one of the league's founding members can be left trailing well behind.
In 2009-10, the gap in revenues between the big-six average and Everton was £120m. In 2024-25, that gap had grown to £442m.
In large part it is the boom in international TV rights.

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport that it has attracted companies prepared to pay large sums to be associated with the Premier League's top clubs.
"The big football brand clubs have global fanbases and that makes them very attractive to global commercial partners, especially for sponsorship and front-of-shirt deals," Maguire said.

"You combine that with the fact that the Premier League is broadcast to 190 different countries around the world, and especially the international audiences - that allows the clubs to negotiate very good prices."
Only 10% of Everton's revenue comes from commercial deals, while for the big six it is 45%.
It means Everton, and other clubs in the league, are heavily reliant on broadcast income. It makes up 66% of their revenue.
For Everton at least, this should change following the move to Hill Dickinson Stadium.
But that is unlikely to be enough to stop the gap increasing.
It has taken a few years, but Aston Villa and Newcastle have begun to increase their revenue.
This is largely thanks to the financial rewards of Champions League football.
But even Uefa has created a system which entrenches the position of the biggest clubs.
When the European Super League plan was torpedoed, Uefa created a new financial deal called the value pillar.
This reserves 35% of all Champions League revenues, or £713m, for the historically most successful clubs.
At the end of the league phase last season City are estimated to have earned £37.9m from the value pillar, Liverpool £35.5m and Chelsea £33.3m. Newcastle received only £13.6m.
The good news for Villa is their coefficient has improved greatly, aided by last season's Europa League win.
Their value pillar is projected to be worth £25m this season. But that will still be less than the big six clubs in the competition.
The cards are stacked against an ambitious club - not just domestically, but in Europe too.
Take a look at the financial trend of the big six and one thing becomes noticeable - Chelsea are beginning to fall behind.
In the past two seasons, and for the first time in recent history, the Blues recorded the lowest revenues of the big six.
Not just by a small amount. They were £74m behind Tottenham, and £200m below Liverpool and Manchester City.
City's matchday income is the lowest, with the club's huge revenues largely due to commercial deals.
City, however, have been found guilty of breaching the Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18, inflating the value by using "sham contracts" with sponsors.
The club deny wrongdoing and have lodged an appealed against the verdict.
Stamford Bridge has a capacity of only 40,000, with no easy scope for expansion. The rest of the big six have grounds which hold at least 60,000.
Chelsea generated an average spend per fan of £80 in 2024-25, the second highest in the league after Arsenal.
Yet with 20,000 fewer tickets sold than their big six rivals, Chelsea's total matchday revenues are dwarfed.
"Matchday spend has become increasingly important," Maguire said. "There has been a flatlining of broadcast revenues, especially since 2017.
"As a consequence, clubs have had to look at alternative methods of increasing revenues, especially with costs both on the pitch and off pitch rising so fast."
Matchday revenue has effectively stalled for Chelsea, rising only £16m over the past 10 years. United's has grown by £69m and Spurs, thanks to their new ground, by £85m.
"Chelsea are far more reliant upon player sales," Maguire said. "There is a growing divide because the global appeal is very much aligned with three or four clubs.

"Arsenal have re-established themselves with their progress in the Champions League. Manchester United are a brand in their own right. And Liverpool have expanded Anfield from 44,000 to 61,000, with many of those extra seats having gone to commercial."
Chelsea's successful player trading model has so far limited the impact.
But there are signs that, financially at least, the big six could become the big five.
You might recall that Villa and Newcastle were not fans of the old profit and sustainability rules (PSR).
PSR forced both clubs to sell some of their best players to balance the books.
That has changed this season with squad-cost ratio (SCR).
There is a key difference with SCR, in that it allows a club to spend the money they generate on players. PSR limited losses so was more restrictive.
"This does make it a little easier for the likes of Villa and Newcastle to spend money," Maguire said. "But it is still heavily weighted in favour of the big six.
"SCR is different to PSR rather than better. For some people, change is advantageous. For others, it isn't."
The big six generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the other clubs. So they can spend hundreds of millions of pounds more on their squads.
This makes the big six even more powerful in the transfer market.
"Look at the clubs who voted against SCR - Brighton, Brentford, Bournemouth, Crystal Palace, Fulham and Leeds," Maguire said.
"It's very noticeable that those clubs have traditionally been very good at player sales, while they have tended to have lower matchday and commercial revenues."
Most of the big six - the outlier being Chelsea - are not remotely close to the Premier League's 85% SCR limit.
If you give clubs more money to spend on transfers, the likelihood is they will do just that. And the numbers back that up.
Premier League clubs spent £3.5bn - not only a highest total for a summer window, but it almost smashed the record for a whole season, the £3.53bn set in 2025-26.
The annual accounting cost of previous transfers, or amortisation, has been rising year on year.
"Over the course of the last decade, transfer amortisation has more than doubled and close to tripled," Maguire said.
"Which means that on average, clubs in the Premier League are now spending, or now have a cost which goes into their SCR calculations of just under £100m."
Uefa fears that SCR will make matters worse, and have an inflationary impact across Europe.
In the summer 13 Premier League clubs broke their transfer record.
Brentford, Brighton, Palace, Leeds and Nottingham Forest all spent more than £40m on a player - unthinkable until recently.
So we have learned that the big six have more money than ever, and the gap is so huge it is impossible for any other club to compete with them, financially at least.
And this is an important point: other than Villa and Newcastle, the other clubs are not trying to compete with the big six.
Clubs like Brentford and Brighton have shown that smart models are just as effective as fat wallets.
They sign the potential stars of the future, nurture them and then sell them to the big six.
Football's ecosystem recycles the big-six money through the transfer market.
But it is a precarious business for these other clubs.
"The smaller clubs have to get it right on a more regular basis than the bigger clubs," Maguire said.
"The big six can afford to make signings which are £60m and £70m, who turn out to be relative flops, and still have those players on high wages for several years."
And this is perhaps the key point about the vast finances of the big six.
The commercial power of the big six does not guarantee success. After all, United sit in the relegation zone.
Yet Mauricio Pochettino, their new manager, may well get the chance to revamp the squad despite the club spending £945m on players in the past five years.
The richest clubs can try to spend their way out of trouble. Again and again.
But the rest of the league are only a couple of bad transfer windows from catastrophe.
And that is the real gap between the big six and the rest.

items.title: The Creality Raptor Pro Max should radically speed up the design of custom car parts
paragraphs: The best 3D scanners have changed the game for custom manufacturing, and they continue to advance. Creality, which also makes some of the best 3D printers, already has a wide range of solutions, including the versatile Sermoon P1S.

Now, it's added to the family a new device that looks set up to speed up workflows for those working in automobile custromisation. The Raptor Pro Max builds on the existing Raptor Pro handheld scanner but almost doubles the number of cross blue laser lines and unlocks a 40% larger single capture range.

The Raptor Pro Max has 42 cross blue laser lines, up from 22 on the Raptor Pro, and it can reach up to 1.26 million measurements, raising the maximum scanning rate by approximately 91% while offering a single capture range of up to 480 × 330 mm at a working distance of 550 mm.

That wider coverage and higher scanning rate mean that you can capture more of a bumper, door or body panel in each pass, which gives successive frames more shared geometry to maintain stable tracking. The expanded coverage also helps reduce the number of markers required by up to 25%.

Creality says the reduction of repeat passes, the need for repositioning and the application of markers means users can complete scans of automotive workpieces in up to 40% less time. That will allow custom parts to be moved into design and trial-fitting work more quickly.

For smaller features, there's also the option to switch to seven parallel blue laser lines to capture edges, threads, and chamfers. Together, the two blue laser modes cover objects from 5 to 4,000 mm in size. Creality cites volumetric accuracy of 0.02 mm + 0.08 mm/m.² The blue lasers can also capture suitable black and metallic surfaces without scanning spray.

During handheld scanning, real-time preview in Creality Scan lets operators monitor coverage as they move around a part. The Blue Laser Line Mode operates at up to 60 fps and the a near-infrared (NIR) structured-light mode at up to 30 fps, with geometry or texture tracking. There's built-in anti-shake functionality to help reduce the impact of hand movement.
The Creality Raptor Pro Max has a suggested retail price of $1,799, which is reduced by around 10% for a limited time to $1,619. There's also a limited-time bundle including a Scan Bridge for $1,799.
Check out the Creality US store or UK store for more details.

items.title: UK firms owed thousands as Saudi-backed LIV paid golfers millions
paragraphs: LIV Golf filed for bankruptcy in September

LIV Golf - backed by more than $5bn (£3.8bn) from Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund - paid millions to players and executives in the weeks before filing for bankruptcy, while leaving a trail of unpaid bills from UK suppliers.
BBC Sport has seen invoices from five small businesses totalling hundreds of thousands of pounds, all of which were overdue before LIV made its final payments to players.
Global Infusion Group,, external a Buckinghamshire company that provided catering at July's LIV Golf UK event, is still owed £321,671, due on 7 August.
Suffolk-based BD365 Clean, external provided 108 cleaning staff and is owed £75,225, most of which was due on 20 July and 13 August.
"It just feels completely immoral," said Bonnie May, chief executive of Global Infusion Group.
"It really matters to a business of our scale. The impact has been huge, both personally and professionally."
Only $2m (£1.5m) has been earmarked so far by the Saudi owners to pay unsecured creditors, leaving many smaller companies unsure if they will receive anything at all.
Yet court filings reveal LIV made 59 payments to golfers on 31 July, amounting to $16.6m (£12.6m) and matching prize money for the same LIV Golf UK event.

A further $34.2m (£25.9m) went to players between 17 August and 3 September following tournaments in New York and Indianapolis, including $6.4m (£4.9m) to 2026 champion Jon Rahm just five days before the bankruptcy filing.
LIV Golf's bankruptcy and its debt to British businesses
Four senior LIV executives also received retention bonuses totalling nearly $3m (£2.3m) in August.
"It's sickening," said Krissi Foskett, owner of BD365 Clean, who described the unpaid bills as "almost an extinction-level event" for her team.
"How can they sleep at night, knowing they are potentially putting companies out of business?"

Meanwhile, public records list more than £3,000 owed to Goodysphere,, external a family-run Yorkshire firm that provides a sensory bus designed to help autistic children who may find busy events overwhelming.
LIV Golf did not respond to our request for comment.
However, in August, LIV chief executive Scott O'Neil said he hoped they would be able to pay their suppliers.
"What I would say to them is we're doing everything we can to make sure we can do right by them and the work they committed."
Players received a total of $16.6m (£12.6m) five days after the LIV Golf UK event
The controversial breakaway league had been owned and bankrolled by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) since its launch season in 2022.
But in April, the fund announced it would end its backing after the 2026 season, putting LIV's future in doubt.
"Our understanding was that the funding would take LIV through 2026," said Global Infusion Group's May, whose company had about 60 staff catering for players and broadcasters.
"We weren't aware the funding had already stopped and there wasn't enough to actually fulfil their obligations."
PIF's multi-billion-dollar investment helped it to lure some of golf's biggest names and disrupt the PGA Tour's dominance of the sport.
"It's Saudi money, that's safe as houses, we thought," said Foskett.
"Their head honchos came along and enjoyed hospitality. We were there cleaning up at one o'clock in the morning then back in at five in the morning, only to be treated like this."
PIF remains the majority owner of Newcastle United, while Saudi Arabia will host the 2034 Fifa World Cup.

"I'm sure the country won't want to be saddled with the characterisation that it doesn't pay its bills," said professor Simon Chadwick, who is an expert in the business and politics of sport across Africa, Europe and Asia.
"I do find it surprising that they would simply walk away. I think they would want to engage in some kind of remedial action, particularly in terms of managing their image and reputation."
Krissi Foskett said her team "went the extra mile" and sifted through waste by hand to help LIV hit sustainability targets
Filmmaker Joe Bentley spent eight days from April working on a video for LIV's YouTube channel that is still online.
He is owed nearly £6,000, with £2,226 due on 31 July.
The video was part of the 'LIV Back' series, set up to "focus on the impact LIV players and teams are making off the course".
He filmed at two schools taking part in 'Little Sticks', a LIV outreach programme which aimed to provide golf equipment and training in areas of deprivation.
"You feel massively deflated, a bit cheated and undervalued," said Bentley.
"Everyone I dealt with at LIV was lovely. The first email I sent chasing was to a production coordinator or a manager and even she was appalled that we hadn't been paid."
Gateshead Council is also owed £1,912, due on 22 August, relating to 'Little Sticks'.
"Transformation is not a short-term process," said Professor Chadwick.
"If you're going to embark on investment programmes in community sport, grassroots sport, you've got to make a long-term commitment and those changes have got to take place."
LIV filed for bankruptcy protection in New Jersey on 8 September.
"The contacts we had sadly all lost their jobs," said Giles Mitchell, whose company, Office Pantry, supplied food to LIV's office on London's South Bank.
"We didn't hear anything from them and then their emails started bouncing back."
There was hope the competition could survive in some form with new investment, but in November LIV announced it was winding down operations.
In the bankruptcy filings, LIV estimated it had between $500m and $1bn (£380m-£760m) in liabilities and at least 1,000 creditors.
The largest 30 unsecured creditors alone were listed with claims of more than $64m (£49m).
"I think the message is loud and clear to somebody like me that, no, we're not going to get paid for any of this," said May.
"If anything did come our way, I'm thinking it's going to be pennies in the pound, nothing which will have any impact, or even cover our legal fees."
Fourteen golfers were among the published creditors with the 30 largest unsecured claims.
Rahm topped the list with a claim of $7.5m (£5.7m), which he agreed to give up as part of his deal to leave the league.
Bryson DeChambeau ($5.7m/£4.3m), Dustin Johnson ($5.5m/£4.2m), Cameron Smith ($4.8m/£3.6m) and Tyrrell Hatton ($3.4m/£2.6m) also featured.
IMG Media, the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, and British golf YouTuber Rick Shiels were each listed with claims of more than $1m (£760,000) too.
Meanwhile, BBC Sport understands the R&A is owed about £500,000 for advice on sustainable maintenance of courses used by LIV.
A hearing is scheduled for January to consider the wind-down plan, but creditors may have to wait longer to find out how much they will get back.
"I've had nights just sat there in tears, thinking, what is the point," said BD365 Clean's Foskett.
"How much comes in will honestly depend on whether or not the business will still be going at the end of January.

items.title: Tammy Shipley was supposed to be monitored in prison. Instead she died after drinking 20L of water
paragraphs: The death of an Aboriginal woman who collapsed after drinking at least 20 litres of water in a New South Wales prison cell was preventable and the result of systemic failures, a coroner has found.
Tammy Michelle Shipley, 47, died at Silverwater women’s correctional centre on 20 December 2022.
State coroner Teresa O’Sullivan ruled on Thursday that her death was caused by low blood sodium levels resulting from excessive water consumption and complications of schizoaffective disorder.
“I’m confident in finding that Tammy’s death was preventable,” O’Sullivan said.

The mother of five had been taken into custody on remand 11 days earlier, after being charged with shoplifting offences, but didn’t disclose her mental health issues to police. Police also didn’t double-check her answers about her health, despite the fact she had attended a police station two weeks earlier and told them she heard her neighbour talking in her head.
O’Sullivan found there had been a missed opportunity to recognise the mental health issues that were present, and to potentially divert Shipley away from the criminal justice system.

When she appeared in a local court over the shoplifting charges the next day, the magistrate was not told she had been refused bail on other charges, so made orders they thought would secure her release.
“There was a clear systems failure,” O’Sullivan found.
Shipley should have been continually monitored – both physically and electronically – after twice attempting self-harm in custody.
It was a serious failure that this had not been done, O’Sullivan said.
“If observations had been carried out at the intervals required, it was likely that Tammy’s excess consumption of water would have been … prevented,” she said.
She deemed it unsatisfactory that Shipley had not been seen by a psychiatrist or mental health nurse at any point during the 11 days before her death.

She added that Shipley should have received medical care from the time she started vomiting, after 10am on the day of her death. Instead, she said, Shipley experienced seizures shortly before noon and was seen lying face down on the floor of her cell around an hour later.
A period of 23 minutes lapsed between when she was first seen lying on the ground and the commencement of resuscitation attempts, which the coroner found was unacceptable.
One corrective services officer had hastily closed the door to her cell after smelling faeces in the room earlier in the day.
“It was completely inappropriate that Tammy, who was known to be suffering a mental health condition, was left in that condition in her cell,” O’Sullivan said.

O’Sullivan made 10 recommendations to NSW police, Corrective Services NSW and Justice Health, including a review of the “austere and depressing” unit in which Shipley was held, which was intended to be a therapeutic space but left the coroner gravely concerned.
She also recommended regular monitoring of footage inside the jail and improved maintenance and cross-checking of records related to mental health conditions.
The coroner acknowledged the jail had already made changes after Shipley’s death.
Outside the court, Shipley’s mother, Vicki, said she hoped the findings would force the system to assess how people are treated.
“I honestly thought that at this stage of our country’s development, we have moved past how convicts were treated,” she said.
“The system – every system – eventually caused trauma to my daughter, until eventually it killed her.”
Vickey Shipley urged the NSW government to quickly implement the recommendations.
“If they’re not made, there will be some other family standing here doing exactly the same thing that I am,” she said.
“All too often we hear the cry: ‘There’s not enough money.’

items.title: Mother whose twin baby died was determined to have home birth despite advice of experts, NSW inquest hears
paragraphs: Baby B’s mother was so determined to have a home birth she ignored the advice of experts – including her own midwife, an inquest has heard.
The inquest heard she was pregnant with twins, which she described as a “wonderful shock”, and didn’t want a hospital birth because she had heard of others’ traumatic experiences.

The New South Wales coroner’s court in Lismore heard on Thursday that the local medical community in the Hunter Valley swung in to action, warning the mother – who cannot be named for legal reasons – that a home birth was risky while also preparing in case something went wrong.
Baby B died of a bacterial infection, while the other baby got sick but survived.

Baby B’s death is part of an ongoing inquest into the deaths of four babies – Baby R, Baby D, Baby DH and Baby B – who were born in free births or home births in NSW’s northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024.

The first three babies died after a free birth – where no medical professionals are present. By contrast, four midwives were part of the birthing plan for Baby B. The main midwife continued to support the woman.
“The alternative was that she would birth at home with no support whatsoever,” the midwife – whose name is suppressed – told the court.
The court heard that expert opinion found that the midwives’ treatment was “reasonable and appropriate”, which was a clear distinction from the other three births being examined at the inquest.
“It will also be clear from the expert evidence that a home birth was still considered by the experts to be not suitable in the circumstances,” the court heard.

Expert witness, Prof Hannah Dahlen, said that was because it was a twin pregnancy, that it had continued beyond 41 weeks, that there had been no specialist review, that the family were far away from the hospital, and that “there was a possible need for urgent operative birth and the need to provide simultaneous skilled care and resuscitation for two babies”.
But the mother declined multiple checks, and her distrust of the medical system was only reinforced as the pregnancy progressed.
She had scans at 12 weeks and at 22 weeks, but chose not to have hospital antenatal care, or to consult with an obstetrician. A local doctor followed up, but she told them she was doing well.
Her midwife recommended monthly ultrasounds, and induction at 36 to 37 weeks. She declined. The midwife told the court she warned the mother about the risks at every visit.
In evidence read to the court, the mother said she had always planned to have a home birth after hearing traumatic birth stories from other people.
“I did a lot of research and found the midwives, so … I felt comfortable to still home birth the twins,” she said.
She said she was “quite selective” finding midwives with home birth experience and had researched the experience online and in books.

The court heard “a lot of staff” at the local hospital were concerned about the plan, and the ambulance service was worried enough to organise a second paediatric resuscitation kit. There was collaboration and communication between the midwife, obstetricians from the local hospital, and a local GP.
In court, the midwife said the mother wouldn’t have hesitated to seek help if it was needed, and that she thought she could convince the mother to go to hospital, or at least somewhere closer to it.
But then ambulance officers – and later, police – turned up at the home to do a welfare check, making the mother angry, upset, and more determined not to enter the health system.
“She felt quite violated because they came to her home,” the midwife told the court. “They were coercing her to attend the hospital.”
The mother went into labour at home, and the first twin was born successfully. Baby B “gave an initial gasp”, “appeared stunned” and needed help to breathe spontaneously.

Everything seemed to be fine, the court heard. The mother said the next night she could hear the baby breathing, and did not notice any changes. But in the early hours of the morning, Baby B was no longer breathing. When emergency services arrived, they noted that Baby B was “pale, unresponsive and not breathing, with no pulse, although she was still warm to touch”.
Hospital records show continued they continued to work for 45 mins to save her once she arrived there, but she was flatlining. Her blood sugar and temperature were low, and she died.
By that stage, the boy twin was limp and grey. He likely had the same infection but it was less severe, and he survived.
The midwife said she surrendered her registration after the death, both because of its effect on her and because of the way the health system treated her.

She said she wasn’t told when Baby B died. When someone from the hospital rang to ask about the surviving twin, she assumed they were asking about Baby B and asked whether she was being transferred to a bigger hospital.
“Oh, she’ll be going to the coroner,” the midwife was told.

items.title: Parents live in fear paedophile nursery worker harmed their children
paragraphs: Parents are calling for mandatory CCTV in nurseries after a worker who looked after their children was later exposed as a paedophile.

Nathan Bennett was jailed in February for multiple counts of sexual abuse, including two counts of rape, against five boys at Partou King Street nursery in Bristol. His crimes were discovered after a CCTV review.
Bennett previously worked as an apprentice for 18 months at another nursery in the Somerset area - which the BBC is not naming – which does not have CCTV.
A number of parents whose children went there said they lived in fear about what could have happened to them at the nursery. The government said a panel was examining the use of CCTV in nurseries.
Warning: This story contains distressing details

Bennett's victims at Partou King Street nursery were two and three years old at the time of his offences. In February 2025, concerns were raised over his behaviour with the children, specifically a group of five who the prosecution said he would "favour".
He was suspended from the nursery after CCTV of him putting his hands down a boy's trousers was reviewed.

There is no evidence he committed any offences while he worked at the Somerset nursery, or that there were safeguarding failures there. Avon and Somerset Police said it had not identified grounds to warrant a criminal investigation at the site.
Det Insp Lucy Forde, who led the investigation into Bennett's crimes, previously told the BBC she feared only a fraction of his crimes could be proven.
"He's worked in childcare and has had access to children for a number of years," she said.
"My worry is there will be other victims that we haven't been able to identify, that are too young to understand what's happened to them," Forde added.

After learning of Bennett's offending, a number of parents whose children went to the Somerset nursery shared their worries about what could have taken place. The BBC has changed their names to protect their children's identities.
Rachel, whose children attended the nursery, said she became suspicious of Bennett after witnessing him being overly tactile with her child in her opinion.
The BBC has seen messages from the time exchanged between Rachel and her partner, in which concerns about Bennett's behaviour were discussed, describing him as "weird".
They discussed raising concerns about him and eventually complained to management about their son being repeatedly left in soiled nappies and being sore.
Rachel said they eventually asked for their child to be moved away from Bennett's care.
"My son was always on Nathan's lap - there would be times where I would see him stroking him on his arm, kissing him on the forehead or cheek," she said.
"There was something inside me that knew straight away that's not right," she added.
Rachel said she saw Bennett taking her child into the nappy changing area alone with the door closed on one occasion.
"I came to pick up my son and I could hear him crying - the changing room door was closed so I waited for a while.
"Nathan came out with him, alone, and said 'I'm not sure what's up with him, he never seems to like his nappy being changed','" she said.
Rachel said healthcare professionals had since referred her child for an assessment by specialists who deal with cases of sexual assault.
If you have been affected by this story or would like support then you can find organisations that offer help and information at the BBC Action Line.
James, whose children attended the nursery at the same time, said he witnessed Bennett being "too physical" with children.
"Most times I went to pick up my children he was holding a child on his lap or making physical contact with a child," he said.
"More often than not, the child looked like they were trying to get away, but he was holding them there. I didn't see other nursery staff with children on their lap," James said.
He said he verbally complained to nursery managers about Bennett.
"I told them I had observed Nathan being physical with children – in my opinion too physical.
"Their response was 'isn't it great how cuddly he is?'," he said.
Bessie Martin, a former colleague of Bennett's at Partou King Street nursery in Bristol, previously told the BBC she had also witnessed him holding children on his lap.
"I would see a child try to wriggle away or stand up and walk off, but he'd say 'sit here and we're going to read a book'," she said.
She became a whistleblower and reported her concerns about Bennett to senior management at Partou.
During his trial it emerged parents had raised concerns to the nursery in the six months before he was caught.
James said news of Bennett's conviction led him to worry about the worker's behaviour when he was an apprentice.
"I was concerned that he didn't become a predatory paedophile when he moved to the nursery in Bristol – I believe he was always a predatory paedophile," he said.
James said CCTV in nurseries should be a "minimum requirement".
"If I was to go through choosing a nursery again, it's something I'd need to have in place," he said.

Another parent, Helen, said she wanted to see mandatory, actively monitored CCTV and stronger safeguards, including higher qualification requirements for staff and strict enforcement of two-person working.
"Mandatory CCTV should not be a problem – especially in places with extremely vulnerable people, where it's most needed," she said.
"Something positive needs to come out of such a horrendous thing," she added.
Helen said the uncertainty of not knowing if anything could have happened had led her to "read into everything".
"Any comments [from my child] about nursery now, you don't know how to interpret them.
"My child will sometimes start a conversation saying, 'mummy, I didn't tell you this thing that happened at nursery' and I start shaking every time she says it," she added.
Katie and John Meehan, whose daughter Genevieve was killed at a nursery in Stockport in 2022, have also been campaigning for mandatory CCTV in nurseries.
CCTV footage showed nursery worker Kate Roughley tightly swaddling nine-month-old Genevieve, strapping her to a beanbag and leaving her unattended. She died of asphyxiation.
John Meehan said that - while CCTV was not a "silver bullet" - use of it could "identify unsafe practices" or provide evidence for the regulator and police when harm occurred.
"For parents entrusting their precious and vulnerable children to a nursery, the confidence and reassurance these safeguards can provide are vital," he said.
The Department for Education said it had strengthened recruitment and safeguarding requirements at nurseries.

It said this included full criminal record checks for staff working closely with children, checks on references before a hire, new safeguarding training and clear processes for staff to raise concerns.
Allegations or concerns that a staff member has harmed a child or is unsuitable to work with children should be reported to the council's Local Authority Designated Officer (LADO).
The nursery where Bennett was an apprentice said one concern was raised following Bennett's conviction, which the LADO confirmed did not meet the threshold for investigation.
The nursery was rated Outstanding by Ofsted at the time of Bennett's employment. The regulator told the BBC there had been no concerns raised during Bennett's employment at the nursery.
In an email sent to parents following Bennett's conviction, the nursery said Bennett was employed as an apprentice and subject to a high level of supervision.

A man who worked at the nursery at the same time as Bennett said he had not noticed any suspicious behaviour but was concerned staff could sometimes be left to work alone, even if they had no previous childcare experience.
"I had never worked in early years or childcare before," he said.
"The chances of being alone when changing a nappy were quite high.
"The door wasn't always open when [Bennett] was changing nappies," he added.
A member of staff who worked at the nursery after Bennett had left, said she had often felt overwhelmed with the number of children she was given to look after.

While she said whistleblowing policies and safeguarding procedures were clearly explained at the nursery and people were encouraged to report anything that did not sit right, she added that complaints she raised about having too many children were not addressed, and she eventually quit her job.
"It was horrendously overwhelming and eventually I couldn't do it anymore," she said.
Rachel said the impact of knowing her child went to a nursery where Bennett was working would be "lifelong".
"The moment I found out he had been convicted confirmed how I had felt that year about Nathan Bennett," she said.

And although she cannot do anything about the lack of CCTV at the Somerset nursery, she said mandatory video monitoring could deter other potential offenders - or provide proof for other families after a crime had happened.
"It didn't deter Nathan Bennett, but without it he would be free to continue committing these crimes," she said.

items.title: Developer accused of 'environmental vandalism'
paragraphs: Councillors Ian Middleton and Fiona Mawson are concerned about the loss of hedgerows and trees
Work to gain access to land for a housing development and a new "super cycleway" has resulted in "environmental vandalism", councillors have said.
Kidlington Green councillors Ian Middleton and Fiona Mawson said residents were concerned by the number of hedgerows and trees recently cut down on Oxford Road.
Adjacent fields have planning permission for 800 homes as part of wider plans for more than 4,400 to be built in the area.
A spokesperson for developer Bellway said all the work had been done with an ecologist on site and complied with outline planning consent.
The trees and hedgerows were cut back on land next to the Oxford Road
The cycleway would help connecting Kidlington to Oxford, running alongside the A4165, Oxford Road.
The route is expected to get busier with significant growth planned for north Oxford, including a potential new stadium for Oxford United.
According to Bellway, the trees and hedges were cut down between 26 October and 6 November to "create access" to the site planned for housing, as well as to "facilitate" the work for the cycleway.
The proposals include "significant landscaping and ecological enhancements" as well as 50% affordable housing and "other infrastructure", it said.
Middleton, the lead member for housing and greener communities at Cherwell District Council, said outline planning permission did not give the developer "unrestricted permission to carry out works".
He also said its actions were "nonsensical" and premature, given the cycle path was not "imminent".
"If all they needed was access, why have they ripped out an entire hedgerow?" he said.
"We knew some of this was going to be taken out, but it's the scale of it that's really impacted people and sent shock waves across the local community."
A spokesperson for Bellway said hit had been working with Cherwell District Council "to agree details of a replacement wildlife corridor," including planting 150 new trees.

items.title: Grade I interiors, gold bars, cost fears: Bank of England faces headache over £160m revamp
paragraphs: Andrew Bailey may spend his days closely watching developments in the strait of Hormuz or US stock markets for signs of shocks to the global economy – but the Bank of England’s governor has a £160m problem brewing much closer to home.

A secretive major revamp of the Bank’s historic headquarters in the heart of London’s Square Mile presents a huge test of Bailey’s project management skills. The central bank, with its reputation staked on carefully counting the nation’s pennies, will be keen to avoid delays, budget-busting or any echoes of the expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that left his former peer Jerome Powell awkwardly clashing with Donald Trump on camera.
Bailey and his senior managers believe they can modernise the Bank’s Grade I-listed structure and interiors while 3,500 staff are still busy at work on site.

By the summer of 2028, 1,400 Bank staff who work in a nearby office at 20 Moorgate will be relocated to Threadneedle Street, have taken voluntary redundancy or have been offered an alternative job in a new outpost in Leeds, also being refurbished.

It appears a unique project for Britain’s struggling building trade: overhaul a site with a globally recognised exterior; preserve its Roman mosaic floors, stone columns and vaulted, ornate ceilings while keeping exact floorplans under wraps, for fear of terror attacks.

The Bank itself began in rented premises in 1694, moving to Threadneedle Street in 1734. Nicknamed the Old Lady of Threadneedle Street after a satirical cartoon of William Pitt the Younger, it has been refashioned and remodelled – first by Sir John Soane between 1788 and 1833 and then again in the 1920s when the interior was largely demolished and rebuilt.

The building is owned by the Bank, which was given independence to set interest rates by Gordon Brown in 1997, and, after the 2008 financial crash, it was later handed responsibility for regulating the banking sector by George Osborne.

Cash to fund the scheme will come from an estimated £100m of savings each year for three years that the Bank says will accrue from 450 redundancies and other cost savings. As one member of Bank staff told the Guardian: “It’s like there is a leaving party every week.”
What the Bank wants to avoid is a repeat of the delays and cost overruns that dogged the Federal Reserve in Washington, which led to Trump threatening the US central bank with court action.

Over the life of the Fed’s renovation project, construction costs have soared. The initial budget of $921m (£696m) in February 2020 was revised several times before December 2024, when it hit $2bn. Construction was supposed to be completed in mid-2024 but is now expected to run until December 2027. The final cost is likely to be nearer $2.5bn.
The Bank’s scheme is on a much smaller scale, and pales against the possible £60bn it will cost to renovate the Palace of Westminster. It is more akin to the £80m Elizabeth Tower restoration.

What Bailey will want to avoid is joining the Elizabeth Tower, which houses Big Ben, as the subject of parliamentary scrutiny after its budget doubled and then rose by a further 20%, giving ammunition to critics who have long accused the Bank of mishandling its core purpose of helping to manage the economy by setting interest rates at the appropriate level.

The Bank project was first announced in July 2025 and work was due to start this month, but it was only in October, with a month to spare, that the construction company Sir Robert McAlpine was awarded the building contract.

Described as an “incredibly complex project”, it aims to transform the neoclassical building, which sits opposite the Royal Exchange and adjacent to the Mansion House, into what some staff hope is a Google-like workplace of friendly office spaces, breakout rooms and in-house cafes.

The Bank says there will be no delays, citing the appointment of architects last November. A project manager, a cost consultant and a firm of engineers were also signed up, and they have already begun evaluating budgets and timescales.

A Bank of England spokesperson said: “As part of our plans to preserve our historic Threadneedle Street office we are considering how best to renovate the site and optimise our running costs. All our procurement processes aim to deliver value for money.”

Bailey’s team – based in a grand part of the Bank known as the Parlours – will need to judge the cost implications of meeting new regulations on fire safety, accessibility, electrical testing – with the fire at Notre Dame mid-renovation still fresh in the memory – new plumbing and the need to have a more environmentally friendly building with heating based on renewable sources.

And that’s not to mention the security of the building while all this goes on. Bailey will be concerned that the 400,000 bars of gold, worth more than £200bn, and £100m of bank notes in the vaults are safe from terrorists and thieves.
A further complication is the fate of the Bank’s museum, which is now open to the public and tucked away in the side of the building, facing on to Bartholomew Lane.

Some senior staff had wanted to relocate the museum into the central quad and have the 100,000 visitors a year – mainly schoolchildren – march through the main entrance. Others wanted to have cafe space near the entrance to make the Bank appear more modern and appealing to visitors.

Vivienne Grafton, the executive director of central operations, told the Architects Journal: “This is an opportunity to breathe new life into a legacy building, not through radical reinvention, but through thoughtful, intelligent transformation.”

But architectural plans have yet to be agreed with the local authority – the City of London Corporation – and Historic England, which must sanction the proposed work on a building considered a cornerstone of Britain’s financial district.

Anna Joynt, a senior architect and heritage expert at the London practice of Allies and Morrison, said it was common for large, complex historic building projects to begin preparatory works before full consent has been given.
“There may be bones of the future scheme in place but the wider scheme may not be developed enough to submit for listed building consent – which needs a lot of detail,” she said.

“It’s fairly common to split out simpler early enabling works and get permission for them in advance of a main scheme. It means work can start earlier and save money as the longer you wait the more things cost.”

There has been some tangible progress on the scheme. The roof of the main portico is clad in scaffolding to allow for repairs. And last year the Bank secured planning permission to overhaul one small section – an area known as the former governor’s secretaries’s offices, which will have their plasterboard walls taken out and the space opened up and modernised.
As for the rest of the 1.4-hectare (3.5-acre) site, staff must wait and see.

items.title: Seaweed earplug among grant-winning Design Museum prototypes
paragraphs: A single-use earplug crafted from seaweed, two plant-based insulation materials and a homegrown timber kit-of-parts for low-rise buildings are among the projects that have been awarded Design Museum grants.
UK-based studios Searo Labs, WeCanMake, Local Works Studio and SY Ecofit have been granted a share of £280,000 from the Design Museum for their “cutting-edge” environmental prototypes.
Described as the “world’s first seaweed-based single-use earplug”, SearoSoft by Cambridge-based Searo Labs is a fully biodegradable and renewable alternative to single-use earplugs.
According to SearoSoft, the soft, mouldable earplugs are made without microplastics or chemicals and designed to hydrate the ear canal, unlike plastic-based products, which can be drying.

Once discarded, they are biodegradable in water or soil after 30 days. As seaweed is a regenerative crop, SearoSoft explained that there is no need for land, freshwater or fertilisers, making the process simple and more sustainable.

Among the other prototypes is a building material project by Sussex-based Local Works Studio. The initiative, named Ferment, will repurpose agricultural waste into an insulating material fit for retrofitting buildings.

Local Works Studio aims to develop an accessible product for farms via what it calls a “harvest-to-house system”, where farmers can produce the insulation themselves using their existing infrastructure, skills and machinery.
Bristol-based studio WeCanMake’s winning prototype, Neighbourhood Factory Futures, is a homegrown timber kit-of-parts system designed to be used for constructing low-rise apartment buildings.
With the Design Museum’s grant, the studio plans to create a neighbourhood factory model, allowing local communities to build and maintain their own homes.

WeCanMake explained it created the system as part of a wider movement aiming to make the UK a “nation of growers, producers and makers” while using reusable materials that store, rather than emit, carbon.

Prototyping PhytoFloc by social enterprise SY Ecofit in collaboration with Phyona and Studio Bio is a zero-waste project that, similarly to Local Works Studio, aims to develop plant-based insulation for building construction.
The project uses biowaste created as a byproduct of phytomining, where former industrial land is rejuvenated by plants that extract pollutants from the soil.
The project intends to recognise the value of post-industrial soils while creating a locally made, low-carbon material.

The grants are part of the Design Museum’s Future Observatory program, which is run in partnership with the Arts and Humanities Research Council. The winning projects were amongst 140 prototypes that were submitted to the scheme.
The museum explained that at a time when supply chains are under pressure, the Future Observatory aims to support designers’ practical research to drive the green transition.
“The climate crisis demands rapid change, and we believe that design is critically important if we are to meet that challenge,” said Design Museum director Tim Marlow.

“The presence of Future Observatory allows us an extraordinary opportunity to get involved with practitioners and problem-solvers and have a direct impact on the development of new technologies at the frontier of current design thinking.”
The four projects will be funded from November 2026 until July 2027. Afterwards, the prototypes will be tested and begin the commercialisation process.

items.title: Who decides that Grand Theft Auto is for adults only?
paragraphs: When playing games in her own time West hates hurting NPCs, but admits at work: "Unfortunately I have to be a bit evil sometimes".
She will typically play a game for several days, checking for blood, suggestive costumes and potentially exploitative in-game purchases.
She says: "Once I'm happy that I've seen everything that would impact the rating, I then go through and I write up a report."
That report is kept on record, while a version without plot spoilers is shared online for parents and players to read.
Examiners follow strict classification criteria overseen by a panel that includes child welfare experts and psychologists.
Ian Rice, director general of the GRA, says the criteria ensure ratings are applied "consistently and fairly".
Violence is only one element that is analysed, but shows how context can affect the classification:
PEGI 3 & 7: Child-friendly, cartoon-like violence, such as in Minecraft, Rocket League, Roblox or Mario.
PEGI 12: Unrealistic violence between humans, this could be games like Fortnite which have no blood or injury detail.
PEGI 16: Realistic violence between humans, can include visible blood and pain reactions.
PEGI 18: These games include what is classified as "gross violence", with high levels of blood and gore, or violence directed at innocent civilians.
Sexually graphic content and the glamorisation of illegal drug use also trigger an automatic 18 rating.
Some might wonder why games need adult content at all. Rice points out games can cover mature themes just like other forms of storytelling.
He says: "Just because it's in a game doesn't mean somebody's making light of it.
"They can cover serious issues, just like Netflix shows or any other kind of media."

items.title: ‘Remarkable luck’: wreck of first Australian-built warship discovered exactly 128 years after sinking
paragraphs: The wreck of Australia’s first locally built warship has been discovered 128 years after sinking off the coast of far north Queensland.
Marine archaeologists found the remains of Ex HMCS Spitfire on 21 August, the anniversary of its sinking in 1898.

Celeste Jordan, the principal heritage officer at Queensland’s Department of the Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation, said it was “remarkable luck”. Rediscovering lost shipwrecks would “help ensure the stories of our past are preserved, celebrated and protected for future generations”, she said.

The 19-metre wooden gunboat, designed and built in Sydney in 1855, was commissioned by the Australian colonial government to protect against Russian warships based at Vladivostok during the Crimean war and amid concern about the French military presence in New Caledonia. It was designed to carry a 32-pounder cannon, although evidence suggests the armament may never have been fitted.
The clipper later served Queensland as a pilot vessel, before it was sold for £300 into private hands as a sea cucumber fishing vessel.

A 1981 article in the Naval Historical Review described the boat as “a sturdy little vessel”. Constructed from ironbark and blackwood, and sheathed in copper, it was designed and built by the Sydney shipbuilder John Cuthbert, and launched by his wife Susan Cuthbert from Darling Harbour in 1855.

On 21 August 1898, Spitfire developed a leak and foundered on a voyage off the coast of Queensland’s Cape York peninsula, according to the Australian National Maritime Museum. Its crew were rescued by the Japanese steamship Omi Maru.

A crew from the Australian National Maritime Museum, the Queensland government and the Royal Australian Navy found the wreck while aboard HMAS Diamantina, a minehunter vessel. The month-long expedition searched an area based on archival records, with sonar picking up the Spitfire as an acoustic anomaly.

The chief of navy, Vice Admiral Matthew Buckley, said the Spitfire occupied a unique place in Australia’s naval history. “For sailors today, this vessel represents the beginning of a story that continues in the Royal Australian Navy.”
The wreck is protected under the Underwater Cultural Heritage Act, and is one of more than 8,000 shipwrecks, sunken aircraft and other heritage sites in Australian waters.

items.title: Tricks! Traps! Riddles! Jan van Eyck’s portraits look vividly real – but are full of secret messages. What do they mean?
paragraphs: At the Barbican Art Gallery in London, there is an exhibition of some of the white paintings made by the US artist Robert Ryman over 60 years from the 1950s. The paintings are square, because a square is neutral, and he didn’t want viewers associating them with the visual language of landscape or portrait. For Ryman, his paintings resolutely were what they were, which is to say, white paint applied to various surfaces and fixed to the wall. Not “windows” through which one could glimpse another world.

At the National Gallery, a couple of miles across town, is an exhibition of 10 works by the 15th-century Flemish painter Jan van Eyck. With one exception – the Arnolfini portrait, which is a one-off in all kinds of ways – they are all A4-size portraits, each angled so that we see more of the left than the right side of their faces. Aside from the likenesses of the people who paid for them in some of his religious paintings, including the Ghent altarpiece, these are the sum total of Van Eyck’s surviving portraits.

In a manner profoundly different from Ryman’s works, Van Eyck’s portraits pull you from our world into his. The precision of his physiognomies is dizzying. In his portrait of his wife, Margaret, recently conserved and on loan from Bruges, she regards you with a steady gaze, her lips firm and decisive. Between her cheek and ear is a blemish, a slight discolouring of the skin; her left eyebrow is bisected by a scar. Her headdress contains seven layers of frothing lace that you want to pinch between your thumb and finger. What must it have been like, to look back at this vision of yourself, in a world in which mirrors were luxury items (and mostly convex, like the one that famously hangs at the back of the Arnolfini portrait)?

We know it’s her, because a very detailed inscription in the painter’s hand on the original frame tells us that “my husband Jan completed me on 15 June 1439” and that “my age is 33 years”. By some stroke of painterly enchantment, is it Margaret herself addressing us? Or is the “me” the painting – a mere arrangement of oil paint on a panel of Baltic oak? The inscription concludes with the words “as I can” – Van Eyck’s motto, a phrase that hovers between extreme modesty and great boastfulness.

All the portraits have something of this uncanny hyper-realistic quality. The pockmark on the slightly shiny, reddish young skin. The lines around the eyes and crinkled cheeks of the old scholar in his red robe, and his ear, purplish with age. The scar between the eyes of the stubbled Baudouin de Lannoy, who worked alongside Van Eyck at the court of Philip the Good, the Burgundian ruler of the Low Countries. The individual hairs of a fur collar as they brush the skin of the neck; the intricate whorls of an ear. You feel that if these people reached out their beringed fingers and tugged you through the frame, you could walk about with them, in the streets of Ghent or Bruges of the 1430s.

Perhaps the most arresting of these faces is the portrait of Jan de Leeuw, who, like Margaret, gazes straight at the viewer. He has such a modern-seeming face that it’s hard to shake the impression that he might have sat beside you on the morning commute. Like Margaret, he has his original frame, around which Van Eyck has painted words that translate as: “Jan de Leeuw who, on Saint Ursula’s day, opened his eyes for the first time, 1401. Jan Van Eyck has counterfeited me. It can be seen when he began 1436.” Beautiful precision, all the more satisfying because the Van Leeuw in question can be found in Bruges’ city archives: from a family of goldsmiths, he was himself the inspector of the goldsmiths’ guild at the time of the portrait. Everything checks out: he’s holding a gold ring.

Except that it doesn’t. Like all the works in the exhibition, its apparent “truthfulness” turns out to be a trap, its mirror-like reality a game of illusion and deceit. “He counterfeited me” – the word is “gheconterfeit” – is such a strange word to use, especially of a man who assessed the quality of gold. In its 15th-century context, it was an ambiguous word, says show’s co-curator Nicholas Flory, also “used in documents to describe a true likeness or reliable copy of a real thing”.

But Van Eyck is also deeply unreliable. The painted words are a trompe l’oeil, convincing you they are inscribed in brass. The man’s name, which means “lion”, actually appears as a cute pictogram, as a little joke. To add to the confounding, certain letters of the inscription are made to look as if they are standing out in relief. If you take these and treat them as Roman numerals, they add up to the dates crucial for the painting: 1401 and 1436. In other words, the portrait, which at first seduces with its “reality”, turns out on second glance to be a highly artificial, self-conscious construct. The paint counterfeits metal for its goldsmith sitter, and sets puzzles for the viewer. The ring De Leeuw is holding is so terribly real – and also, so desperately fake.

The Arnolfini portrait is another example of apparent clarity melting swiftly away to complete bafflement. It is one of the best known works in the National Gallery, so familiar to British art lovers that it is possible to forget how strange it is. For centuries, this image of a man taking hold of a woman’s hand was known as the “Arnolfini marriage”, because it was assumed to commemorate an actual wedding ceremony. In the 1930s, Erwin Panofsky posited that every item in the busy domestic interior (the oranges, the wooden overshoes, the mirror, the dog, the burning candle and the guttering candle in the beautifully painted chandelier) was weighted with matrimonial symbolism.

But in truth, no one even knows for sure whether it represents members of the mercantile Arnolfini family (the identification was made based on 16th-century inventories in which the picture said to portray “Hernoul le fin” or “Arnoult Fin”, which were thought to be corruptions of the name Arnolfini). And more recently, many critics have pulled back to accept a more straightforwardly materialist interpretation of the scene: the oranges, the ridiculously voluminous green dress, the fine furnishings, are all markers of status, rather than symbolic as such.

As for the inscription – it reads: “Johannes de eyck fuit hic [was here] 1434”. Again, it seems so clear – but where on earth is “here”? Does it mean Van Eyck was witness to some actual event that he depicted? Or that he painted himself as one of those figures dimly visible in the convex mirror? Or that the main figure is actually a self-portrait, and that this pale man with the large hat and flared nostrils – also the subject of a second portrait in the show – is Van Eyck himself? The inscription breaks the fourth wall: it seems to be hovering on the picture plane itself. So is “here” the metaphysical “here” of the artist’s imagination?

There is one certain self-portrait of Van Eyck, and that, characteristically, is another trick.
