It is not in this exhibition, but rather in a religious work in the Groeningemuseum in Bruges, the Virgin and Child With Canon Joris Van der Paele. Van Eyck hid in his painting in a tiny image of himself – identifiable by his paintbrush – reflected in the metal shield of Saint George. The ageing canon has removed his spectacles, perhaps the better to appreciate the supernatural vision of the Virgin and child.

The National Gallery’s show opens with a work from its own collection that is frequently regarded as a self-portrait. The realist details are bewitching, intimate: the bloodshot red eyes, the fine lines around them, the stubbled cheeks, the exuberantly painted red hat. On its original frame is painted a signature (“Jan van Eyck made me on 21 October 1433”) along with the motto “as I can” – the position of which, where one would often find the name of the sitter, helps build the case that the work depicts the painter himself. Here, the writing appears to be deeply incised into the surface, playfully implying that the frame is of solid gold, rather than the gilt that it really is.

The more you crane and gaze at these paintings, admiring the wrinkles and the spots and the all-too human flesh, the more you trip up on Van Eyck’s tricksiness. The slippage between being fooled by the illusion and recognising that you are being fooled is part of the pleasure. The more you look, the more you feel you’re having a conversation with the painter – and that he is having the last laugh.

items.title: Datacentres to create 70% more carbon emissions by 2030, IEA report warns
paragraphs: The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth.

The Paris-based agency found that the breakneck pace of the industry’s growth means that within four years AI datacentres will consume an extra 350 terrawatt-hours of electricity every year, or more than the annual electricity consumption of Great Britain.

Its influential annual report warned that the world’s energy future was less certain after the impact of the Middle East war, which it has described as the greatest energy market disruption in history.
“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said the IEA’s executive director Fatih Birol.

Instead, it will be reshaped by the policy decisions governments make after the crisis to meet the increasing demand for energy to power a growing global population, the rising need for air-conditioning and a booming AI economy, the IEA said.

Datacentre developers have emerged as the world’s biggest corporate buyers of renewable energy to help fuel their servers which have a connection to local power grids. Despite this, the report showed that the appetite for fossil fuels is expected to grow even faster, particularly in the US and China.

By the end of the decade, around half of the electricity needed to power China’s AI datacentres will come from coal power plants, according to the IEA. The rest will come from renewable energy, with smaller amounts from nuclear reactors and very little from gas plants.

In contrast, the US is expected to rely on gas to provide about 60% of the electricity for its datacentres by 2030. There were plans for about 180GW of new gas-fired power plants linked to US datacentres in August this year, the agency said. That is almost as much new gas capacity as the total now installed across the European Union.
As a result of the growth in fossil fuel generation for datacentres, emissions associated with this sector were on track to rise by 70% by 2030, the IEA said.

The appetite for gas power among US datacentre developers is more than 16 times higher than in Canada, where the IEA identified plans for 11GW of gas generation to power their servers. In the rest of the world, AI developers have put forward plans for new gas plants with a combined capacity of just 4GW, the agency said.

This is because renewable energy is expected to play a greater role in supplying datacentres outside the US and China. In the EU, the IEA expects datacentres to rely on renewables for about 70% of their electricity by 2030 – followed by nuclear power, gas generation, and a very small amount of coal power.

The agency based its forecasts for the notoriously opaque industry on data showing the annual global shipment of AI servers, which have climbed eighteen-fold since 2020. It also used space-based imagery to track the buildout of 93 large “AI factories” around the world.

Its analysis suggests that the world’s datacentre capacity has climbed tenfold in the last 24 months to 17GW. By the time the AI factories were completed, their combined capacity was likely to be about 50GW, the IEA said.

The world’s existing stock of datacentres, including those with AI-optimised servers, now stands at 120GW, with 80% of this capacity in China, the US and the EU. A further 120GW will be built by the end of the decade under the IEA scenario often considered its central base case, of which three-quarters will be AI datacentres.

items.title: Programa software tracks everything from product dimensions to material quantities
paragraphs: Studio operations software Programa has redesigned its programme to rethink how interior design studios operate, giving practices more flexibility and freeing up their time.
According to Programa, beautiful interiors are built on “hundreds of decisions”, which take long periods of time to decide upon and update across multiple spreadsheets.
Each decision brings specification details, quantities, pricing and revisions that studios must keep updated as a project develops.
These include minute, precise details such as dimensions, materials, finishes, technical requirements, and component quantities.

Programa‘s redesigned programme keeps a record of each item used in an interior project, from furniture and lighting to hardware and finishes, and optimises their organisation based on how the project runs.
The company explained that increased AI use is making convincing images “easier to generate than ever”, yet clients often run into logistical issues when using this alone.

For example, the AI model doesn’t take into account whether a wardrobe or sofa fits through the door, suits the needs of the people living there, or whether the overall design takes full advantage of a space’s natural light.
With Programa, the designer can smoothly make these judgements using the software’s organisation of specifications, cost, quantities and overall project coordination.

The company explained that if a designer updates a product’s shared specification once, the change appears in the Programa schedules that include it, while quantities can be individually allocated by room.
For Austin Carrier of Californian design studio, Hommeboys Interiors, this is particularly helpful.
“We use schedules for everything from lighting and hardware to plumbing fixtures and furniture, indoor and outdoor,” Carrier explained.
“For furniture, we can break down every room, then the pieces within that room, and give clients several options to reject or accept,” he added.

As a result, the software aims to cut the “gruelling amount of work” updating schedules, preparing presentations, and communicating with suppliers. It also reduces repeated data entry, freeing up time.
The platform is defined as an “alternative to spreadsheets”, which often have to be made from scratch and reformatted for different presentations.
“The issue with the spreadsheet is that it’s like a blank cell,” added Los Angeles-based designer Paul Chan. “You can put anything in there – it doesn’t carry from one project to another.”
“With Programa, I can take a format from one project and move it into the next,” Chan continued. “There’s consistency between each project.”
Specifically, the Programa Schedule function details the items’ code, supplier, finish, dimensions, quantity and price.
It offers a streamlined place to reference drawings, get client approval and work with contractors to meet on-site deadlines.
The company explained that one of its platform’s main benefits is that it can be used from early product decision-making through to final delivery.
Here, the studio manages the specification and controls what is shared, whereas the clients review selections and provide approvals. Collaborators also receive the information relevant to their work.

“Once we get all of the information in there, we can send it out in one email to all of our vendors, and then they are able to get us pricing back very easily,” added Tana Nesbitt-Hayes of Studio 8 Architect.
“If we’re exceeding our budget in one area, we can tailor it back. It’s always up-to-date.”
“We share our Programa Schedules with the millworkers and the engineers,” she added. “They can see the refrigerator we’re going to put in, and they can make the panels to fit.”
Programa offers a free trial for all studios. To learn more, visit its website.

items.title: This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls
paragraphs: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are meeting for a historic trilateral summit
China correspondent Reporting fromShenzhen
Xi Jinping will believe he has achieved something no other world leader could in securing a historic summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen.
For decades, Washington and its western allies shaped the world order.
Yet it is China that has orchestrated the remarkable diplomatic spectacle of three of the world's most powerful protagonists sitting around the table.
And surrounding it all is the futuristic display that is Shenzhen, with driverless cars cruising past as drones fly overhead and robots - literally - dance in the streets.
Ostensibly, this is an economic summit for Asia Pacific leaders. But for Xi, it is also a demonstration of China's grip on the global economy and world politics.
His country is no longer just reacting to decisions made in Washington, London or Brussels - instead Beijing is at the heart of conversations which are reshaping the international order.
But this meeting is not without its pitfalls for Xi as there are many things he does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.
First, China is not keen for the war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year, to be on the agenda.

This is a delicate balancing act for Xi who is aware his relationship with Putin may damage China's connections in Europe. The EU is a key market, especially now when the Chinese economy is heavily relying on exports.
However Xi also doesn't want the war to end in a way that will destabilise Russia, a key ally and neighbour.
Beijing is still trying to maintain that it is neutral in this war and has repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's full-scale invasion.
Russia's invasion of Ukraine, now into its fifth year, has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives

The US, especially under the previous Biden administration, and Europe have accused China of sending Russia components that it could use in its war in Ukraine, while also propping up the country's economy by buying oil and gas.
Xi wants to keep Putin close, but not too close because he also doesn't want Russia's problems to become China's problems.
Donald Trump has already made it clear he wants the three leaders to discuss limiting the world's supply of nuclear weapons.
The US and Russia possess the world's largest stockpile of nuclear warheads. But China is rapidly expanding its own arsenal, which is raising alarm bells in Washington.

The last major US-Russian arms control treaty, known as New START, expired in February this year, triggering fears of an arms race. The agreement had set a cap to control the number of nuclear weapons in US and Russia's arsenal.
Trump would like China to be included in any new agreement, but Beijing has pushed back.

Xi's argument will be that his arsenal is considerably smaller than what Washington and Moscow own, and, therefore, it would be unfair for Beijing to be bound by their limits. China also believes it should have the freedom to develop its own nuclear capabilities.
China unveiled intercontinental nuclear missiles at a military parade in 2025
This subject could complicate Xi's bid for China to be recognised as a leader on the world stage - because the US could argue that the status includes being a responsible nuclear power.
Xi will want to control the optics of this meeting, from start to finish.
Chinese officials like to nail down agendas with talking points and produce carefully choreographed speeches.
But in this unprecedented summit, Xi will have to live with two very unpredictable leaders.
Both Trump and Putin have their own agendas and the US President has already threatened to go off script.
There is a risk that they both dominate the meeting and Xi ends up looking like a host, rather than the architect of a major diplomatic moment.
Of course, Xi may be ready for this. It may even play into his hands.
The Chinese leader has been trying to portray himself as a stable global leader - at this summit he will be flanked by two men embroiled in wars they cannot seem to end.
So any unscripted moment could serve to highlight his preferred role as senior statesman.
For all the attention, this meeting of three men with vastly different agendas is unlikely to yield any significant outcomes.
But the power it projects is important for Xi as he heads towards next year's Communist Party Congress, where he is expected to secure a historic fourth term as leader of the party and country.
A job fair in Jiangsu province: China has been battling youth unemployment in a sluggish economy
He may hope to use this as propaganda at home, given the country is grappling with huge domestic challenges.

A country-wide property crisis has dented consumer confidence. Local governments are heavily in debt. Manufacturing has slowed and more of China's workforce has become dependent on flexible jobs with no pension or social security. One in five young people are thought to be struggling to find work. Frustration and anxiety about the future bubble up routinely.

Xi does not have to deal with elections, and the country has not seen major protests in decades. But he will be concerned about his popularity within the party elite as these problems - and the palpable frustrations they produce - grow.

At a time like this, a photo-op with Putin and Trump may offer him proof that his country's "century of humiliation" is over. China is no longer a rising power, he can argue - rather, it is increasingly shaping the rules of a new era.

items.title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
paragraphs: One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.

In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.

Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.

“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”

The Maputo protocol, a landmark treaty adopted by the African Union in 2003, guarantees women’s rights and obliges states to protect women from violence. It affirms that marriage must be based on full consent and guarantees women’s right to health.

“The underlying principle is unambiguous: sexual intercourse without free and voluntary consent constitutes sexual violence, including within marriage,” said Murunga. “Marriage does not create perpetual or implied consent. A woman retains the right to decide whether, when and how she engages in sexual activity”.

He said that as a first step rape laws across the continent needed to change. According to Murunga’s 2024 report, rape within marriage is not criminalised in some African countries. Seven countries expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Some countries, such as Tanzania and Eritrea, only criminalise marital rape when the couple do not live together.

In countries where child marriage is permitted and marital rape is not criminalised, children are left unprotected. A legal loophole is created for what, outside marriage, would be classed as rape, and young wives have few options when it comes to protecting themselves from sexual violence and exploitation. In Gabon, for example, when a man has married a child he abducted, he can only be prosecuted after the marriage is annulled.

Underpinning these laws is the mistaken belief that marital rape does not exist as a concept because, by marrying, wives are assumed to have permanently consented to sex with their husbands. In many areas, religion plays a key role in affirming these beliefs.

Alimatu Dimonekene, founder of A Girl At A Time, an organisation supporting adolescent girls in Sierra Leone, said a conversation around consent in marriage had yet to begin in Africa. “We’ve not even started the conversation [around marital rape],” she said. “Women will never call it rape; they make excuses for it or even blame themselves.”
She added: “In west Africa, sex is seen as an obligation in marriage. You must do whatever your husband demands.

“Once he has paid your bride price [a traditional marriage custom in which the bride’s family are paid money, livestock or goods by the groom], he owns you and you cannot reject his demands. Whatever he wants, he gets, including in terms of intimacy, finances and raising the children.”

items.title: ‘Most extraordinary virtual world’: critics hail Grand Theft Auto VI as masterpiece
paragraphs: Good things clearly come to those who wait. After 13 years of anticipation, Grand Theft Auto VI is finally here – and, according to critics, it’s a masterpiece.

The trailer for the video game, which returns players to Vice City, Rockstar’s fictional version of Miami, attracted more than 90m views in 24 hours when it was released in December 2023. Excitement continued to mount, with two release delays and a steady stream of leaks and speculation keeping the game in the headlines.

Now, Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100 – tying with Nintendo’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record for the best reviewed video game since 1998.
In a five-star review, the Guardian’s Keza MacDonald said: “In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen.”

MacDonald praised the fictional state of Leonida as an extraordinarily detailed world, populated by incidental encounters and activities that make it feel alive. But for all its violence and grotesque humour, what stood out was the relationship between Jason and Lucia – GTA’s first female protagonist.

She said: “I was rooting so hard for Jason and Lucia by the end that I felt quite sick with worry about what was going to happen to them, pacing back and forth in front of my TV throughout the final missions. Among all the expectations I had for GTA VI, I did not expect it to make me so emotional.”

In a 10-out-of-10 review, IGN’s Luke Reilly called it “the single most impressive video game I have ever played”. He praised its graphics, driving mechanics and the sheer amount of detail in its world.

He said: “I see no real limit to the amount of time I could spend here, endlessly exploring and interacting with Vice City and the massive area surrounding it. While the well-paced story effectively nudged me around the map, there are still vast sections of it that I’m yet to even visit – despite hitting the credits after almost 120 hours of hijinks.
“Frankly, I’ve never played anything that’s hit quite like GTA 6 – and right now I have zero plans to stop playing it.”
In its five-star review, Eurogamer said Rockstar had “pushed back the horizon of video games once again” with its graphics, storytelling and world building.

Chris Tapsell wrote: “It’s about big ideas, themes, places – America, society, love – and also about individuals. It’s ridiculous and puerile, and also sometimes mature. Tender and violent. Deep and shallow. Novel and, in places, surprisingly familiar.”
For the New York Times, the game was “about love and relationships, their joy and heartache, and the work required to make them successful”.

Yussef Cole’s review said this reflected a maturation of a series that had “generally only told stories about men solipsistically chasing after their own success”. Whether you’re controlling Jason or Lucia, he added that “much of what you can do – apart from activities routine to GTA like stealing cars and robbing banks – is taking action to care for and nurture your romantic partner”.

The Washington Post’s Gene Park awarded the game four stars, saying it “raises the bar at every level”. He highlighted its unusually convincing portrayal of human behaviour, with more than 33,000 individual non-playable characters and interactions shaped by race, class, gender and money.

Writing for Forbes, Paul Tassi singled out the relationship between Jason and Lucia as one of the game’s greatest achievements, saying: “I can’t say I’ve ever seen a better video game relationship than the one they share.”
Bloomberg’s Jason Schreier gave the game five stars, calling it a “masterpiece”. “It’s hard not to be astonished by what Rockstar has done here. There’s nothing else like it,” he said.

GamesRadar+ also awarded it full marks, calling it “the ultimate time vampire”, and VGC suggested its influence will be felt across the games industry for years to come. Reviewer Jordan Middler described Rockstar as operating at “the absolute peak of its power”, adding that GTA 6 was “one of the best video games ever made”.
Grand Theft Auto VI officially launches on Thursday. Rockstar has not revealed the cost of the game, but some estimates put the figure north of $1bn (£760m).

In the UK, the standard edition costs £69.99, rising to £89.99 for the Ultimate Edition. The research firm Sensor Tower estimated that the game had generated $1.54bn (£1.2bn) in digital pre-orders by 17 November, while analysts have forecast that it could generate between $3.25bn and $5.2bn in sales during its first week.

items.title: Elon Musk says record spending on US midterms was 'pretty foolish'
paragraphs: Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.
The Tesla and SpaceX CEO was the election's top individual donor, giving $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.
Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.
Democrats won control of the both chambers in the US Congress, flipping both swing seats and making historic gains in places that have for decades been controlled by Republicans.
The election was seen as a bruising defeat for Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living in the US.
Musk was speaking virtually, external at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.
"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.
He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."

For several months at the start of Trump's second term in the White House, Musk served as an unpaid "special government employee" and Senior Advisor to the President, leading the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) to cut government spending.
In October 2026, the Pentagon named Musk as a co-lead of a future of warfare study called Project Meridian, while he continued to travel with and advise Trump.
Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.
The large number of Republican losses could have implications for Musk and his businesses.
Democrats coming into power in both the Senate and House of Representatives have pledged greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the building of controversial data centres.

In Georgia, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the newly elected Democrat governor promised to limit the rollout of the massive buildings, as well as the tax breaks tech companies often get to build them.
Democratic lawmakers have also suggested that SpaceX, which has gained an estimated $10bn in new government contracts since Trump was re-elected, should be investigated.

items.title: Vincent van Gogh painting auctioned for record $190.4m after dispute over Nazi era sale
paragraphs: A Vincent van Gogh masterpiece sold for a record-breaking $190.4m (£144.9m, A$285m) on Wednesday after a dispute between the seller and the heirs of a previous Jewish owner who sold it in the Nazi era, Sotheby’s said.

Chataigniers en fleurs (Chestnut Trees in Blossom), which was painted in 1890 in Auvers-sur-Oise, France, set a new record for the Dutch post-impressionist and became the most expensive work auctioned off so far this season.
The New York Times reported that William Acquavella, art dealer and head of Acquavella Galleries, bought Chataigniers en fleurs.

The previous auction record for a painting by Van Gogh was $117.2m for the 1888 work Orchard with Cypresses, sold at Christie’s in New York in November 2022. But the New York Times reported on Wednesday that another 1888 painting by Van Gogh, Le Zouave, sold for “around $190m” in a private transaction through Christie’s less than a year ago.
An influential German publisher, Samuel Fischer, acquired the painting in Paris in 1909 and his family sold it in 1936.
His heirs had previously opposed the sale, saying Fischer’s family parted with the painting only because of financial losses suffered under the Nazis.
The heirs’ Berlin-based lawyer, Gunnar Schnabel had called on Sotheby’s to prove the painting was sold at its market value and that the family would have sold it regardless of the political context.
The Blaquier-Arrieta family acquired the painting in 1975 and has owned it for more than half a century, according to Sotheby’s.

But on Tuesday, Sotheby’s said “an agreement has been reached between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and all of the legal descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer regarding the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Chataigniers en fleurs.”

Schnabel told the New York Times in a statement after the sale: “The family hopes that the considerable public interest in this case, and its fast and fair and just resolution, may offer some encouragement to other families who have faced persecution during the Nazi era.” However, he said, the mood at the auction was “no Champagne atmosphere”.

According to Sotheby’s, the Fischer heirs said they were “grateful for the trusting and fair negotiation and collaboration with Sotheby’s and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which make it possible to acknowledge the suffering of the Fischer family during the Nazi era and honor Gisela Berman Fischer’s history of seeking justice for her family.”

items.title: AI giant Anthropic valued at up to $1.5tn ahead of stock market debut
paragraphs: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has quickly become a big name in the tech industry
ByKali HaysTechnology reporterSamira HussainNorth America business correspondent and Osmond ChiaBusiness reporter
Anthropic is poised to hit a value of up to $1.5tn (£1.14tn) when its shares start trading on the stock market on Thursday.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the popular chatbot Claude said its shares will be priced at $83 each when it lists on the Nasdaq, a tech-focused stock exchange based in New York.
That price will make it one of the most highly valued companies in the world.

It will be the first US firm focused exclusively on AI to go public, marking a crucial test for the fast-growing industry, which faces questions over whether the huge investment poured into the technology will be profitable.
The AI firm said earlier this month it would likely offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each, which valued the company at up to $1.3tn.

But demand for Anthropic's stock debut - commonly referred to as its initial public offering, or IPO - is very high, according to one early investor in the company who spoke with the BBC on condition of anonymity.
The person said shares were more than 10 times oversubscribed ahead of the public listing, meaning demand for Anthropic shares exceeded the number of shares available.
If that turns out to be the case, Anthropic's valuation could quickly blow past its target on Thursday when trading begins.

Depending on how strong that demand is, Anthropic could even exceed the early market valuation of Elon Musk's SpaceX, which was the world's most highly valued stock debut when it went public with a value of $2.2tn in June.
However, in the weeks that followed, SpaceX shares fell significantly in price.

As it stands, Anthropic's listing will see the firm raise more than $68bn from its initial investors. It is also expecting another $26bn from private placements. So the total amount the company will raise is expected to be $94bn.
The amount of cash Anthropic has raised from its listing is already more than SpaceX raised in June.
OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year.

Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology, or one that was founded and built around AI tools and products. Its scope is different from tech giants like Google and Microsoft that also develop AI but are involved in other tech services.
There is excitement around Anthropic's listing, but also some concern from investors around its ability to generate revenue and profits going forward.

Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue for Anthropic is whether its business "can keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.
"Nevertheless, it is not an everyday occurrence for public investors to gain direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity," Wang said.

While nearly every other major tech company is pouring huge amounts of money into the technology and infrastructure required for their own AI tools, they are built around social media or online retail or online search. AI tools and applications are secondary.
"Anthropic going public gives us a whole new window into what AI demand looks like," Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower, told the BBC.
Anthropic was started by a group of co-founders, led by siblings Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei, all of whom left their work at OpenAI to start a new AI firm.
The company has carved itself out in the ongoing AI race as more focused on building the technology with safety top of mind.
It refused to comply with a demand by the US Department of Defense that Anthropic's tools be used in an essentially unrestricted way.
CEO Dario Amodei has been outspoken in his belief that AI tools may soon be so powerful that they present a threat to human existence.
The company has urged developers to slow the development of AI, arguing that advanced systems could pose "catastrophic" risks to humanity if they are not handled with appropriate safeguards.
Rival firm OpenAI has also voiced similar concerns about the technology's risks and delayed its plans to list on the stock market to address AI safety concerns.
Nonetheless, Anthropic is looking to grow quickly and gain more access to financing through the public markets in order to do so.
Claude is Anthropic's widely-used AI chatbot
Norton said Anthropic going public now, in a time of market volatility comes down to the simple fact that the company needs access to more money.
"AI is financially demanding," Norton said. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more, and so the time has come."

But broader anxieties have started to grow about the AI industry's business model, which is reliant on expensive computer chips that are in short supply. The technology is also dependent on controversial data centres and funding such operations require deals with other tech companies.

The Federal Reserve Bank has expressed concern about the rapid growth of AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss a potential rate rise.
A few of the meeting's participants also noted that "AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms".
With additional reporting by Rachel Clun and Osmond Chia

items.title: 'Feudal' leasehold system set to be scrapped in England and Wales
paragraphs: ByTarah WelshHousing correspondent and Jade Thompson
The government is to introduce new laws to scrap the way flats are built in England and Wales.
Under the proposed bill, most new leasehold flats will be banned and replaced with commonhold, where residents collectively own and manage their buildings.
Matthew Pennycook, the housing minister, said the current leasehold system was "blighting lives" and was an "anachronism in the twenty-first century".
The legislation follows Labour's 2024 election manifesto to "bring the feudal leasehold system to an end" - with further details expected to be set out later.
However, freeholders argue the policy is "unjust" and will have a detrimental impact on investment markets.

The proposed Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill will also include capping ground rent - the annual fee paid by current leaseholders to their freeholder - at £250. That will then be reduced to a "peppercorn" rate - which is effectively nothing - after 40 years.
Fozia Malik lives in a one-bedroom flat in Oldham and says her ground rent will go up from £150 to £300 in January. That is alongside service charges of more than £4,000 a year.
Malik says her block of flats has been plagued by a number of problems, including fire safety issues and rising costs.
The managing agent for her building says the service charges are due to costs that are out of its control and high insurance because of fire safety issues.
But Malik says she would "never" buy a leasehold flat again, describing it as a "continuous torture cell".
Fozia Malik says she would "never" buy a leasehold flat again

When she bought her flat, Malik assumed the system would work in the same way it does in Pakistan, where she grew up, and in most other countries, where buying a home also means owning a share of the land it sits on.

However, in England, most flats are sold on a leasehold basis. That gives the buyer the right to occupy and use a property for a set period of time, but the freeholder retains ultimate ownership of the building and the land.

Systems based on shared ownership and collective management - such as commonhold - are already standard in many parts of the world, including Australia, New Zealand, the US, Canada and much of continental Europe. They give residents ownership of their home and a stake in the building's common areas.
The government says its reforms are intended to bring England and Wales more closely in line with other international models.
It comes as more than 1,000 leaseholders have contacted the BBC over the past two years with complaints about the current system.
Campaigners have welcomed many of the reforms, but questioned what happens to the millions of people who already own leasehold homes.

While the legislation is expected to reshape ownership for new developments, converting existing leasehold buildings into commonhold is far more complicated. And it has led to concerns that current leaseholders will be left behind.
Giles Grover, from the campaign group End Our Cladding Scandal, says there is a risk the proposed changes will create a two-tier system of those buying new homes and existing leaseholders.
He began campaigning on behalf of flat owners following the Grenfell Tower tragedy. He says: "It's so complicated, will the measures that are being introduced actually benefit everyone?"
Giles Grover, from the campaign group End Our Cladding Scandal, says there is a risk the proposed changes will create a two-tier system

The government says the bill will make it easier for existing leaseholders to convert to commonhold, abolish forfeiture - so people cannot lose their homes over relatively small debts - improve transparency around service charges and crack down on estate charges.
Pennycook says it will transform "the experience of homeownership for existing leaseholders by giving them greater rights and protections and providing them with easy and effective escape routes".
However, the issue about how existing leaseholders can move into commonhold and how freeholders should be compensated remains unresolved.
A spokesperson for the Residential Freehold Association, which represents the UK's largest freeholders, says £18.7bn "could be wiped out from investments overnight".

items.title: Elon Musk tries to explain what’s going on with Ukraine and Starlink
paragraphs: is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Elon Musk said Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy is lying about disruptions to Starshield in Ukraine and that he’s trying to misuse SpaceX’s consumer service, Starlink, for military purposes. Musk made the comments at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday as he tried to explain the conflict following weeks of back and forth between Zelenskyy, Musk, and the US government.

“From the beginning, I’ve said that Starlink is a civilian system,” Musk said. “It is not meant to be used for offensive drone strikes that kill people. If you want to do that, you need to do Starshield, which is a separate system that is controlled by the US government. But do not ask me as a private individual to make kill decisions.”

Musk also said that “if they want to do something that’s an offensive military action, it needs to be the Starshield system where the kill decision is that of the War Department, perhaps ultimately the president, and not mine.”

The interviewer, Andrew Ross Sorkin, said that President Zelenskyy refers to the system as Starshield and is claiming that is the system that was slowed down. “That’s false,” Musk said, claiming that Zelenskyy is “not always truthful.”
Sorkin asked, “So when President Zelenskyy talks about using Starshield, he is not using Starshield, or he’s lying?”
“He is lying,” Musk said. “What he is actually saying is he wants to use Starlink for offensive military operations.”
Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

items.title: Crimean Bridge attacked again, Russian official says
paragraphs: Final moments before stretch of Crimean Bridge collapsed after Ukrainian attack
The Crimean Bridge has been attacked by Ukraine for the third time this week, a Russian official has said.
The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that traffic was temporarily suspended following another strike on the bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea.
The critical bridge had already been hit twice earlier in the week resulting in severe damage and part of the bridge collapsing into the water.
The important infrastructure has long been targeted by Ukraine because of its significance as a logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.
A screengrab of the damaged Crimean bridge in the Kerch Strait on 17 November
It comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin meets US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday for landmark talks in China.
Aksyonov confirmed the strike on the bridge in the early hours of Thursday via Telegram, adding that assessment of the damage was under way.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian sources have continued to issue air raid alert warnings overnight for districts just outside of the capital Kyiv.

At least three people were killed in a Russian drone attack on Odesa on Wednesday, according to the regional state administration. Officials described the attack as "brutal and deliberate... directly targeting people and their lives".
President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge as an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Ukraine used drones and missiles against it on 17 November which brought down a key section of the road.
That section of the double-arched, 12-mile bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.
In response, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".

While Ukrainian forces have struggled to close the bridge for good, recent attempts have brought them closer to destroying the bridge's crucial road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line.
Russian forces have also targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv in recent days.
Russian strikes hit the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges causing traffic closures, partial damage to the metro system and some power and water outages.

items.title: Van Gogh painting sells for record $190.4m after row over its Nazi history
paragraphs: It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.
The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a value of $180m (£136m) prior to the sale, was put up for auction as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.

Sotheby's announced in the hours before the auction that it had resolved a dispute between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - regarding the sale.
Representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family had claimed the painting may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

A lawyer for the family's heirs reportedly wrote to Sotheby's on their behalf, telling the auction house that the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.

"In recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement," Sotheby's said on Wednesday.
Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.
It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.
The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotheby's said.
The Blaquier family acquired it in 1975 and owned it for more than half a century before the latest sale, the auction house said.

items.title: Is your child lying to you? That might not be a bad thing
paragraphs: Prof Hoicka's daughter Ada tries to sneakily eat cookie dough aged two when she thought her mum wasn't looking
When drawings appear on the wall or biscuits disappear from the tin, your child might blame the dog or claim there was a ghost - even if they are clutching crayons or covered in crumbs.
Children telling fibs is something most parents experience, but such dishonesty and deception is an important part of mental development.
"It's actually a skill that they're developing and that they will play with in order to get better," clinical psychologist Dr Jade Redfern tells the CBeebies Parenting Download podcast.
Here, experts explain why learning to lie is a sign of healthy behaviour - and how to help encourage honesty.
Prof Hoicka's daughter Juno also deceives her aged three by hiding under a table to eat marshmallows
Young children aren't quite sophisticated enough to lie, says Redfern, but they are capable of deception before the age of one.

One of the studies mentioned on the podcast comes from the University of Bristol, external, which found that around a quarter of children appear to understand some form of deception by the time they are ten months old.
Prof Elena Hoicka, who led the study, says it was fascinating to see how "surprisingly young" kids could be so adept and cunning, including her own.
"As a mother of three, I can certainly vouch for how artful and wily they can be.
"Hiding under the table or in the bathroom to eat sweets or chocolate is their common ploy."
Hoicka says that the kind of deception a child uses from the age of two is quite basic - like pretending not to hear their parent or denying they've done something.
Clinical psychologist Dr Jade Redfern explains why young children may lie and Traitors winner Rachel Duffy discusses how she encourages hers to tell the truth

"It could also extend to doing forbidden activities in secret," she says. "For example, looking in a bag they were told not to look in when no one is apparently watching, or making excuses, such as claiming to need the toilet when asked to tidy up."
By the age of three, they have become much more proficient and creative in their deceptions, showing a deeper understanding of language and how other people's minds work.
She says they also start to withhold information. For instance, truthfully telling their parents that their sibling has hit them but omitting the fact that they hit their sibling first.
These deceptions are a sign of them developing something Redfern calls "theory of mind".
Ada, age two, deceives her mum by hiding in the bathroom to eat chocolate she had stolen
"As children grow up, we want them to learn and develop the skill that they are their own human being with a separate mind and intentions," she explains.
"This is how [they] develop the skills in empathy, or being able to think about another person's thoughts and feelings that might differ from their own."
Another reason a child might lie is self-preservation as they don't want to upset or disappoint their parent.
"All human beings are driven by attachment," says Redfern. "[Children are] driven by being able to preserve that relationship with their caregivers as they depend upon it."

Early on, they learn what brings them closer to their caregiver and what pulls them apart, she says. With this in mind, Redfern thinks you can encourage honesty by creating a safe environment for a child to tell the truth.
"[We] have to think about ways we can help children feel safe enough to tell us the truth [when] they've made a mistake... and they don't want to disappoint us."
This is something Rachel Duffy, who won the latest series of The Traitors, tells the CBeebies Parenting podcast the she has been trying to do.
Prof Hoicka with her daughters Ada, now aged six, and Juno who is three years old
The mum-of-three recalls one occasion when her eldest son borrowed his brother's bike and broke it after crashing it into a car. Initially, he tried to lie about what happened.
"I said to him, 'You'll not get into big trouble when you tell me the truth.' I just left and gave him a little space.
"And he went, 'Yeah, that was me.' And then he knew that space was safe. We had a conversation - no raised voices, no roaring or shouting."

Redfern says this is a good example of how to deal with such a situation and that there are occasions when a lie, or nuance, might be appropriate - such as when they receive a gift they don't want or describe other people physically.
"My kids delightfully told me recently that I was very wrinkly," she says. "Again, I try to take it with open curiosity."
She does this by talking about why they think she is wrinkly.

"I think just being able to explore as children get older, just having open, curious conversations - it really develops empathy for somebody else's feelings when they've been shown and modelled empathy over and over again."

items.title: Mike Lynch’s superyacht had unidentified vulnerability to high winds, report finds
paragraphs: The superyacht Bayesian, which sank in a storm off Sicily killing seven people including the tech tycoon Mike Lynch and his teenage daughter, was vulnerable to knockdown but crew were not aware as it had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down, the final report from the UK’s Marine Accident Investigations Branch (MAIB) has said.
The 56-metre (184ft) vessel was anchored near the fishing port of Porticello when it sank during a violent storm shortly before dawn on 19 August 2024.

Lynch, 59, had been enjoying a voyage around Sicily with family and friends after his acquittal in a long-running fraud case regarding the sale of the technology company he founded, Autonomy, to Hewlett-Packard in 2011.

He and his 18-year-old daughter, Hannah, died, as did lawyer Chris Morvillo and his wife, Neda, banker Jonathan Bloomer and his wife, Judy, and the yacht’s chef, Recaldo Thomas. Nine other crew members and six guests were rescued.
The MAIB final report, published on Thursday, appears to contrast with recent reports from Italy, where prosecutors have reportedly blamed errors by the crew.

The MAIB report details how the yacht was hit “by extreme winds that were not explicitly forecast” of about 70 knots (80 mph), which knocked it on to its side in less than 15 seconds. It sank 18 minutes later.

Investigators found that the yacht’s vulnerability to strong winds had never been assessed for the conditions in which it was anchored, with its sails down and its retractable centreboard raised. The centreboard is a large underwater structure that helps a sailing vessel remain stable.
The extreme weather was most likely caused by a downburst – a powerful blast of air from a thunderstorm that hits the sea and spreads out with enormous force, the report said.

None of the life rafts on board automatically inflated or released from the vessel. The crew managed to release one manually. Survivors were rescued by crew from a nearby yacht, the Sir Robert Baden-Powell.

Rob Loder, the chief inspector of MAIB, said: “This accident developed with extraordinary speed. In just 14 minutes, calm conditions had given way to winds of at least 68 knots, which in less than 15 seconds pushed the yacht on to its side.

“Our investigation found that Bayesian had a vulnerability to high winds that was not recognised, because the yacht had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down. The extreme winds that night were also not explicitly forecast, so the crew had no warning of the risk.”

The report conveys the desperate minutes as the Bayesian was knocked down. Crew were alerted by sudden and severe winds of up to 30 knots at 03.55, and within two minutes the yacht listed starboard and the vessel began to drag anchor before the wind suddenly increased to about 70 knots.

“At 04.06 Bayesian violently heeled over 90 degrees to starboard, taking less than 15 seconds to do so. People, furniture and loose items fell across the deck. The generators shut down immediately and battery-supplied emergency lighting automatically turned on,” the report said.

Some guests, awoken by the listing and who had left their cabins, escaped. One couple used furniture drawers as an improvised ladder. Guests who managed to get to the flying bridge were instructed to swim away from the vessel and warned to stay clear of the mast and boom as it sank.

Passengers and crew who made it out gathered in the water, using a torch on a mobile to search for others. A crew member managed to swim back to the yacht to manually release one life raft from stowage. By 04.24 the life raft was inflated.

The investigation found that, with no sails set, Bayesian was vulnerable to knockdown in severe winds. This vulnerability was affected by its loading condition, apparent wind angle and the position of the centreboard, but had not been identified in the originally approved stability information available to the crew.

It said information contained in guidance provided to mariners did not provide sufficient detail of the impact of possible weather conditions to support decision-making. The weather forecast also did not indicate the risk of downbursts from the thunderstorms it predicted, it said.
Inquest proceedings in the UK are looking at the deaths of Mike and Hannah Lynch and Jonathan and Judy Bloomer, who were all British nationals.
The Maritime and Coastguard Agency is also investigating the sinking.

items.title: McDonald's sex abuse: 'They were waiting for the younger girls to turn 18'
paragraphs: A former McDonald's worker who says a manager failed to protect her when she was being sexualised by customers, has called on the firm to “change the way they treat younger employees”.

Hope, who worked at a branch in the West Midlands in 2023, also told BBC News she saw older colleagues eyeing up 16- and 17-year-old workers, and talking about wanting to sleep with them when they turned 18.
Hope is one of hundreds of workers bringing a discrimination claim against McDonald's. This week, a judge ruled against McDonald's attempt to have their claims struck out, a move that Hope welcomed.
McDonald's said: "Ensuring a safe, respectful and inclusive working environment across our restaurants and offices remains a fundamental priority."
The latest developments come after a BBC investigation in 2023 which heard that workers, some as young as 17, were being groped and harassed.
Last year, McDonald's staff told us they still faced sexual abuse and harassment.
McDonald's workers speak out over sexual abuse claims
McDonald's boss on abuse claims: 'I don't want to talk about the past'
Every McDonald's warned over staff sexual abuse
Hope, who is now 22, says that her branch of McDonalds had a very sexualised, "toxic" environment.
She spoke of a time a manager came up behind her and put his hands on her shoulders. From then on, whenever she saw him coming over, she says she "moved quick" to get away from him.
Ex-McDonald's worker: "You need to fix it so it doesn't happen again"
Another time, she says a manager failed to protect her when she says she was being sexualised and objectified by two customers on a night shift.
Hope says she told the manager what was happening, but he told her to "just suck it up and deal with it".
Her main concern, however, was for the younger teenagers, who she says weren't being looked after.

"You could tell there were other staff members waiting for their 18th birthdays. That sort of like toxic culture where it's like, 'Oh, you know, it's not illegal now.' It was that feeling from quite a few of them," she says.
"And why would you? That is literally a child still."
Hundreds of current and former McDonald's employees are bringing a discrimination claim against the firm.

The fast-food chain had attempted to have the complaints thrown out but this week at the London Central Employment Tribunal, Judge Glennie ruled that 450 cases can go ahead and they are now expected to be heard at the Employment Tribunal in April.
The BBC understands that these relate to indirect discrimination, not sexual harassment.
Hope told us she was not taking part in the legal case for money, saying they didn't know if they were going to get anything.
Instead, she said it was to try and "change the way they treat younger employees".

"It's going to change the way they treat allegations. It's going to shake up the whole internal process and make life easier for the kids who are now having their first jobs. And it's going to make it a lot safer, I think, as well. And that's something you can't put a price on, the safety of the young these days.''
She also accused McDonald's of trying to "delay the inevitable" by attempting to have the claims thrown out.
"And the judge quite rightly looked at them and said: 'No. We're not going to do that.'"
The claims were presented by law firm Leigh Day, which is acting for the current and former employees.
The claims focus on the vulnerability of young or female workers in the workplace and follow allegations of widespread harassment and discrimination across McDonald's restaurants in the UK.

Leigh Day partner Kiran Daurka told the BBC: "We're really delighted that the judge has found that these claims can go forward to a full hearing. It's really important for access to justice that these cases are heard."
A McDonald's spokesperson said they could not comment on the specifics of ongoing legal proceedings.
In a statement, they said the company had "embedded an extensive set of robust and far-reaching initiatives" as part of its "steadfast commitment" to its staff, adding that this work continues.

"Any form of harassment, discrimination or inappropriate behaviour is unacceptable and has no place in our restaurants or offices. We are confident that with the guidance and partnership of external experts, we and our franchisees have industry leading safeguarding measures in place," the spokesperson added.

items.title: Anthropic IPO raises record $81.3 billion on strong AI demand
paragraphs: Anthropic's shares will start trading publicly on Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. Idrees Mohammed/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

The artificial intelligence company Anthropic said on Wednesday it sold more than 956 million shares at a price of $83 a piece in a record-breaking initial public offering that makes it one of the most valuable companies in the world.

The five-year-old AI powerhouse raised around $79.4 billion through the offering, exceeding the $75 billion IPO haul of Elon Musk's SpaceX earlier this year. Anthropic said in a statement that "certain stockholders" also sold more than 23 million shares as part of the IPO, bringing the total haul to more than $81.3 billion.
Anthropic's shares will start trading publicly on Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.
The listing was oversubscribed, despite coming at a time of growing concern about a possible AI bubble and volatility in tech stocks.
The number of shares sold and the price exceeded Anthropic's original expectations. The listing prospectus targeted a sale of 825 million shares at $70 to $78 per share.
Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.

items.title: Four Maryland high school students sue after AI mistakes Doritos bag for gun
paragraphs: Four current and former students at a Maryland high school have filed a lawsuit a year after armed police detained them, prompted by an AI alert that mistook a bag of Doritos for a gun, in an incident that left them “fearing for their lives”.

The plaintiffs sued Omnilert, the company behind the AI gun-detection system, Baltimore county police, the board of education, individual officers and the school principal, alleging unlawful detention and search because of technological and human errors.

“These students were failed not only by a technology that is prone to false alerts, but also by the very adults meant to keep them safe when we send them to school,” said Damon Hewitt, the president and executive director of the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, which is representing the students. “Instead of this protection, they were met with guns and traumatized. And it could have been even worse.”

The incident took place last fall. The students had just wrapped up football practice on the evening of 20 October when their coach passed out bags of Doritos to the team, according to the complaint. Taki Allen, a junior at the time, took several bags and was with his friends near the picnic tables waiting for their ride, when six local police cruisers emerged with lights flashing. Many officers unholstered their weapons and the students put their hands in the air, the complaint said.

The legal complaint stated that the plaintiffs “were in shock and feared for their lives after being stopped, ordered to their knees, handcuffed and searched” by armed officers. One officer allegedly told them as he left the scene: “Hey, thanks for not running away, that would have been a real problem.”

The complaint described a chaotic series of events in which Omnilert’s AI gun-detection system flagged the chips bag as a firearm with 90% confidence. Omnilert Gun Detect system scans security footage for signs of firearms. “That alert kept going even after school staff and local police reviewed the image and determined it was a mistake,” the lawsuit stated.

While Omnilert markets its product as reliable and leading to “fewer false positives”, the lawsuit states that Maryland’s office of the inspector general for education “found that more than 99% of OGD Alerts in Baltimore County Public Schools were false positives that required no police response”.
Omnilert, the school principal, Baltimore police and the board of education did not immediately respond to a Guardian request for comment.

An Omnilert spokesperson previously told the Baltimore Banner that the company was reviewing the lawsuit and was “truly sorry for the fear they and their families experienced. We understand why they want answers.” A spokesperson for Baltimore county told the New York Times that the district cannot comment on pending litigation.

The lawsuit included texts from the school principal making light of the incident in messages to fellow administrators that contained emojis of a smiley face crying with laughter. The complaint said she did not apologize to the students.

One officer allegedly said as he began to leave the scene: “Fucking Omnialerts” and: “Stupid AI cameras.” His colleague allegedly joked to the plaintiffs: “Be careful on school property, especially holding stuff like that … be careful with your chips bags.”
The students didn’t find that funny, and reported feeling pain from tight handcuffs, as well as lasting emotional distress, according to the complaint.
Taki Allen said he no longer feels safe waiting for rides or hanging out at school after hours; he often pays for rides home to avoid waiting for rides from friends or family.

Freida Winfield, whose son Keith is part of the lawsuit, was en route to pick up him and his friends when they were detained. “No child in Baltimore county should face this kind of danger while waiting outside his own school for a ride home from his mother,” said Winfield.

items.title: Why has Waymo pulled all its driverless cars from US freeways?
paragraphs: The vehicles currently operate in 15 US cities, though freeway rides are only offered in a handful, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.

items.title: Crimea bridge has been attacked again, says Russian-installed governor
paragraphs: A key bridge connecting annexed Crimea to Russia has been attacked again, a Russian-appointed regional governor has said, two days after Ukrainian strikes caused serious damage to it.

“Following a new attack on the Crimean Bridge, traffic has been temporarily halted. All relevant services are on site and at work. An assessment of the damage is under way,” Sergei Aksyonov, the Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, wrote on Telegram.

Wednesday’s ‌attack is third this week on the highly symbolic bridge that links Russia with Crimea, which ​it seized from Ukraine in 2014. A 227-metre section of the road spanning the Kerch strait was destroyed this week, but the rail corridor appears to be operable despite sustaining some damage.

The strike comes just hours before an unprecedented meeting between Russian president Vladimir Putin and his Chinese and American counterparts, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump, in China. One source in Ukraine’s armed forces said this week’s attacks were designed to embarrass Putin on the world stage. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” the person said.

For Ukraine, the bridge is a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Ukraine has previously declared that the bridge across the Kerch strait, built eight years ago, is illegal. Kyiv had tried twice to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.

Earlier, Ukraine critically damaged the road section of the bridge in what President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed as an “unprecedented” military operation. A span of the bridge’s road section collapsed, but the railway line was still standing.

Zelesnkyy described the earlier attack as the culmination of a long and complex campaign to demolish the bridge, involving domestically produced drones and ballistic missiles. Palianytsia drones hit the road section of the bridge, while Neptune and other missiles targeted the adjacent rail section, he added.

items.title: The nation’s largest school districts consider ditching Google Search
paragraphs: New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago schools are considering Google alternatives after the company said it will disable Search for schools that opt out of its AI features, according to The New York Times. Starting next year, schools will not have the option to disable Gemini-powered features without also disabling Search. Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president of education, told the Times that, “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” and that schools that turn off Google’s AI features “will not have access to Search.”

Many elected officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Senator Bernie Sanders, responded harshly, calling Google’s behavior “extortion.” Mamdani had recently announced a policy that barred 2-K-8 students from using AI in the classroom. In a statement to the Times, New York City schools chancellor Kamar H. Samuels said, “If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options.” Chicago’s public schools have also reportedly told Google that if it can’t provide a version of Search without AI, “the district will look to other search solutions.”

In a statement to The Verge, Google spokesperson Laura Breen said, “We hear parents and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to shortcut learning, and we share the same goal: help students learn. To improve Search for the classroom, we’re starting to pilot Guided Learning capabilities in Search this month to walk students step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers. Next year, we’re also updating our approach to controls for schools to address feedback we’ve heard from educators, so Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools decide which services to enable. We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers.”

Educators are wary of AI’s effect on students’ critical thinking skills, and some studies have shown that students who use AI generally perform worse on tests. There are also concerns about the mental health effects on children who develop relationships with chatbots at a young age. But Google is deeply embedded in classrooms across the US, which rely on Google Classroom, Chromebooks, and other services, and going fully Google-free might prove difficult.
Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

items.title: Hunger Games fan, 13, to get artwork shown on cinema screens before film
paragraphs: Freja, who "didn't expect to be chosen" as the winner, beat more than 1,000 entries from across the UK
A teenage Hunger Games fan has met the cast of the new film after her artwork won a competition, meaning it will be displayed at every cinema screening across the UK.

Freja Brown, 13, won the British Board of Film Classification's (BBFC) create the card competition, which ran ahead of the release of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping - the sixth film in the franchise.
Freja, from Cardiff, beat more than 1,000 entries from across the UK and said she was "so grateful" to be chosen.
Her design will be the official BBFC black card, which displays the age rating and classification details of the film before every cinema showing.
Freja's winning design will be shown as the official BBFC black card before every UK cinema screening
The Year nine student, whose favourite subject is art, only started oil painting three years ago.
Her mum Marie recalled the moment Freja found out about the competition while scrolling on social media.
"She just squealed and said, 'there's this competition where you can create a piece of art' and she loves making art. So, she was like, 'I'm gonna do it'."
"She's read all the books and watched all the movies, so being able to combine her love for the Hunger Games with her own art sounded really fun."
Freja and her mum attended a fan screening event for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on The Reaping in London
Joseph Zada, Mckenna Grace, and Whitney Peak, who play Haymitch, Maysilee, and Lenore Dove in the new film, announced Freja's winning design in a specially recorded video.
Freja said: "I couldn't believe it. I knew that there were lots of other people who had sent in their artwork, so I didn't expect to be chosen and I am so grateful I was."
As part of her prize Freja was also invited to attend a screening of the film in London, where she met some of the stars.
Showing the work to Elle Fanning, who plays Effie Trinket, the actress said: "Oh my God, I thought it was a photo."
Actor Ralph Fiennes said: "It looks wonderful, it's really amazing, I love it."
Freja only started oil painting three years ago, but her mum says she has always been a creative person

Speaking of her inspiration, Freja said: "I was inspired by this specific part in the trailer because it shows the Hunger Games arena to be a beautiful place and not the killing machine that it actually is."
Marie, who is a photographer, said her daughter has always been a creative person and "makes stuff all the time", filling their home with her creations.
Marie said her daughter spent more than a month on the piece and worked until the day of the deadline after she "locked in for a whole weekend" to get it done.
She added that she was "so proud" of her daughter.
"It's not just a random piece of art somewhere, it's something that her and her friends get to see, which is fantastic."

items.title: Tibetan exile leader sees little hope for China-Tibet dialogue, warns of threats to Tibetan language and culture
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

Penpa Tsering, the political leader of Tibet's exiled government, the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA) in India, says prospects for resuming substantive political dialogue with Beijing remain bleak, despite informal contacts between the two sides.

In an interview with VOA on November 11, Tsering said informal contacts with Chinese representatives, initiated by Beijing, are ongoing. He said the CTA will continue participating as long as the Chinese side remains willing.However, he played down their significance, saying the exchanges mainly allow Beijing to learn about the CTA's activities and, in particular, the Dalai Lama's situation.

"Beyond that, it's just conveying messages, trying to understand what each side wants to know more. Nothing more than that," he said, adding that he had few expectations for these back-channel discussions.
Formal dialogue between Beijing and representatives of the Dalai Lama took place between 2002 and 2010 but produced no concrete results. Official communication has remained suspended since then.
Informal contacts continue, but expectations remain low

Tsering said China's current political climate offers little room for meaningful negotiations, whether concerning Tibet or other regions such as Mongolia. He expressed hope that a future Chinese leadership would be more open to rational dialogue, or that the current leadership might change its position.

Beijing considers Tibet an internal matter involving China's sovereignty and territorial integrity and does not recognize the CTA as a political entity entitled to negotiate with the Chinese government. In April 2024, China's Foreign Ministry reiterated that Beijing was willing to engage only with the Dalai Lama's personal representatives, not the CTA.
The CTA advocates the "Middle Way Approach," which seeks genuine autonomy for Tibet within the People's Republic of China rather than independence. Beijing has rejected the proposal.
The Dalai Lama's reincarnation a major point of contention
Tsering also criticized Beijing's efforts to influence the selection of the next Dalai Lama.

"On the one hand, they control all religious activities in Tibet, and on the other hand, they want to get involved in reincarnation because they know that it's politically important," he said. "They believe that if they can control the reincarnation of the next Dalai Lama, then they can control the whole of Tibet."

China maintains that the reincarnation of Tibetan Buddhist spiritual leaders must follow what they describe established religious rituals and historical conventions, and receive approval from the central government.

In July 2025, shortly before his 90th birthday, the Dalai Lama declared that the institution of the Dalai Lama would continue. He said responsibility for recognizing his successor rests with the Gaden Phodrang Trust.
Beijing subsequently reiterated that the search for his reincarnation must take place within China and comply with Chinese laws and regulations.
Tibetan language and cultural preservation under pressure
Tsering also warned that China's policies on ethnic affairs and education continue to threaten the transmission of Tibetan language and culture to younger generations.

He said the CTA would continue seeking a negotiated solution to the Tibet issue while strengthening its administrative institutions, sustaining the Tibetan exile community and securing international support, particularly from the United States.
He pointed to Beijing’s Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law, adopted in March 2026, saying it could further restrict the space for preserving Tibetan language and cultural traditions.
"The ultimate objective is assimilation," he said, saying that children as young as four are being sent to boarding schools where Mandarin dominates the educational environment.
"When our kids come home, they refuse to speak Tibetan. That is the biggest danger for us," he said. He described this as “a... cultural genocide at least.”

Chinese authorities maintain that promoting ethnic unity and Mandarin-language education helps improve communication, educational opportunities and economic development. Beijing also says minority languages are legally protected and that boarding schools are established to address geographical challenges and uneven access to educational resources.
VOA contacted the Chinese Embassy in Washington and the U.S. State Department for comment on Tsering's remarks but had received no response by publication time.
Tsering praises bipartisan U.S. support for Tibet
Tsering described relations between the CTA and Washington as strong.
“The United States is the only government that has a law on Tibet…. Our relationship with the U.S. government remains very strong,” he told VOA.

He cited the 2002 Tibet Policy Act, the 2020 Tibet Policy and Support Act, and the 2024 Resolve Tibet Act, which strengthened U.S. policy supporting dialogue between Beijing and Tibetan representatives and opposing Chinese interference in the Dalai Lama's succession.
The legislation also provides for sanctions against Chinese officials involved in imposing a successor to the Dalai Lama.
China has condemned the U.S. legislation as "interference in its internal affairs" and accused Washington of using the Tibet issue to pressure Beijing.
When signing the 2024 legislation, then-President Joe Biden reiterated Washington's call for Beijing to resume direct dialogue with the Dalai Lama or his representatives without preconditions.

items.title: EU proposes €45bn loan for Ukraine to avert cash crisis and boost defences
paragraphs: The EU executive has proposed a €45bn (£37.5bn) loan for Ukraine to help with a looming cash crisis and reinforce its defences, as Russia’s relentless bombardment continues.

Announcing the plan to lend Kyiv the money in 2027, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said: “We think this is the best way to give Ukraine a strong hand at the negotiating table. And Ukraine only needs to repay once Russia pays for the damage it has caused in Ukraine.”
She expressed confidence all 27 member states would stand behind the loan, despite four central and eastern European countries having already ruled themselves out.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he hoped for the swift adoption of the loan and was counting on the support of all EU member states: “Strong support for Ukraine is the best signal to Russia that this war must end,” he wrote on X.
Zelenskyy convinced EU leaders last month that his country faced a €70bn funding gap in 2027. The EU pledged to cover €45bn and wants Ukraine’s other allies to cover the rest.

Only 11 months ago, the EU agreed a €90bn loan for Ukraine, which was intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv’s military and civilian needs in 2026 and 2027. But as Russia’s attacks have escalated, the cost of Ukraine’s defence and the toll of economic disruption continue to rise.

Andrius Kubilius, the EU defence commissioner, said Ukraine’s military spending was increasingly dominated by drones. Ukraine, he told reporters, expected Russia to use 10m drones this year and 20m in 2027. “Ukraine with EU assistance needs to match – and will match,” he said.
The EU loan is split into two parts: €25bn for weapons and €20bn for civilian needs, including funding essential services, such as schools and hospitals.
