Von der Leyen expressed confidence that all member states would support the loan because “all 27 member states say very clearly that they want to support Ukraine”. She said member states could choose to support Ukraine’s civilian needs, rather than military spending.

Slovakia, Czechia, Hungary and Bulgaria, however, have said they do not intend to take part in the latest funding round for Ukraine, prompting a warning from the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, that he would block the EU’s seven-year budget unless all countries got onboard.
The four central and eastern countries are net beneficiaries of the EU budget, while Germany is the largest payer and Ukraine’s biggest EU donor.
The EU wants Ukraine’s non-EU allies – such as Norway, the UK and Canada – to find €25bn for Kyiv in 2027.

The EU proposal included provisions “to help other countries to help us”, a senior commission official said. Brussels has proposed that G7 countries that provide new loans get guarantees that the borrowing can be repaid with future profits from Russia’s frozen assets.
The profits from the Russian assets are being used to repay a €45bn loan issued by the G7 to Ukraine in 2024.

Countries with a triple-A credit rating could opt to provide guarantees to the EU budget up to €5bn to expand European borrowing for Ukraine on capital markets. The commission has identified six countries that fall into this category: Australia, Canada, Liechtenstein, Norway, Singapore and Switzerland.

EU officials previously said the UK and other allies needed to do more to support Ukraine in 2027, arguing that the EU was shouldering too much of the burden. The UK subsequently pledged a £10bn economic and military support package for Ukraine.

Zelenskyy said: “The UK, Canada, Japan, and Norway have been helping tremendously in our defence of life, and establishing clear rules under which they can provide further aid in conjunction with the EU will help even more.”

Britain said on Wednesday night it would send 1,000 long-range attack drones to Ukraine as part of a further £260m military aid package, a day before prime minister Andy Burnham was due to travel to Berlin to co-chair a meeting of Kyiv’s European allies.

The commitment to support Ukraine’s deep strike campaign into Russia emerged a day after the US argued that Kyiv’s attacks on refineries and warehouses were ineffective and counter-productive, earning criticism from the UK and Germany.
“The UK will do everything we can to ensure Ukraine is able to defend itself,” Burnham said.

items.title: Littler shocked by brilliant Wattimena at Grand Slam
paragraphs: Defending champion Luke Littler suffered a shock early exit at the Grand Slam of Darts after a stunning display from Jermaine Wattimena.
The Dutchman was in tears after securing a remarkable, and thoroughly deserved, 10-8 victory in the second round in Wolverhampton.

Having looked imperious as he won six legs on the spin to take a 7-2 lead, 16th seed Wattimena showed signs of nerves as the finish line approached, but dug in to stave off a late Littler comeback and progress to the quarter-finals.
"I think I played really incredible, I played my best game on this stage and I'm really proud of it," an emotional Wattimena told Sky Sports.
"He started playing well at the end. Last leg, [I had] one dart for the match - amazing."

Wattimena finished with an average of 101.70 having hit a staggering 10 180s and, such was his level for the majority of the match, he might feel the margin of victory should have been more comfortable.
The 38-year-old twice threatened nine-darters and had two darts for an 8-2 lead, with Littler rarely even given a look at a double.
However, the 19-year-old world champion sensed an opportunity and showed his class with a 10-darter to break throw as Wattimena finally stuttered a leg from victory.
But a dramatic comeback fell just short as, with Littler waiting to pounce on 65, Wattimena hit tops to take out 77 for the match and reach the last eight of the tournament for a second time.
Wattimena will face compatriot Kevin Doets in the next round after the world number 23 saw off Scotland's Cameron Menzies 10-5.
Doets averaged 101.51 and matched Wattimena's 10 maximums as his relentless scoring made up for an off night on the doubles.

items.title: Florida pastor found guilty over 2021 assassination of Haitian president
paragraphs: A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted on Wednesday of US charges arising from the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse.

Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced a total of eight charges including conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.
He faces up to life in prison at sentencing.

Federal prosecutors said south Florida was a hub for planning and financing the plot to oust Moïse and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing. The government said Sanon was the conspirators’ initial choice for Moïse’s replacement. Prosecutors also said Sanon helped raise money for the conspiracy and arranged travel to Haiti and lodging for himself and others in that country.

Sanon acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moïse, but pointed out that the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill Moïse.
Sanon was born in Haiti and moved to the US as a teenager. He testified that he worked with churches in Haitian immigrant communities in Florida and the midwest.

Haiti has not had a president since authorities said that a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers killed Moïse and wounded his wife in a night-time raid at their home on 7 July 2021. The poorest country in the Americas, Haiti has a history of dictatorship, political upheaval and foreign intervention that has long hindered democratic rule.
The election of a new president is scheduled for next year.

Prosecutors said the scheme to kill Moïse included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from US government programs that were intended to help businesses during the Covid pandemic, according to court records. US prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.

The plot to oust Moïse began taking final shape in April 2021, when Sanon met in south Florida with a former Haitian senator and several US businesspeople, according to an indictment. The group agreed that Sanon, once in power, would award contracts to two Florida-based companies – Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security, collectively known as CTU – for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment, according to investigators.

CTU initially hired about 18 Colombian nationals with military training to provide security for Sanon, according to prosecutors. Conspirators also spent months obtaining weapons and body armor and attempting to build ties with Haitian gangs, officials said.

By June 2021, the conspirators realized Sanon had neither the constitutional qualifications nor sufficient popular support to become president. They shifted their support to Wendelle Coq Thélot, a former Haitian supreme court judge who died in January 2025 while a fugitive.
Sanon was previously scheduled to be tried with four other men who were convicted earlier this year, but his case was separated from theirs and delayed for health reasons.

items.title: UN highlights what it calls "learning poverty" in Afghanistan
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.

Afghanistan's education system is facing a deepening crisis, with the United Nations warning that the quality of education is deteriorating as millions of girls remain barred from secondary schools and universities.

Daniel Timme, Chief of Communications at UNICEF Afghanistan, told VOA that a major problem facing Afghanistan’s education system, besides the ban on girls’ education, is “learning poverty,” which refers to children's inability to read and understand a simple text by age 10.
“The two most pressing issues in the education sector are certainly the ban on adolescent girls attending secondary school and the general problem of learning poverty,” said Timme.
A joint UNESCO and UNICEF report in 2025, based on 2022 data said that more than 90 percent of 10-year-old children in Afghanistan were unable to read even a simple text.

“Learning poverty in Afghanistan is among the highest globally," the report concluded, "with 93 percent of children at the end of primary unable to read and comprehend a simple age-appropriate text.".
“What is especially worrying is that this problem exists regardless of whether children attend school,” Timme said.
According to a U.N. statement early this month, of the 11.5 million Afghan primary school-age children, only 6.6 million are enrolled in formal primary schools in 2025.
The report said that although the enrolment of primary-age children is higher than it was in 2022, when the Taliban took power, it has not kept pace with the growing primary school-age population.
“The priority is to expand the education system’s capacity fast enough to meet growing demand,” the report added.

After returning to power in August 2021, the Taliban banned girls’ secondary and tertiary education in Afghanistan, with primary education the only level of formal schooling accessible to girls. Despite this, girls' enrollment in primary schools remains lower than boys’ enrollment.
According to a U.N. report released in October, some 2.9 million girls were enrolled in formal primary schools last year, while 3.7 million boys were enrolled.
Timme said that improving the quality of learning should be a top priority.
“More importantly, we need to train teachers and ensure that they can provide quality education,” he added.

The U.N. report noted several challenges affecting the quality of education, including an acute lack of qualified teachers, particularly female teachers, inadequate teaching and learning resources, ineffective assessment and monitoring mechanisms, and significant deficiencies in school infrastructure.

The report also said that “Nearly half of schools lack essential facilities such as clean water, sanitation or heating, while over 1,000 schools remain closed due to conflict or damage. Climate shocks and displacement further disrupt continuity, exacerbating inequities in access and outcomes.”

Afghanistan is also facing significant infrastructure and access challenges. Nearly half of schools lack basic amenities such as clean water, sanitation, and heating, while more than 1,000 remain closed due to conflict or physical damage, the report said.

Timme said improving school conditions matters because schools are places where children learn but also “develop social skills, learn to interact with others and begin to understand their roles in society.”

items.title: Waymo pulls driverless taxis from freeways across the US after California ban
paragraphs: Waymo has stopped offering driverless taxi rides on freeways across the US indefinitely. The Alphabet subsidiary pulled its vehicles from highways nationwide after California banned them from freeways in response to recent traffic incidents.

Waymo had allowed riders to hail its robotaxis for freeway rides in the San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles, Phoenix, Miami and Austin. The California-based company offers rides on city streets in many other areas, including Las Vegas, Dallas and Denver. Those rides remain unaffected by suspended freeway service.

A Waymo spokesperson wrote in an email that the company has “temporarily restricted commercial freeway rides in all markets where we operate that service”, though it’s “continuing freeway testing with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel”. The suspension was implemented last Wednesday, according to the spokesperson, but they didn’t say how long it would last.

Waymo’s voluntary suspension came the same day as the California department of motor vehicles banned the company’s robotaxis from the state’s freeways. The ban followed two traffic incidents, including one in which three Waymo driverless vehicles drove into a construction zone, a DMV spokesperson, Jonathan Groveman, said in a statement.

The construction zone incident occurred on 5 November, and the second incident, which involved California highway patrol vehicles, occurred the next day on a highway in San Francisco, according to Groveman.

Video of the 6 November incident circulated widely on social media last week. In the footage, a Waymo vehicle can be seen trying to bypass California highway patrol vehicles conducting a traffic break.

“The department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present,” Groveman said.
Groveman added that “similar incidents” previously occurred on 18 May.
The Waymo spokesperson said the “recent freeway construction zone encounters on US 101 in California” did not “involve any injuries or collisions”.

California’s restrictions bar Waymo from operating and testing its driverless vehicles on the state’s freeways, according to Groveman. He said the restrictions will remain in effect until “Waymo demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions”.

items.title: Democrats skip a vote on adding Brendan Carr’s adviser to the FCC
paragraphs: Senate commerce committee Chair Ted Cruz (R-TX) began a meeting Wednesday meant to confirm President Donald Trump’s nominee to the Federal Communications Commission with a lopsided dais. To his right sat all 14 Republican members of the panel, including Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD). To his left were about a dozen empty chairs — every Democratic member of the panel was absent.

Cruz said he’d learned the night before that Democrats intended to boycott the vote, though Democrats say they’d repeatedly raised their concerns about advancing a Republican FCC nominee without a Democratic one. “The administration has shown it’s willing to move Democrats,” Cruz said, pointing to Senate votes scheduled on bipartisan pairs of nominations to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and the Securities and Exchange Commission. And even though the Supreme Court confirmed his power to do so, Cruz said, Trump has not moved to fire any Democrats from the FCC, as he did at the Federal Trade Commission. “This is an ordinary nomination to fill a vacancy previously held by someone in the same party,” Cruz said.
“This is an ordinary nomination to fill a vacancy previously held by someone in the same party”

But in statements and comments to reporters outside the committee room, Democrats said that the process has been far from normal. Senate committees often vote on nominations to historically independent agencies in bipartisan pairs. Confirming Danielle Thumann Severs, senior counsel to FCC Chair Brendan Carr, to become a commissioner at the agency would put the FCC at four total members — three Republicans and one Democrat, Anna Gomez. Gomez’s term has technically expired, though she can remain on the commission through next year unless she’s replaced. But Democrats fear that by confirming a third Republican to the FCC, Trump might finally fire Gomez, because he’d no longer need her present for a quorum to vote on key actions.

Democrats asked for Thumann’s confirmation vote to be withheld until her nomination could be paired with a Democratic nomination. One way to do that would be to renominate Gomez. But so far, the president has not offered any Democratic nominees for the commission. Democrats said they made their concerns clear to Cruz, and added, “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In addition to the procedural concerns, Democrats worry about Thumann’s work as an adviser to Carr, and whether she was truthful about the matters she worked on. In a letter asking Cruz to delay her confirmation vote, Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-NM) detailed his concerns. At the November 10th hearing where Thumann answered committee members’ questions, she testified that she had “not worked with the Chairman on any media-related issues,” Luján noted in the letter. But documents obtained via a Freedom of Information Act request show that Thumann was “looped in” on various media matters, and “helped draft Skydance’s commitments that facilitated the 2 FCC’s approval of the Skydance-Paramount merger,” Luján wrote. “She also played a role in processing informal complaints related to CBS 60 Minutes alleged news distortion and she apparently orchestrated the Commission’s response to consumers regarding the Jimmy Kimmel controversy.” The FCC did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the matter.

Even Cruz admitted concerns with Carr’s handling of Kimmel’s comments in the aftermath of conservative activist Charlie Kirk’s killing. But at Wednesday’s meeting, he said he “emphatically agree[s]” that Thumann had resolved any lingering worries about that. He added that his JAWBONE Act, which the committee previously passed, could directly address First Amendment violations by government agencies of either party. The bill would let individuals sue government officials if they illegally try to compel social media or broadcast companies to remove their speech. Sen. Jerry Moran (R-KS), who’d similarly expressed concern over the Kimmel incident, said he found Thumann’s responses on the subject “comforting,” including in a phone call earlier that morning where he said he’d expressed his “serious interest in how the FCC protects and promotes free speech, including free speech on broadcast.” On the call, he said, “she was able to satisfy me once again in her answers, including an explanation for her role at the FCC and her lack of engagement on this type of issue as the FCC made decisions.”
“If she was lying about this, what else is she lying about and what else is she hiding?”

Speaking to reporters outside of the hearing room ahead of the meeting, Luján accused Thumann of lying to the committee. “The questions that I have is if she was lying about this, what else is she lying about and what else is she hiding?” he said. Luján said he wants both Thumann and Carr to appear before the committee by the end of the year to answer lawmakers’ questions. Asked if he’d support using the committee’s subpoena power or even pursuing impeachment against Carr when Democrats regain power next year, Luján said his vote to confirm Carr as a commissioner under President Joe Biden is among his biggest regrets, and that while he hopes Carr will testify voluntarily, “everything should be on the table here to be able to get answers for the American people.”

When it came time to vote on whether to advance Thumann’s nomination for a final step of a vote on the Senate floor, all 15 Republicans voted “aye.” That gave Thumann enough votes for her nomination to advance to the Senate floor, where it’s expected to pass along party lines once scheduled. Still, the clerk listed off the names of the 13 Democratic committee members whose seats remained empty. There was no response.

items.title: Anthropic sets share price at $83 for stock market debut, above expected range
paragraphs: Anthropic set the share price for its debut on the US stock market at $83 on Wednesday, positioning the artificial intelligence company for one of the biggest initial public offerings in history. The firm is slated to begin trading on Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT, with CEO Dario Amodei and other co-founders ringing the bell to open the Nasdaq exchange.

The pricing is above Anthropic’s earlier estimates. Last week, the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, set its preliminary share price at $70 to $78. With all shares counted, those prices put Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) from $1.26tn to $1.41tn. Elon Musk’s SpaceX debuted on Wall Street in June with the biggest market offering ever at $1.77tn. With Anthropic setting its share price at $83, it could now surpass SpaceX.
Amodei is planning to sell about $260m worth of shares with the IPO, as are his six fellow co-founders. At the top of the price range, the co-founders’ stakes will be worth more than $18bn each.

When Anthropic filed for its IPO last month, the company detailed rapidly rising revenue in its prospectus: $41m in 2023, $386m in 2024, $4.585bn in 2025 (an increase of more than 1,000%), then $16.286bn in the first six months of 2026 alone. The company disclosed that, as of the end of June, it had raised $141.1bn.
Despite the increasing revenue, Anthropic disclosed a net loss of $80bn for the first half of 2026.

Anthropic’s main expenditure listed in its investor prospectus is computing power from datacenters. The company has compute purchase commitments and lease agreements of more than $70bn over the next 12 months and more than $450bn by 2030, with a further $450bn due by 2045.

Anthropic is the first company at the forefront of the generative AI boom to go public, and its performance is likely to affect investors’ enthusiasm. Its competitor OpenAI was slated to hit Wall Street later this year, but CEO Sam Altman has said that the company opted to delay its IPO until it can overcome safety concerns.

Anthropic’s IPO comes during a volatile time for AI and the stock market. Last month, the industry saw a broader slowdown, with share prices dropping at several companies amid growing concern about the technology. Then, last week, Nvidia, which designs the chips AI companies use to power their chatbots, was racked with a scandal that led to CEO Jensen Huang resigning after reports of multiple extramarital affairs.

items.title: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
paragraphs: It was during November 2020 that somewhere in San Francisco, a woman called Daniela Amodei phoned a friend, asking for advice.
Daniela oversaw safety and policy at OpenAI, one of the most talked-about AI companies in the world.
But Daniela and her brother Dario - who worked there too - had misgivings over safety levels at OpenAI and thought it could be time to walk away.

So she did what many do when we can't make a decision about something, she phoned a friend. The friend's reply was direct and to the point: "You don't need to be on the phone with me. You already know the answer."
The Amodei siblings and a handful of other colleagues quit. Together, they set up a rival – Anthropic.
Six years on and Anthropic, the maker of leading AI model Claude, has predicted revenues of $52bn in 2026 and $135bn in 2027, according to analyst estimates.

It is about to sell shares to the public for the first time in what's known as an Initial Public Offering or IPO, aiming for a valuation of an estimated $1.4tn (£1tn), which would propel it straight into the top 10 of the most valuable US companies.
The sale comes at a crucial time when many are wondering whether, amid increasing concern about the potential of AI, the industry's bubble is showing signs of bursting.

Where once investors were "all in" on a technological revolution to rival the railroads, the car, electricity and the internet, some are now hedging their bets, amid arguments that AI prices will be driven down as the technology becomes more common and concerns that a hefty wedge of the AI investment is tech giants investing in each other.

Shares in companies that supply the raw computing power behind AI, like Coreweave and Nebius, have seen their value cut in half while even the mighty Nvidia has lost its crown as the world's most valuable company with its shares down 30% - a staggering $2tn fall in value.
So could the Anthropic IPO reinflate the bubble or will it be remembered as the last gasp of a boom that is heading for a bust?
At an event last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told JPMorgan Chase's CEO Jamie Dimon that his guiding principle was to "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's worth".

The company is selling roughly $65bn worth of shares to the general public and a further $26bn on to other big tech companies. It is comfortably the single biggest money raising event in US corporate history.

It's an old adage that during a gold rush you should buy companies that sell the picks and shovels as opposed to those staking everything on striking gold. In AI's case that's the chip makers, the data centre builders, the energy providers. But Anthropic is arguably the gold itself and this IPO will see what value people put on it, according to Fiona Cincotta.

"I think the reason that this IPO is so important is basically it's the first ability for the public investors to access a pure play AI trade," she says, adding that previous offerings have been about "other parts of the ecosystem, which are, the semiconductors, the chips, the, data centres. But this is the first time that we were actually able to access the AI provider."
Daniela Amodei helped set up a rival company to OpenAI
What a company is worth depends almost entirely on predicted future earnings.
It's that calculation that many think presents the sharpest needle to the AI bubble.

Will current and future users of AI be prepared to pay enough to justify the trillions being spent on the chips, data centres, energy and employees, some of whom can command annual salaries of over $100m?

"AI is certainly in a financial bubble. While LLMs [large language models] offer genuine utility and are undoubtedly here to stay, the economics don't add up," said Gary Marcus, Professor Emeritus at New York University and author of Taming Silicon Valley, speaking earlier this year.
"[The] more companies build AI models, the [more the] technology becomes commoditised, eliminating meaningful competitive advantages and driving down prices."
So far, the growth rates in Anthropic revenue are extraordinary.
But these explosive growth rates hide a potential problem. Around a quarter of that revenue came from just a handful of companies, among them Google and Amazon.
It's also concentrated in the US which accounts for two-thirds of its revenue.

There is also the staggering network of circular financing found in the AI world. For example, Anthropic has agreements to buy or lease hundreds of billions of dollars worth of chips and computing power from a handful of companies including Broadcom, Google, Amazon. Many of those firms are also investors in Anthropic and major customers of its products.
It's not just some Wall Street investors questioning whether the AI boom is all it's cracked up to be. Out on Main Street, ordinary Americans have concerns too.

With the US driving so much of global AI growth, a growing public backlash against a technology that threatens to replace millions of jobs and hoover up vast amounts of energy and water became a factor in the recent midterm elections in the US.

Many areas in the US have passed moratoriums on data centre development and many candidates deemed too close to big tech found that association a political liability rather than an asset. Many Democrat candidates publicly opposed data centre development and won.

Added to that, the Pied Piper of AI, chip maker Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang, resigned last week after admitting to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.
Dario Amodei is one of Silicon Valley's big beasts

Huang's spectacular fall from grace and Nvidia's 30% fall in value from its peak have left AI investors looking for a new champion for the AI boom that has underpinned the US stock market and arguably much of its entire economy for the last two years.
If Anthropic – and its CEO are to be AI's new Pied Piper, he will be playing a different tune to the relentlessly upbeat, leather jacket-clad talisman Huang.

While Huang wanted AI development to continue full throttle, Anthropic was built on misgivings over the levels of safety and responsibility the OpenAI leavers felt were being exercised over the development of society-changing technology.
Amodei has warned that AI capabilities could enable biological weapon development, mass surveillance, authoritarianism and the replacement of millions of white-collar, tax-paying workers.
He has called for a slowdown in its development as its powers are growing at such an exponential rate that it could very soon elude any human oversight.

That said, his paternalistic overtures have been sceptically received by those who point out that the pace of Anthropic's development of new more powerful models has shown no sign of the slowdown he's advocating for the rest of the industry.

But for all the concerns, just as with Elon Musk's SpaceX before it – the hype and the FOMO (fear of missing out) on an undoubtedly profound moment in technological and perhaps human development – means that buying interest is high.
It's reported that orders to buy shares exceed the number on offer by over six times.
With demand outstripping supply by such a margin, a first-day jump is likely given the oversubscription, but it doesn't tell you much about long-run return.
Using SpaceX as an example again, shares initially rose nearly 70% from its IPO sale price of $135 to $225. Shares in SpaceX are currently back to $145.
The Anthropic IPO could be wildly successful and blow a bit of fresh new air into what some maintain still looks a lot like a bubble.
Eileen Burbidge, founder of tech investors Passion Capital, is one of those who reject the notion that AI is a bubble about to burst.

"Maybe the growth of the bubble has slowed down a little bit, but actually I wouldn't be willing to say that it's about to burst yet," says Burbidge. "I think this IPO could actually mean everyone could be off to the races again."

Fiona Cincotta believes Anthropic's IPO is about far more than just Anthropic. "I think what's going to be really interesting here is I think it can actually be used as a valuation benchmark for the entire AI ecosystem," she says.
"That's why I don't think this is just going to affect the share price of Anthropic. I think this is going to have much wider implications across the whole AI trade."

Two things can be true at the same time. The Anthropic IPO could be wildly successful - FOMO is a powerful emotion in financial markets. But its probable success won't soothe the unease in some quarters that not every company, every investor and every citizen will think of AI as the answer to humanity's problems.

items.title: Absolute Batman can save DC Studios
paragraphs: With James Gunn and Peter Safran out as the co-heads of DC Studios following Skydance’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, it’s unclear what will become of the cinematic universe that was building around movies like last year’s Superman. Though Gunn’s Man of Tomorrowfeature might still come out, it seems like his larger vision for the DC Universe may be tossed out by DC Studios’ newly appointed CEO, Jeremy Latcham. Gunn was taking his time fleshing out the DCU with relatively less high-profile characters like Peacemaker, Supergirl, and Clayface. But Latcham has reportedly received a mandate from Skydance CEO David Ellison to fast-track a new version of the Justice League featuring more popular heroes like Wonder Woman and the Green Lantern.

This drastic shift in priorities will likely change what the DCU looks like in the coming years as Skydance attempts to parlay its comics IP into projects that can help it get on top of the $80 billion of debt the company is now responsible for after acquiring WBD. Ellison’s instinct to whip out the A-list superheroes is probably right from a business perspective. Most casual DC movie fans are more interested in stories about the Trinity than obscure characters like Gorilla Grodd. But after two iffy attempts at creating interconnected DC movie franchises, that audience might not have much of an appetite for yet another full-on reboot.

Rather than starting from scratch, DC Studios should probably keep some of the things that worked well during Gunn and Safran’s tenure, like presenting Superman as a compassionate person with a strong moral compass. But if the studio really wants to take this franchise in a new direction that gets people excited, it should also be thinking about tapping into the energy of some of DC’s most successful recent comics. Though the WBD merger prompted Skydance to begin laying off almost 2,000 employees last month, DC Comics — which Skydance gained control of as part of the deal — was reportedly left unscathed because the publishing arm’s business has been performing surprisingly well. Much of that success seems to have been driven by strong sales of comics created by DC’s Absolute Universe imprint.

Launched in 2024, the Absolute Universe comics reimagine DC’s heroes and villains as wildly different versions of their classic selves. Absolute Wonder Woman is a witch raised in Hell, Absolute Superman first arrives on Earth as a teenager who remembers his childhood on Krypton, and Absolute Batman is a working-class civil engineer rather than a socialite born into immense wealth. The Absolute characters’ worldviews and approaches to enacting justice are all distinct from their mainstream universe counterparts. But as much as the Absolute comics diverge from established canon, they each capture the essence of what makes their central characters iconic pillars of the DC brand.

Wonder Woman aside, there have been so many cinematic portrayals of DC characters based on their classic selves that it has often seemed like Warner Bros. was stuck in a kind of rut. There have been slight stylistic differences between the various big-screen iterations of Superman and Batman over the years, but for the most part, they have all come across as the products of a studio that’s averse to trying new things.
Absolute Batman is compelling because it inverts the established power structures that define most classic Batman comics.

That’s part of what made Matt Reeves’ The Batman— which didn’t bother to rehash Bruce Wayne’s tragic origin story — feel somewhat like a breath of fresh air when it debuted in 2022. Robert Pattinson will reprise his role as the Dark Knight in The Batman Part II, but it’s not really clear whether that version of the character will have any bearing on the DCU’s future.

Between Reeves’ Batman films existing in their own universe (similar to Todd Phillips’ Joker features) and Pattinson presumably being busy now that he’s been cast as Amazon’s new James Bond, it doesn’t seem likely that that version of the character will be incorporated into the DCU. Ellison obviously intends to put out more projects featuring Batman, though, and DC Studios could tell a riveting story if it took some cues from the hero’s Absolute incarnation. What makes Absolute Batman such a compelling series is the way it inverts the established power structures that define most classic Batman comics. In those books, Bruce Wayne is part of Gotham’s marginalized underclass, while the Joker is a moneyed elite whose villainy is highlighted in the way he manipulates various industries.

This inversion puts Absolute Batman in a position to operate as a vigilante with a much deeper connection to the ordinary people he has sworn to protect. Monstrous supervillains like Poison Ivy and Bane are still major threats, but the comics also spend time pitting Absolute Batman against more ordinary evils like corrupt police departments infested with white nationalists fixated on terrorizing minorities. Absolute Batman’s progressive political overtones might not gel with Ellison’s personal sensibilities, and the comic’s brutality probably doesn’t align with Latcham’s approach to making films. But Absolute Batman’s phenomenal sales have made it abundantly clear that readers are enjoying these stories, which is likely a big part why DC Studios announced earlier this year that it has plans to produce an animated series based on the comics.

Those plans might change in the wake of Skydance acquiring WBD, but an Absolute Batman series would give DC Studios an organic way to introduce the character into its tentpole films. Having characters jump back and forth between TV and the big screen was one of the stronger ideas Gunn introduced to the DCU, and it’s a strategy that could continue to benefit DC Studios under Latcham’s leadership. Turning Absolute Batman into the next flagship Bruce Wayne would be a bold move on Skydance’s part. But if the studio really wants to prove that this megamerger was the right decision, it needs to show the public that it has the guts to take exciting chances.

items.title: UK government asks for Russell Brand's YouTube account to be removed
paragraphs: The UK government is asking for jailed rapist Russell Brand's YouTube account to be removed after his wife posted a video with a message from him claiming his innocence.
A justice minister met with Google, which owns YouTube, as first reported by Sky News.
The comedian is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

On Sunday, his wife Laura shared a video on their YouTube channel, and read out a handwritten message from Brand, in which he claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening."
The message prompted an investigation into whether Brand broke prison rules.

Downing Street previously called the message "clearly appalling", adding: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."

Mia Latter, a woman who has made allegations against him, said she found the message shared on the couple's Sunday Service show "upsetting" and was appalled to hear "this Christian message alongside absolute lies".
In recent years, Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer and has a large following.
Latter, 37, has alleged she was raped by the comedian when she was 16. She was not a complainant in his recent criminal trial and he denies her claims.
"I just felt for those women that stood trial and everything they went through," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme this week.
She is one of a six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.
Education Secretary Lucy Powell criticised media outlets earlier on Wednesday for playing extracts of the message, saying they should not have "amplified" his words.
Speaking to LBC, she described Brand as "someone who's not showing a jot of remorse, a jot of any sensitivity at all to their victims".
As things stand, the Brands' YouTube account is still active.
Meanwhile, his social media accounts on Meta platforms - Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp - were disabled last week.

items.title: Hegseth uses Venezuela visit to boast of Maduro’s capture by US military
paragraphs: Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since US special forces abducted its former president, Nicolás Maduro, to boast of the dictator’s capture during what he called “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America”.

Maduro was controversially seized by Delta Force operatives in the early hours of 3 January, setting in motion an improbable rapprochement between Washington and Venezuela’s anti-imperialist “Chavista” regime, which has ruled since 1999.

Speaking outside the recently reopened US embassy in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Wednesday, Hegseth said: “It’s a great honor to be here as the first United States secretary of war this century to set foot in Venezuela.​ Just one year ago my presence here … would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable.

“In fact, exactly one year ago today … [Maduro] stood on a stage not too far from here and yelled mockingly, ‘Come and get me!’” Hegseth recalled, before adding sarcastically: “Well, we answered that call.
“The reality is that … January 3 is the day that will go down in history as a day of liberation for Venezuela,” Hegseth claimed, although Maduro’s allies continue to hold power with US support.
Earlier in the day, Hegseth was welcomed to the Miraflores Palace by Maduro’s former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who became acting president with Donald Trump’s blessing after his abduction.

In the aftermath of the deadly US attack, Hegseth was one of the bluntest Trump administration voices when it came to celebrating the invasion. “Maduro had his chance … he effed around and he found out,” the defense secretary bragged.
Speaking at the palace, Hegseth struck a more conciliatory tone as he vowed to deepen cooperation with Venezuela’s new leaders in brief comments that were broadcast by the state broadcaster VTV.

“I stand here on behalf of President Trump, who sends his greeting and looks forward to the opportunities, not just militarily … but also economically: the incredible resource capabilities that your country has, that we look forward to unlocking together with you,” Hegseth told Rodríguez and senior cabinet members, including the defense and foreign ministers, Gustavo González López and Oliver Blanco.

Hegseth said his visit to Rodríguez’s “beautiful country” was designed to re-establish and increase “defense cooperation” between “two great militaries” that less than a year ago were briefly at war. Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that Trump officials were trying to negotiate a long-term US troop presence in Venezuela as part of their push for regional hegemony.

“I appreciate your leadership and commitment to your country,” Hegseth told Maduro’s successor, a once outspoken anti-imperialist leftist who has overseen an unlikely realignment with Washington since her ally was grabbed.

During her five-minute address, Rodríguez, whose oil-rich country is widely seen to have become a US protectorate after January’s invasion, made no mention of Maduro, who is behind bars in New York City.

But referring indirectly to his capture and the subsequent reconciliation with Washington, she told Hegseth: “Thanks to the political and geopolitical maturity of our governments, we have – in a very short period of time, just a few months – turned what were very difficult and very tough times for our people, into an extraordinary space for cooperation and mutual benefit.”

Rodríguez hailed the “historic” energy deal her government recently struck with Trump, who has called it “the biggest oil deal in world history” as well as “the spoils” of his “conquest” of Venezuela.
Hegseth claimed the agreement, which reportedly involves 65bn barrels of reserves, “makes the strait of Hormuz a non-factor for the western hemisphere”.

Critics of Rodríguez’s political movement painted Hegseth’s visit as a humiliating act of genuflection for a president with no choice but to roll out the red carpet for the man whose troops captured her boss.
Writing on X, Luz Mely Reyes, a prominent Venezuelan journalist, said Hegseth’s visit was designed to underscore Washington’s “direct administration” of her country.

“Ten months after Nicolás Maduro’s capture, Washington no longer needs to fire shots to remind everyone who is in charge: the mere presence on Venezuelan soil of the architect of the January incursion reaffirms that the country’s operational sovereignty is subject to the White House’s directives,” Reyes said.

Reyes suspected the visit also carried a message for members of Venezuela’s armed forces. “Domestically, the trip forces the military high command to legitimize the man who directed the extraction of their former commander in chief,” she said. “In this regard, I wonder whether it might be a message of discipline intended to prevent any pockets of resistance in the barracks.”

Trump’s attempts to expand his Shield of the Americas anti-cartel coalition of Latin American governments suffered a major blow last month with the defeat of his far-right ally, Flávio Bolsonaro, in Brazil’s presidential election. The leftwing winner, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has indicated his country will not join the initiative.

But Venezuela’s interim government is in little position to resist. During his surprise visit to Venezuela, Hegseth said Venezuela had gone from being “our most aggressive regional threat to [being] a compliant security partner”. He praised Rodríguez for working “closely, pragmatically, and diligently with the United States to stabilize Venezuela”. Hegseth claimed US and Venezuelan armed forces would work together to attack “narco-terrorists” operating on Venezuelan soil, vowing: “We will hunt you down. We will find you. And we will kill you.”
Concluding her speech at the palace, Rodríguez told her foe-turned-friend: “Thank you, secretary, and I wish you a lifetime of happiness.”

items.title: German knives, English socks: 13 gifts beloved globally that Americans are missing out on
paragraphs: Our editors and writers have lived across the globe, from Abu Dhabi to Toronto to São Paulo. So when we asked them to share beloved gifts from outside the US, the answers were as varied as our home towns.

This is the stuff we bring home in our suitcases and press into friends’ hands. Take the “workhorse” German paring knives or the bright red tortilla press that makes homemade masa feel effortless. There’s a 3lb tub of Maldon salt that is absurd yet practical, and a set of Australian linen sheets that get softer with every wash. They’re all delightful discoveries that don’t require a plane ticket to bring home.
Visit our ultimate holiday gift guide for more gift guides and holiday shopping ideas for everyone on your list.

For more than 30 years, my parents have used these trusty German knives in the kitchen of our 10th-floor apartment in Abu Dhabi. Every household I know in the UAE has a set. You can pick up the whole collection at a local grocery store for next to nothing (they come in different colored handles!), and they’ll last a lifetime. They are incredibly versatile too – from slicing fruits and vegetables to cutting luggage tags and fixing things around the house. They don’t rust or lose their shape. Whenever I fly back from Abu Dhabi, I bring sets as gifts for my US friends. As a good friend in New York once put it: “They’re the perfect workhorse knife.” Maya Yang

There’s something really special about a fresh, homemade tortilla. They taste better than anything you can get at the supermarket and are shockingly (at least I was shocked) simple to make. To make your masa (dough), just add water to your harina (maize flour) and roll into little balls. Though you can realistically flatten these balls with a rolling pin and some parchment papers, a tortilla press gives you consistent thickness. Plus, the bright red finish brightens up any kitchen. Danielle Renwick

I first discovered Hunter Candles when a colleague introduced me to their tucked-away storefront in Sydney’s tree-lined Surry Hills neighborhood. Their scents are fresh and never overpowering, with unique, earthy notes inspired by ingredients such as shiitake mushroom, river mint, blue gum trees, mountain ash and grapefruit rind (who would have thought!). I also love that customers in Australia can return empty candle glasses for refills. My favorite is Daisy, a bright scent with delicate florals and summery hints of peach. Maya Yang

When I moved to Los Angeles, one of the first things that I bought was a linen sheet set from Dazed but Amazed, a small Australian company. The small-batch color combinations they offer are striking and unexpected; the sheets themselves get softer and softer with use. There’s a Pacific sensibility in everything the brand offers – they make my bedroom feel like it opens right on to the beach. Lois Beckett

For your friends with caviar taste on a McNuggets budget, let me introduce you to the 3lb container of the UK’s Maldon sea salt flakes. While small boxes of Maldon salt are widely available at grocery stores around the US, loyalists to the stuff (me) know that the 3lb tub is a whimsical necessity in any good kitchen. It’s not only a visually fun gift to receive (it comes with a cute little handle!), it’s absurdly practical! I use a smaller salt cellar on my counter, but knowing there’s plenty to refill it with at all times? A thrill! It’s also roughly $30, making it a cost-effective gift for someone desperately seeking seasoning in their life, a white elephant offering or a cheeky pre-holidays gift from you to you. Jenna Amatulli

This sustainable knitwear brand, founded in east London during the pandemic, produces a beautiful array of striking, vintage-inspired socks. There are bold checks and tasteful stripes in a wide array of colors. I craved a pair as soon as I saw them. LB

I lived in Brazil in my 20s and 30s and to this day crave cheesy, gooey pão de queijo. This addictive treat, originally from the state of Minas Gerais, is a mix of tapioca flour, cheese and eggs. If I’m feeling particularly nostalgic I’ll pair them with some açai. I was delighted to find that this dry mix comes in bulk and tastes just like anything you’d find at a Brazilian padaria. DR

“Despite my Italian heritage, it took a temporary move to Rome to discover the magic of the moka pot. I instantly fell in love with this Italian coffee maker’s ability to brew a beverage on par with the $10 lattes found at my favorite cafes,” I wrote in my guide to achieving a perfect cup of iced coffee. In the chillier months, I rely on mine for achieving steaming cups of coffee, topped with frothed milk and a dash of cinnamon. It’s far less expensive than an espresso machine, but makes coffee nearly as strong.
While I own two sizes, the colored option would make for a particularly great gift (I have red). Lauren Gould

In the nearly 15 years I’ve lived in Toronto, I’ve never been more than 15 minutes by bike or streetcar from the city’s best outdoor spots: Trinity Bellwoods, or a ravine. These beautifully illustrated jigsaw puzzles that capture my favo(u)rite city scenes are a dream to play, each piece snapping easily into the next, and the poster is so lovely I have framed it. Jessie Willms

If you’re looking for a non-Amazon alternative to the Kindle, let this be your sign to get a Kobo. (These e-readers are widely available outside Canada, but it’s nice to tell people that Canadian tech extends beyond the BlackBerry – RIP.) Then load it up with your favorite Canadian books, from Margaret Atwood to Rachel Reid to all the Emily St John Mandels. Does it also snow terribly from early December to May where you live? Get cozy under this quilt, in these sweatpants and this bunny hug (an endearing Saskatchewan regionalism for hoodie. Light a Province of Canada candle and read until spring. JW

If you’re a millennial looking to (finally) upgrade and unify your tablewares, consider Fable. The Canadian company makes lovely ceramics that feel much more luxurious than their price point. The plates and bowls are a lovely foundation if you want to pair them with your existing eclectic tableware. While I would die to have all my tableware from Michelle Organ or Toni Darling Frank, budget (and my likelihood to drop breakables) prohibits it. A mix of makers big and small is the sweet spot. JW

El Dorado rum comes from Guyana, where I’m originally from. Growing up, El Dorado was always a name we knew and took pride in. Guyana is known for its demerara sugar, and El Dorado rum is one of the great products that comes from the ingredient. When I give it as a gift, I love that I’m sharing a little piece of home and introducing someone to something special that represents my country. It’s a great rum. Keisa Caesar

Scandinavia’s best contemporary art museum is tucked away in the Danish countryside, a short train ride outside Copenhagen. Luckily, its online store of stunning art prints ships to the US – and you can get them framed or unframed. There’s something for every art lover: reimagined maps and manuals of Dominican-American artist Firelei Báez, eerie figures of Kaari Upson, classic landscapes by David Hockney and more. For a holiday gift, I might choose one of these ocean plant cyanotypes by 19th-century British botanist Anna Atkins. LB

items.title: Trump’s latest land grab is an AI hub in the Philippines
paragraphs: President Donald Trump was greeted by no less than five beauty queens when he landed in the Philippines on Tuesday, according to local news outlet Rappler. As he stepped onto the tarmac, a child handed him small US and Philippine flags. A band played “YMCA,” a staple at Trump rallies, as more girls in traditional bell-sleeved blouses and young men in wide-brimmed hats danced to the song.

Outside the airport, hundreds of protesters packed streets bearing signs — and at least one prop casket — saying “Trump out.” Others say “Reject Pax Silica,” the name for the US-led international initiative to secure chips and critical minerals used in the hardware fueling the AI boom.

“Pax” comes from the Latin word for “peace, stability, and long-term prosperity,” the Pax Silica website proudly says. Yet the unspoken question — peace and prosperity for whom? — explains the whiplash between the Philippine government’s warm welcome of Trump and the public fury raging outside.

Trump says he wants to “win AI” — whatever that means. As such, the US needs data centers full of GPUs to do it. With Americans increasingly opposed to data centers and chip factories being built in their communities, the US is now recruiting less affluent nations to take up some of the slack. Lawmakers from both the US and the Philippines are promising a slice of the riches that advances in generative AI are supposed to create. And that’s supposed to be worth the land razed, homes destroyed, and natural resources lost in the name of technological progress. In the Philippines, that’s taking the shape of a proposed 1,620-hectare (4,000 acres) hub for chip factories, processing plants for critical minerals, and data centers.

At least two dozen countries have signed on to the Pax Silica initiative, and Trump was expected to pressure more to join while in the Philippines for events related to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. With Pax Silica, the US aims to insulate itself from China’s dominance in manufacturing semiconductors and processing critical minerals needed to make those chips. Trump held a bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. Wednesday before heading to Shenzhen to meet with China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin.

Philippine and US officials are expected to sign a framework agreement by the end of the year for the jointly developed Pax Silica Economic Security Zone. The details are still murky and shrouded in NDAs. The Philippines’ Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) overseeing the plan expects an economic boom from minerals processing and chip manufacturing, with perhaps a data center or two on site. Meanwhile, human rights advocates who oppose the project warn that it will displace Indigenous residents, cutting them off from water resources on which they rely.
“How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood?”

“We do not want to give up our community,” Petronila Capiz-Muñoz, chieftain of the Indigenous Aeta Hungey tribe, told Human Rights Watch. “How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood? This is where we source our water, this is where we plant.” Capiz-Muñoz said BCDA officials have told residents that they’ll need to relocate by December to make way for development. Small farmers are also afraid the semiconductor hub will push them off their lands, according to Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch.
There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here.

The Aeta are among the first people to inhabit the Philippines, believed to have arrived around 30,000 years ago. And yet the Aeta Hungey tribe has been trying since 1994 to secure an official certificate recognizing its ancestral domain in one of the areas now facing industrial development. But since the tribe hasn’t been granted that certificate, the BCDA can still claim the AI hub will be built “outside titled ancestral domains.”

The agency says the project will be located on public land located at the former Clark Air Base built in the early 1900s when the Philippines was a US territory. The Philippine constitution now only allows its own citizens to own private land. But the BCDA can offer leases lasting as long as 99 years to foreign developers. The agency expects to rake in close to $1 billion USD (about 60 billion in PHP Peso) from lease income over the first 25 years.
There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here

The BCDA was in talks with around 30 different companies interested in setting up shop in Clark’s proposed AI hub, then-BCDA President and CEO Joshua Bingcang told reporters in July. He couldn’t name names, he said, because of NDAs — creating the same kind of opacity that has turned Americans against data centers on their home turf.

He did mention, however, that an American energy company was conducting a feasibility study into building a liquefied natural gas (LNG) line and plant to meet the hub’s enormous electricity demand. Bingcang called LNG a clean fuel, but that’s provably false. LNG is primarily methane, a smog-forming pollutant that is an even more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide.

Bingcang said in September that the Philippine government wanted to invite Nvidia, TSMC, and Apple. While one or two data center developers had expressed interest, according to Bingcang, most of the companies interested were “high tech” manufacturing firms. He has also described chip manufacturing as a “clean” industry, echoing corporate spin that’s been around since the start of Silicon Valley.

At the first chip fabs in California, workers — many of them Filipino immigrants — donned “bunny suits” to assemble sensitive chips in environmentally controlled “clean rooms.” Little did they know that the gear they wore offered little protection against the harsh chemicals used in manufacturing, which also leaked out of storage tanks to contaminate soil and groundwater. When studies came out in the ’90s documenting disproportionately high rates of miscarriages among workers, companies pledged to phase out some of the chemicals linked to reproductive health risks. Around the same time, chip manufacturing started to move out of the US to Asia, where similar health problems stemming from the same chemicals cropped up even decades later.

Chipmakers say their fabs have gotten much safer over the years, in part because more work is automated. Even so, the BCDA estimates that the AI hub will create up to 190,000 direct jobs. The BCDA, White House, and Philippine’s Malacañang Palace did not immediately respond to questions from The Verge.

“I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great,” Trump told President Marcos during his visit. Marcos’ parents are estimated to have stolen up to $30 billion from government coffers over decades of rule before a people power movement ousted the current president’s father from the same office in the 1980s. But public memory, it seems, can be short.

And skyrocketing demand for more powerful chips used for generative AI has raised fears among environmental and labor groups that history might repeat itself. Companies move fast and break things, leaving a toxic mess in their wake. And when Americans decide they’ve had enough in their own back yards, the industry sets up shop somewhere else where they think their customers aren’t paying attention and politicians are happy to look the other direction.

items.title: What’s next for Nvidia? Whatever doesn’t rock the mind-bogglingly profitable boat
paragraphs: If someone handed you $8,300 every second, what would you do? That’s how much pure profit Nvidia now makes. By the time you finish reading this paragraph, Nvidia will likely have cleared $45,000 and change.

It’s easy to look at Nvidia, a company that just lost its visionary founder CEO due to a series of scandals, and think that the company and maybe the entire AI industry are in terrible trouble. Perhaps so?

But I want you to understand: Nvidia isn’t your average semi-successful company that might tempt a new CEO to fix things that are broken. It is a company so staggeringly, mind-bogglingly successful it’ll do everything in its power not to rock the boat. There is so much money at stake.

It’s so much money that when I heard about Jensen Huang’s resignation, my first thought was: I need a way to visualize this jaw-dropping amount of money for you. I want to show you that Nvidia has risen so far, so fast, that rival chipmakers AMD, Intel, and Qualcomm barely qualify as competition now.

If you’re on a desktop OS, you could mouse over each dot in our chart above to see the staggering sums. But we built another way to visualize the rise of Nvidia I like even better. It’s a horizontal bar graph that not only puts Nvidia’s revenue growth in perspective, but shows you its monster profits right alongside them — plus the world events that made Nvidia a star.

TL;DR: The crypto boom and the great GPU shortage have nothing on the AI boom. Those earlier periods saw Nvidia’s profits briefly peak at $1.24 billion and $3 billion a quarter respectively, while the rise of data centers has driven them to $65 billion per quarter with no sign of stopping.

Yes, Jensen may have set a trillion dollars of Nvidia’s market cap on fire — from around $5 trillion at the start of November to “only” $3.6 trillion now — but the smoldering company is raking in $700 million in profit a day on average.

Put another way: Nvidia could give a $1 million bonus to every one of its 42,000 employees, every three months, without running out of cash. Or, you know, Nvidia could end world hunger or provide clean water for everyone, now that it’s making over $200 billion in pure profit a year.

But even if we stick to self-serving capitalism, you’re probably still a happy investor if you bought Nvidia a decade ago. A $1,000 investment 10 years ago is now worth over $67,000. You’d have over $1 million if you invested $15,000 back then.

And make no mistake, Nvidia is sticking to capitalism. Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress just promised to return as much money to investors as possible on the company’s November 17th earnings call. “Going forward, we intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders,” she announced. “All” is a lot more than the 50 percent baseline that Jensen promised five months ago.

Nvidia isn’t the only company whose fortunes have risen this dramatically. RAMageddon revealed that just three companies — Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron — controlled nearly 90 percent of the entire global DRAM market, and those three have repeatedly signaled that they’d prefer to celebrate record profits instead of ramping up production too fast.

But while their revenues and profits have been skyrocketing even faster over the past year or so, even Big RAM hasn’t caught the AI wave quite the same way as Nvidia. Samsung, of course, doesn’t just make memory — its revenue numbers include phones, tablets, TVs, home appliances, chips, displays, camera sensors, audio, networking equipment, medical equipment, and more.

In the most recent quarter, Micron made $37.7 billion in profit, SK Hynix made $29.8 billion, and Samsung came in at around $55.3 billion, but they’re all shy of Nvidia’s $65.3 billion. Historically, RAM has also been a bit more cyclical: Both Micron and SK Hynix actually lost money in 2023 because they produced too much memory.
On its latest earnings call, the first since cofounder Jensen Huang’s resignation, interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress reinforced the idea that Nvidia expects the good times to keep on rolling.

Asked how things might change under new management, she suggested that they wouldn’t: “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual,” she said. She added that the company has secured the backing of customers and suppliers including TSMC, the all-important firm that actually fabricates Nvidia’s chips.
“Our momentum is real, our demand is accelerating, our supply is growing. Our customers and partners are with us, and employees are committed,” she claimed. “We’ve got this.”

Nvidia claims it’ll rake in even more money next quarter, with projected revenue of $130 billion. Profit may be proportionally smaller since gross margins are estimated to drop to 71–72 percent (compared to nearly 75 percent), but Kress said Nvidia intends to get them up as high as 73 percent next year.
In other words: This astounding gravy train isn’t going anywhere. At least that’s the plan.
Stevie Bonifield contributed to this story.

items.title: Sony’s impressive Bravia 8 II OLED hits a new low price ahead of Black Friday
paragraphs: is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Black Friday is a great time to save on a new OLED television for your winter movie nights. Though, it turns out that you can already get a great deal on the 65-inch Sony Bravia 8 II, one of our favorite OLED televisions. It’s currently discounted by $1,100 at various retailers, including Amazon, Best Buy, and directly from Sony. That discount brings the price under $2,200, the lowest we’ve seen. You can also save $800 on the 55-inch model, which is typically $2,599.99 (Amazon, Best Buy, Sony), but now costs just under $1,800.

The Bravia 8 II was chosen as the “king of TV” by a panel of judges (including The Verge’s own Nilay Patel) in Value Electronics’ 2025 shootout. The OLED TV has excellent color accuracy, a bright panel, and a 120Hz refresh rate.

My colleague John Higgins praised the Bravia 8 II for its excellent image quality and engaging picture, though those positive traits are consistent with almost all OLED TVs. What sets this one apart is its impressive image processing, the bold colors from its quantum dot-equipped OLED panel, and that it looks great right out of the box (although he recommends using Professional mode). The screen was awarded the top spot at 2025’s Value Electronics TV Shootout, beating out similar offerings from competitors like Panasonic, LG, and Samsung.

For gaming, the panel can reach up to 120Hz at 4K, with both variable refresh rate and automatic low-latency mode to ensure that your content looks and feels good to play. The connectivity includes two HDMI 2.1 (one with eARC), and two HDMI 2.0 ports, giving you plenty of inputs for consoles and a Blu-ray player, among other gadgets. We spotted some color fringing of certain colors in dark scenes, and lamented the lack of a but it’s an otherwise excellent screen we can easily recommend.

items.title: Instagram now lets you edit your stories after you post them
paragraphs: is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Instagram’s latest update will allow you to edit your Stories without losing your views, likes, or replies. You can now edit the text, music, stickers, and drawings for up to 15 minutes after sharing your Story, Instagram head Adam Mosseri has announced.

Reverse engineer Alessandro Paluzzi first spotted Instagram working on this feature in April, but now it’s official. Previously, you had to delete and repost your Story to fix a typo or add a song that you forgot to include.
You can edit your post by opening your Story and selecting the three-dot menu in the bottom-right corner. From there, tap “Edit Story” to start making changes.

In addition to editable Stories, Instagram announced that it’s launching new fonts, colors, and shapes for stickers, as well as presenting them on sticker sheets that are supposed to be easier to browse. The platform is also making changes to the way you select multiple photos and adding new blur, colors, and gradient background options.
