items.title: I gasped at the new Tin Can phone – I’ve been looking for a solution like this for months
paragraphs: Yes, I genuinely gasped when the Tin Can press release landed in my inbox this morning, as it is exactly the product I've been searching for.

While I'm committed to a smartphone-free childhood for my children, I empathise with my children's need to communicate with their friends outside of school. They're also a bit young for the best dumbphones, but I still gatekeep my phone, only allowing occasional texting to other parent's phones in order to reach their pals. And I suddenly realised how unfair this is.

When I was nine, as my daughter is now, I was using our landline to call friends every day, honing valuable communication skills, and the lack of a home phone in my house means that my daughter is unable to do the same. As a new product, it's filling a very real gap in family life – and it's beautifully designed as well.

The Tin Can is already available in the US and Canada, and it's now making it to the UK. It runs on Wi-Fi, so no costly extra landline charges on your broadband (the route I was all set to go down), it looks simple to use, is crucially screen-free, and comes in a variety of delicious colours. It also has helpful parent controls, including restrictions like 'quiet time', you can only call other Tin Can handsets (for free), as well as parent-approved numbers (as part of a monthly subscription), and emergency numbers.
Of course, for best results, your children's friends also need to have a Tin Can – so I'm off to convince the parents I know to put it on their Christmas lists.
Pre orders are open for the UK, and it will arrive with you from 30 November.

items.title: Batman to James Bond: The clues about what to expect from Robert Pattinson's 007
paragraphs: He has been in big-budget blockbusters like Twilight, Tenet and The Batman, as well as a string of quirky arthouse films - so what clues can Robert Pattinson's past roles give us about what he might be like as James Bond?
Every actor creates a new James Bond, and Pattinson is one of the best in the business at crafting a memorable character.
The British actor can be an action man or an anti-hero, a romantic lead or a comic fool. He can be granite-faced or goofy, and everything in between.
"I was thinking about what the aspects of James Bond are, and he's done all of those throughout his career," says Paul Tweddle, host of the Heavy Spoilers film podcast, external.

He cites Pattinson's performance as a brooding heartthrob in teen vampire franchise Twilight, his suave and quick-witted secret agent in Christopher Nolan's Tenet, the withdrawn and focused title character in The Batman, and the ruthless and manipulative Antinous in Nolan's The Odyssey.
Pattinson has "often been drawn to really dark fare", says Anna Smith, film critic and host of the Girls on Film podcast, external.

"Wouldn't it be interesting to see Bond go a little bit darker?" she suggested to the BBC's World Service. "But also what he's got, and I'd like him to do more of, is comedy. And goodness knows, we need a Bond who can handle humour."
Unusually for a James Bond actor, one word that has cropped up frequently is "weird".
Earlier this month, Pattinson was described as "the weirdest guy in Hollywood" by the Celebrating Cinema podcast, external.
"Pattinson is an actor who makes bold, interesting, risky choices. For such a handsome guy, he can bring the weird, and then some," wrote Chris Hewitt in Empire, external.
"About 0.07 seconds after the announcement, people were already anticipating the weird with his Bond. And they may well get their wish."
Pattinson (right) starred with Willem Dafoe in The Lighthouse in 2019

Variety's chief critic Guy Lodge said, external Pattinson's reputation as an actor "has been considerably enriched by his predilection for playing, frankly, losers and weirdos", such as in more offbeat films like Good Time, The Lighthouse, Primetime and Mickey 17.

"Even his blockbuster assignments are more interesting when he lets his inner freak out to play," Lodge added. "His big, heightened, leeringly villainous turn in The Odyssey is off on its own beam entirely."
Associated Press film critic Jake Coyle said, external smaller films like The Lighthouse and High Life show "Pattinson's proclivity for pushing boundaries".

"He's certainly the funniest and quickest to laugh James Bond we've had in decades," Coyle continued. "It will be interesting to see how much of his personality bleeds into Bond, or how much the tux stifles it."
So what do Pattinson's performances in some of his biggest films tell us about what to expect?
Pattinson in Tenet with Himesh Patel (left) and John David Washington (right)
Pattinson plays a dapper and enigmatic British agent in Christopher Nolan's time-bending 2020 thriller, as adept at bungeeing off an arms dealer's tower as he is delivering some deliciously dry wit.
"He's very suave, he's thinking on his feet," Tweddle says. "He's someone who's holding his cards close to his chest and not necessarily giving the game away.
"Tenet is the obvious one where Nolan's basically doing a kind of James Bond movie."

The Times' chief critic Kevin Maher agrees, external: "Pattinson has effectively played Bond already, when he effortlessly inhabited the role of the suave yet nonetheless lethal British spy Neil in Tenet.
"For many observers (including this one) that was the role. That was the audition. There was no turning back after Neil."

New York Times critic Alissa Wilkinson noted that Pattinson has picked up other "Bond-adjacent" roles. "The most obvious is Bruce Wayne, a.k.a. Batman, the wealthy playboy with a lair of tech toys and his own gussied-up automobile," she wrote, external.
"Wayne and Bond have a lot in common on paper, but in Pattinson's hands Wayne becomes emo, reclusive, awkward, with the hair of a '90s grunge rocker."

The Guardian's Peter Bradshaw also pointed out, external parallels with how Pattinson played "the darkly conflicted caped crusader Batman in Matt Reeves's 2022 film, lurking athletically in the shadows - like Bond, used to working in secret".
Like Tenet, The Batman proved Pattinson is an expert at action scenes, whether that be jumping off a building or being involved in an explosive car chase with The Penguin.
"Batman is a really good example of where he's a withdrawn figure, someone who has his mind focused solely on a task, and I think that's a big part of what James Bond needs to be," Tweddle says.
However, Pattinson's 007 should be a little less brooding and aloof than his stony-faced Batman and Bruce Wayne.
Although Pattinson plays the villain in Nolan's Greek epic, Antinous's menace and ruthlessness could come in handy when playing Bond, according to Tweddle.
"I think Robert Pattinson also has quite a psychotic side to him, which a lot of the James Bond books delve into - how he's a killer, and he needs to have that side to him," he says.
"What he's done in The Odyssey shows he can be manipulative, and connive and make certain plans, which is what a spy needs to do."
Collider's Collier Jennings named, external The Odyssey, along with Tenet and The Batman, as films that show Pattinson is "the perfect" fit for Bond.
"All three roles carry an element that makes James Bond work," Jennings wrote.
"Batman has the combat skills and subterfuge you'd need to be a spy of Bond's caliber, not to mention the cutting edge hardware.
"Neil has a great grasp on the intricacies of pulling off complex covert operations.
"Antonius walks with a swagger and arrogance that either makes you love him or hate him."
Pattinson's current film sees him play real-life NBC journalist Chris Hansen, who carried out sting operations on suspected paedophiles for TV show To Catch a Predator.
It again demonstrates Pattinson's range as an actor and his ability to take on complex roles - he balances the portrayal of Hansen not as a villain but equally not as a hero.
"He's very much face-to-face with the predators in the room, and he's controlling the situation," Tweddle explains.

"It's very confrontational and demands a certain amount of power. Being able to control the room like that is also quite transferable to James Bond, and interrogations are a big part of what he does."
Pattinson will next be seen playing shape-shifting villain Scytale in the forthcoming third instalment of the epic sci-fi series - directed by Denis Villeneuve.
The pair's reunion for the next Bond movie is not a coincidence. Villeneuve's experience of working with Pattinson on the film may have been the deciding factor when casting James Bond.

"The thing I adore with Robert Pattinson is that when you roll cameras, there's always a certain moment where you have no idea what will happen. He is an explosion in front of the camera," the director told Time, external before the Bond casting was announced.
"He has an incredible imagination and is a very playful actor, and a very creative actor, always trying to bring new ways of expressing himself and always trying to surprise me."
Surprising, bold, weird? One thing is for certain, Pattinson's James Bond is going to be interesting.

items.title: Anthropic IPO: how can I buy shares, and is it worth it?
paragraphs: The technology company Anthropic is heading for a blockbuster stock market listing this week in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history.

The company is a leader in artificial intelligence, and is best known for its chatbot Claude. The float, which is expected to value the business at $1.4tn (£1tn), comes at a volatile time for tech stocks, yet it has been reported that the shares could be six times oversubscribed.
When a company floats it issues a prospectus for would-be investors that details its activities and lays out the share offering, including an estimated price.

Anthropic’s prospectus explains that the shares on sale will be 825m of class A common stock, and that the initial public offering (IPO) price will between $70 and $78 a share. However, the final price will be set on Wednesday.

The shares will come with voting rights, but, if all the shares’ votes are combined they will only represent 49.9% of the total vote available, so will not allow buyers to be able to force any changes in the way the company is run.
The shares will be listed on the Nasdaq in New York on Thursday, and will be available to individual investors alongside big institutions.

In the UK, several investment platforms are offering customers the chance to subscribe to shares, including AJ Bell, Hargreaves Lansdown, Robinhood and eToro. At Robinhood and eToro the minimum investment is $250 (£189), at Hargreaves Lansdown the minimum investment is £250, and at AJ Bell investors will need at least £1,000 to apply. AJ Bell is closing applications at 1pm on Wednesday, while Hargreaves Lansdown and Robinhood will close at 3pm. All say they could close the doors early without notice.
Once the IPO has happened and the shares have been listed they can be bought at any point, and through platforms that have not been involved in the IPO.

Yes – in fact, there are already funds which own stakes in the company. In the UK they include the Baillie Gifford US Growth and Scottish Mortgage investment trusts, while Fidelity has investments held in funds available to US investors.

Once the IPO is over, the stock will ultimately find its way into some tracker funds – although some will be quicker than others – and managers of actively invested funds could also choose to buy shares. That means people might well end up investing in Anthropic even if they do not attempt to buy any shares directly.
Anthropic’s prospectus includes 92 pages on potential risks to the company and its industry, so it is not an investment for the faint-hearted.
Recent weeks have highlighted the fragility of the US markets, and tech stocks in particular, so this is one to consider very carefully.

Nils Pratley, the Guardian’s financial editor, has raised questions about the company’s governance structure, saying it “represents an extraordinary concentration of power in the hands of a few individuals”.
Jason Hollands, the managing director of the investment platform Bestinvest by Evelyn Partners – which is not participating in the IPO – highlights some other things investors need to consider.

“Anthropic would give most retail investors the first opportunity to have a direct stake in a frontier AI developer. But it remains a capital-intensive business, and it has yet to establish a consistent path to profitability,” he says. “Investors will need to judge whether the company can turn demand for its models into durable earnings.”
Hollands says if demand for shares exceeds the limited supply, “that could support the price initially with a ‘pop’, but it does not guarantee a strong debut or lasting gains over the coming months”.

He adds the SpaceX listing in June “is a reminder that a hotly anticipated IPO and early enthusiasm can quickly be followed by volatility: its shares have traded below their IPO price at points since listing”.

When we asked Claude whether to buy shares in Anthropic it was upfront about why it is not a great source of investment advice: “I can’t tell you whether you should buy. I’m not a financial adviser, and I’m also made by Anthropic, so I have an obvious conflict of interest here.”

It went on to present a few facts about the IPO, and some useful questions that any investor should be considering before buying an individual share in an IPO. Can you cope with a loss if it goes down in value? How much of your portfolio will an investment in it represent? Will you already have exposure to the share through a tracker fund?

items.title: Dezeen launches 20x20 project to identify the architects and designers to watch over the next 20 years
paragraphs: Today is Dezeen’s 20th birthday, and to celebrate we launch our 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler. For the series we’ve asked 20 architects and designers who have had a major impact over the past 20 years to each select an architect or designer that they believe will have the biggest impact over the next 20 years.
Called 20×20, the project aims to celebrate the past 20 years of Dezeen while looking forward to the names and faces we’ll be seeing much more of in the next 20 years.
We’ll be revealing the selected architects and designers on Dezeen over the next four weeks, getting to know them and their work in a series of interviews.
The series launches today with a profile of Russian-born, Paris-based designer Harry Nuriev, who was selected by Danish architect Bjarke Ingels.

He will be followed by the selections of Es Devlin, Faye Toogood, Francine Houbine, Frida Escobedo, Huberto Campana, Iris van herpen, Jeanne Gang, Kelly Wearstler, Lesley Lokko, Ma Yansong, Marc Newson, Mariam Kamara, Marina Tabassum, Nendo, Neri&Hu, Patricia Urquiola, Philippe Starck, Sabine Marcelis, Sou Fujimoto and Yasmeen Lari.
All of the interviews will be listed below as they are published:

items.title: ‘She set out to buy a painting a day’: on the trail of Peggy Guggenheim’s legendary shopping spree
paragraphs: Peggy Guggenheim, art enthusiast and socialite born into a wealthy New York family, was often photographed outside her palazzo in Venice with a handbag dog and outré sunglasses. The Peggy Guggenheim Collection as we now know it, however, was nearly not in her Venice palazzo but London, evidenced by a short-lived and largely overlooked period between January 1938 and June 1939 when she ran Guggenheim Jeune in Cork Street. This exhibition posits that this initial gallery’s activities were far more influential in the shaping of contemporary art than previously recognised. Guggenheim Jeune mounted a flurry of 20 exhibitions including such UK firsts as a group show dedicated to collage, and solo exhibitions by Wassily Kandinsky, Jean Cocteau and Yves Tanguy.

How to demonstrate the pioneering qualities of a gallery that is now a ghost? With reassembling and contextual padding, it appears. The catalogue states that at least 60% of the artworks in this exhibition were originally shown at Guggenheim Jeune, though only a handful of captions list definitive instances. Does this imply that where not stated, they are included for illustrative purposes? This may be due to relevant works being difficult to obtain; for the segment representing Jean Cocteau’s exhibition in January 1938 we have one of his ink drawings for his 1937 play Les Chevaliers de la Table Ronde, and another in reproduction only.

Kandinsky’s knockout Dominant Curve, we are told, was purchased by Guggenheim directly from its 1938 retrospective appearance, but what of the other, wonderful, Kandinskys also present? His ectoplasmic Green Figure of 1936 is loaned from the Pompidou: was it at Guggenheim Jeune or not? The same may be said of the magnificent – and massive – Mondrian Composition No 1 with Grey and Red 1938 and Composition with Red 1939, explicitly stated as included in the Exhibition of Abstract and Concrete Art in May 1939 and then acquired by Guggenheim for her collection. It’s shown next to César Domela’s Relief no 11 C, a light relief of painted wood and concentric ellipses and honeycomb textures, which by contrast has no contextual anchoring in its text. If an exhibition deliberately cites a prior one, accuracy is crucial. One is inclined to be forgiving however with the inclusion of such rare treats as a tiny 1931 Salvador Dalí, and the barely visible oil on board Old Man Running completed by Lucian Freud apparently aged 15.

In contrast with a previous show at Petersfield Art Gallery about Guggenheim’s time living in West Sussex, which more heavily focused on her social life and affairs, this show is more academically flavoured and less is expounded on her social networking and activities, though they are inextricably bound. The clue is in the show’s subtitle: “the making of a collector” not curator. As such, we glean a sense of Guggenheim as facilitator and promoter of existing players moving within her orbit rather than a visionary selector. She famously set a goal to buy a picture a day, which sounds not unlike someone declaring themselves an intellectual for owning a large library. It was actually Winifred “Wyn” Henderson who managed the gallery, deciding on the name, finding the Cork Street location, shaping its promotional graphic design and using her professional network to bring artists into its circle; and Marcel Duchamp behind the scenes shaping its opening, educating Peggy on the difference between abstraction and surrealism.

We have then among big names that are well established in the art historical canon – Tanguy, represented here beautifully in dreamlike biomorphic landscapes, is said to have been Guggenheim Jeune’s only commercially successful show – lesser known surrealists such as Grace Pailthorpe and Reuben Mednikoff, who were suggested by Wyn and perpetuated what they called “psychorealism”: a mix of automatic drawing with psychoanalysis. Similarly, probably the only reason a sequence of monosyllabic portraits by Cedric Morris were exhibited, featuring the same flat modelling and blank expression, was because he was friends with Guggenheim and delivered a hundred of them to the gallery, of which mercifully only a handful make it here. A revelation however is Wolfgang Paalen’s delightful, macabre umbrella made of sponges, experiments with candle smoke and a gun made out of “poultry and mammal bones, brass and velvet”, mounted so high you’d be forgiven for missing it.

The show was pitched by the Peggy Guggenheim Collection Venice curator Gražina Subelytė and independent curator Simon Grant, so it is useful to bear in mind an underlying purpose serving the Guggenheim estate; it would be instructive to be able to compare Guggenheim Jeune’s purported influence on London contemporary art with other players – such as the Redfern Gallery or Mayor Gallery – beyond such amusing anecdotes cited here that customs were so flummoxed by avant garde art that it was demanded it be imported according to its base materials. Making tangible and cohesive a short but brilliant burst of activity, a precursor to what is now a cultural behemoth in Venice, was clearly a feat enough.
Peggy Guggenheim in London: The Making of a Collector is at the Royal Academy, London, 21 November to 14 March

items.title: Meet Harry Nuriev, Bjarke Ingels' pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years
paragraphs: BIG founder Bjarke Ingels has selected Harry Nuriev for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler. In this interview, the Russian-born, Paris-based architect and designer explains how he constantly aims to reinvent himself and his work.
Nuriev established his studio, Crosby Studios, 12 years ago with the aim of shaking up the world of interior design.
“First, it came from this game of rejection,” he told Dezeen from his house in Tuscany.

“Let’s say everyone likes to use wood – I won’t have any wood. If everyone likes beige or brown – I won’t have beige or brown. People are confused with a material, so that’s exactly the material I’m going to use.”
“I’ll bring exterior to interior, interior to exterior,” he continued. “I’ll mess everything. My colours will be inspired by fashion, my texture will be inspired by architecture.”
“You can’t be safe. You always have to risk.”

Over a decade later, the strategy appears to have worked. Nuriev was recently named Designer of the Year at French design show Maison&Objet and has a client list that many designers would envy. Among his recent works are a sofa for Balenciaga, a pop-up store for Skims, a reflecting pool for Gucci and a puffer-jacket-filled virtual sofa for Nike.

Now Ingels, arguably the world’s best known architect, has selected him as the designer that he believes will have the biggest impact over the next 20 years, as part of our new series marking 20 years of Dezeen.
Nuriev established his own studio after freelancing and working on other people’s projects for many years, with the aim of being able to pursue his own creative interests.
“When you work freelance just to pay bills, you don’t really have particular voice,” he said. “You have nothing really too specific to express.”
“I was like, hold on, I actually need to pull all the things together to express myself, whether it’s comfortable for everyone or not.”
At the time he established his studio, Nuriev recalls the interior design landscape being constrained and dominated by a couple of key, predominant styles that he was determined to break out of.

“Twelve years ago interior design was just minimalistic Japanese style or classic,” he said. “Maybe there were some alternative, very vague and obscure styles, but there was literally just two, maybe two and a half camps.”
“I remember that in interior design, and in particular the industrial area, there was no room to express yourself in a fashion or an art way,” he continued.
“[I realised] there is no way that everyone needs to live the same way, have the same living room and sit in the same sofa. I thought that I will create something different.”
Rather than identify a target market or clients that wanted a particular style, Nuriev simply set out to create his own individually styled interior spaces and objects.
“It was really a big experiment,” he said. “In retrospect, looking back now, I really think I was lucky.”

“By then I had learned classic and traditional way of doing it, so I knew the marble game and wood game and all of the, let’s say, Architectural Digest alphabet. But my idea was that my personal voice, my internal conversation, was very different, I didn’t know if people would like it or not,” he continued.
“Then, to my surprise, some people liked it.”

Much of Crosby Studio’s work utilises stainless steel, and has an appearance that is cold and almost uncomfortable. However, although this aesthetic is now associated with the studio, Nuriev is keen to ensure that his work continues to evolve.
“I understand we’re responsible for this whole stainless steel, futuristic, uncomfortable, Instagramable aesthetic,” he said.
“In a certain way we keep in our DNA our signature things that people already liked, even though they’re kind of retired for me and maybe I want something different,” he continued.
“But we always experiment because that’s the part of the formula, part of the recipe, to always have this little spice in every project.”
His metallic, almost cold aesthetic is partly born of the idea that you can create spaces that people can be enjoy without necessarily being comfortable.

“It’s bullshit because there’s no such a thing [as comfort],” he said. “I remember after a nightclub at 2am, sitting on a sidewalk, eating some hot dog and being extremely happy, but also I remember being in the most refined, beautiful restaurant, sitting in the most comfortable chair with soft cushioning and feel miserable.”

“I developed this mentality that comfort is actually not really healthy,” he continued. “Sitting comfortably in a sort of like sleeping environment, where you can relax all the way, can pull the strength out of you.”

The competition to create something new and attention-grabbing has intensified in the past 10 years, but Nuriev believes that it is still possible to find new ways of reinventing materials and forms through a process of experimentation and reinvention that he calls “transformism”.
“[I tell myself] ‘don’t fool yourself, you can’t create anything new, Harry,'” he said. “What you can do, you can find an existing thing and you can reinvent it. You can find a new life.”
“I’m trying to find new materials, and it’s becoming harder and harder because we explore quite a lot of different things, but surprisingly, there is always something,” he continued.
“It’s like music – every year there is new songs, there is new combinations of the same notes that we have known since Mozart, Bach and Chopin, but it’s still different.”
After more than a decade, Nuriev has a clear idea of his and Crosby Studio’s strengths, as well as the limitations of his creations.
“They are dessert-ish in their nutrition level, kind of like the entertaining side,” he said. “You don’t expect a full meal from Crosby.”
“You come to experience emotion,” he continued. “You want to have this sweet or salty or spicy something, and then you get it and you go. It’s not a daily situation.”
He believes that his work translates best at the medium scale – an installation, store, room or hotel lobby.
“I think I have found my scale,” he said. “We work in big development projects, which is fine. We can deliver it easily, but there are so many great people who can do it better than us.”

“Rather than we just distribute all our juice everywhere, and then maybe it will have less energy, [for example in] a huge building, let’s just do this lobby so crazy that people will feel the emotion.”

As Crosby Studios has established its reputation, the profile of its clients has risen considerably to include some extremely well known and demanding brands, though Nuriev says these projects can be the most creative.

“The calibre of clients is changing dramatically,” he said. “And you know it’s just like in a computer game, you feel like you’re on a different level, they speak in different vocabulary, it’s just complete different game.”
“Now I’m working with big sharks, and obviously their expectation is different. They’ve been working before me with bigger artists, so it’s also challenging. But this is the challenge of growing.”

Nuriev believes his most important role at Crosby Studios now is to maintain the “rebellious spirit” that it was launched with – something that inevitably becomes harder as a studio grows and the clients change.
“I think the game now is to constantly remind myself that we’re not an Armani Casa with steel, no matter how old we are, and to keep this spirit,” he said.

“I think that’s my job as the founder to remind my team, yes, we have gained professional skills, we know how to talk to people, we know how to draft a contract, we know how to deliver on time, but nevertheless, we still want to keep our rebellious spirit.”
His biggest fear? Becoming a pastiche of himself and rolling out designs in an unchanging signature style.
“My nightmare is to become a replica of my own self and just retire, becoming an established artist who just found his own voice and just puts his signature everywhere. This is not what I want.”
“As Coco Chanel said, once you feel comfortable, it’s the time to change completely. So to reinvent yourself is an exercise, and it’s pretty much my daily life.”

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.
Photography by Jenia Filatova unless stated

items.title: Giant lunar sculpture has visitors over the moon
paragraphs: The Moon sculpture is hanging at the St Helier Methodist Centre
People visiting a large illuminated sculpture of the Moon have said it is an "amazing" sight.
ArtHouse Jersey has brought Luke Jerram's artwork to the St Helier Methodist Centre until Sunday 29 November.
The 6m (20ft) wide display, which has been shown around the world, features detailed imagery of the lunar surface from photographs by Nasa.

Arthouse CEO Tom Dingle said: "Something that makes the most of a public space, that makes us think about the world around us, about ourselves, but also something that we can all share together all at once, is really exciting."
Eva, nine, said it was "cool" to see a sculpture of the Moon up close
The Moon follows a similar public artwork display in Jersey in 2023, when more than 31,000 people visited the Floating Earth on Queen's Valley Reservoir.
The installation features light and sound displays, which ArtHouse said would allow people "to encounter our closest celestial neighbour in an entirely new way".
Nine-year-old Ava thought the moon was "cool" and "like a big spot in the middle of the sky".
Primrose Keenan also enjoyed the exhibit, saying it was "amazing".
"We saw the Earth on the lake as well a few couple of years ago and that was amazing too," she added.
Toby Balderson said: "It does make a difference being able to see everything in such detail.
"We always just see little snapshots of it."
Youngsters Aquila and Starla, who are sisters, said it looked "really good" and "very big".
Dingle added: "Sometimes to stop, to take a pause and to reflect on the wider things, to think about the world out there, is actually really healthy and therapeutic."
He said the exhibit also showed the importance of free public artwork: "It enlivens our public realm, it gives us something to do together.

"It actually can change the pace for a day. It can give somebody a moment to reflect and it can mean something different to everybody - and yet we have the same universal experience at the same time."

items.title: Maybelline's new slogan is a crime against copywriting
paragraphs: Normally it's a visual rebrand that gets hackles raised online. A new logo can draw furious ire, as brands like Jaguar and Cracker Barrel have discovered in recent years. Less controversial tends to be copywriting tweaks. But beauty brand Maybelline's 'new' slogan has infuriated me more. Than. Any. Other. Rebrand. This. Year.

“Maybe she’s born with it, maybe it’s Maybelline," was one of the most famous jingles on TV for a while. It first debuted in the 1990s (see the original below), and is burned onto the consciousness of countless viewers. But now, in a attempt to remove its so-called "ambiguity", the slogan has been updated. Nay, butchered. One of the best pieces of copywriting, this ain't.

The new slogan reads: "Maybe. We’re born with it. Maybe. It’s Maybelline." Yes, "she's" has been changed to a more inclusive "we're". But it's that stuttering punctuation that's bothering me. Why does it suddenly sound like it's being recited by somebody struggling to walk up a hill?

According to Sandrine Jolly, Maybelline's global brand president, the original jingle "was giving ambiguity – it was more of a question". Well, yes. That was rather the point. The word 'Maybe' is, by its very nature, an ambiguous word. Its synonyms include 'possibly' or 'perhaps'. Its entire meaning is uncertainty. You can't change that by giving it a full stop. Trying to remove the ambiguity from a slogan built entirely around ambiguity is a bit like changing Nike's 'Just Do It' to 'Please. Consider. Doing. It.'
Maybe. We're Born With It. Welcome to the beauty of infinite possibility. - YouTube

And there's nothing wrong with changing 'she' to 'we'. It's a perfectly reasonable attempt at inclusivity, and one that could have been achieved without completely murdering the rhythm. Instead, Maybelline has taken one of the catchiest jingles of all time and made it sound like a hostage reading out a statement. Four sentences where there used to be two. Does that really make for more certainty?

What makes it all so infuriating is that this feels like change for change's sake. The original slogan was clever, memorable and instantly recognisable. The new one needs an entire press release to explain what its punctuation represents. In an era when brands are realising the importance of their heritage branding assets, maybe, just maybe, Maybelline should have left its slogan. Alone.

Daniel John is Design Editor at Creative Bloq. He reports on the worlds of design, branding and lifestyle tech, and has covered several industry events including Milan Design Week, OFFF Barcelona and Adobe Max in Los Angeles. He has interviewed leaders and designers at brands including Apple, Microsoft and Adobe. Daniel's debut book of short stories and poems was published in 2018, and his comedy newsletter is a Substack Bestseller.

items.title: SSdH "renegotiates light" in Melbourne warehouse transformation
paragraphs: A double-height glass atrium draws light into the open-plan interior of Tucker, a former warehouse that Australian architecture practice SSdH has turned into a residence and exhibition space in Melbourne.
For the project, SSdH wanted to focus on adaptation over replacement and aimed to work as much as possible with the existing warehouse structure.
The studio designed a raised courtyard, a steel-mesh external stair tower and a double-height atrium to draw more natural light into the 770-square-metre space.
To help retain the character of the former warehouse, SSdH fitted the main entrance into its loading bay and preserved a ghost sign overhead.

The Galvabond-clad entry was designed to act as a “deliberately compressed” holding zone, SSdH said, suspending visitors within a relatively unlit area before opening onto the light-drenched central space.
“Light was a big part of the original brief, with the existing boundary walls, limited openings and previous additions leaving much of the warehouse interior quite dark”, SSdH told Dezeen.
“We liked the idea of being held for a moment, making the shift in scale and light feel more surprising”.
Next to the main entrance, SSdH placed a double-storey external stairway that leads to a roof terrace. This was clad in steel mesh to allow for natural light and views from the first-floor interiors.
The ground floor interior is dominated by a double-height glass and steel atrium that was angled against the original floor plan of the warehouse to let light into the open-plan living area.
“Our approach begins with looking at what’s already there rather than trying to make something entirely new”, SSdH said.
“We were interested in how the building could continue to evolve through smaller adjustments rather than extensive demolition”.
The studio designed the interior of the home to be “continuously adaptable”, with the ground floor able to be used as an exhibition space.
Much of the floor plan is given over to open space, with a curation of select furnishings anchoring it.
In the living area, built-in sofas line the perimeter of the atrium wall next to the courtyard, and are accompanied by an industrial-informed timber and shearling bench by design studio BMDO.
In the kitchen, SSdH added a monolithic travertine island that is complemented by spotted-gum-timber and stainless-steel cabinetry that was fitted against a preserved painted-brick wall.
“Throughout, the material palette is honest, refined and robust, allowing the characters of the original warehouse to remain present”, said SSdH.
A wooden staircase set within a double-height void leads to the first floor, which features wraparound circulation and is home to the private bedrooms and bathrooms.

Spotted-gum and big-river timber cladding was used across cabinetry, extended doorways and flooring, with exposed roof trusses visible throughout. Both bedrooms receive ample light from south and north-facing windows, with the primary bedroom overlooking the atrium and courtyard below.
The main bathroom is fitted with wraparound marble and features a glass brick exterior wall that SSdH added as part of its aim to “renegotiate light” within the existing framework of the warehouse.
“We were drawn to the thickness and form of the glass, which catches, holds and releases light in a way that conventional textured glazing doesn’t quite achieve,” the studio said.
Overall, SSdH hoped to preserve the charm of the original warehouse while creating an adaptable, contemporary space.
Many decisions were “made on site as the building revealed itself”, the studio said.
“We wanted the spaces to remain open to different ways and possibilities of living, allowing the building to adapt without needing to be completely reworked in the future”, it concluded.

Other Melbourne homes recently featured on Dezeen include a studio with a “lantern-like” glass-block facade, a century-old corner shop transformed into a family home and a home comprised of a cluster of red-brick volumes.

items.title: Hi-tech Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit
paragraphs: In a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping, is basking in its neon glow.

On the sidelines, a series of high-profile bilateral meetings and the announcement of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have cemented Xi’s status as an agenda setter on the global stage.

The broader Apec summit, meanwhile, provides an opportunity for China to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms “unilateralism and protectionism” – that is to say, trade measures taken against Beijing by countries such as the US.

All this is set against the futuristic backdrop that is Shenzhen, a city that perhaps better than no other embodies China’s rise into a confident, technologically innovative power central to the global economy.
A photo display in the Apec media centre charts Shenzhen’s transformation from sparsely populated marshland, calling it “a miracle in the history of world development created by the Chinese people”.

“[Xi] wants people to go home Chinamaxxing,” said Prof Astrid Nordin, of King’s College London. “Shenzhen is itself part of the message. It’s a showcase of Chinese technological and economic achievements, and of China’s claim that it offers opportunities for prosperity in a world increasingly characterised by uncertainty and conflict.”

Like the light show, the summit is being carefully coordinated. The Financial Times cited people familiar with the matter as saying it would be one of the most tightly controlled in the organisation’s history, with leaders having to travel to a state guesthouse beside Shenzhen’s tiger safari park to meet Xi. The paper said diplomats had grumbled that the format “seems designed to reduce the free-flowing discussion characteristic of prior editions”.
Setting out its expectations for the summit, China’s foreign ministry has said it looks forward to “practical results in key areas such as trade, connectivity, digital economy, AI and so on”.

Already, Xi has announced trade wins with Canada’s Mark Carney, extending remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.

A meeting with Papua New ⁠Guinea’s leader, meanwhile, showed how Beijing’s geopolitical priorities have been absorbed and reflected by its allies, with James Marape recounting to Xi how he had closed Taiwan’s office in his country despite domestic challenges in doing so.

The most important meeting will be between Xi and Trump. The leaders of the world’s two superpowers are expected to tackle a broad range of issues including AI and trade. In a move that could strain the fragile tariff truce that the two leaders first agreed last year, the Trump administration said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips.

Christopher Adams, a senior adviser at the law firm Covington who was at the centre of trade negotiations with China for the Obama and first Trump administrations, said: “The trade truce may increasingly look like a ceasefire in a war where major combat operations remain on hold but skirmishes are escalating to the point where the line between peace and war is blurred.
“I don’t see pressure to announce a further extension of the trade truce in Shenzhen. If a significant extension is announced, that would be an upside surprise.”

China has not hesitated to leverage Apec’s multinational platform in service of its arguments. A commentary by the state news agency Xinhua on Tuesday said: “Amid deepening geopolitical rivalries and growing global divisions, [China’s hosting] sends a clear signal that great-power competition need not be a zero-sum game, and that one country’s development need not come at the expense of another.”

The chair of the Apec senior officials’ meeting, Chen Xu, said Beijing had made trade “openness” a key focus of its Apec year and looked forward to “achieving more practical outcomes on the trade front”.

The much anticipated trilateral summit with Trump and Putin, on the other hand, could prove largely symbolic. For Xi, “it provides the appearance of China shaping the world order as an equal to the United States,” said Dr Kevork Oskanian, an expert on Russia at the University of Exeter. “Agreement on substantial issues, which would, in any case, require extensive preparatory negotiations, is unlikely.”

For China’s ruling Communist party, the political pomp has another key purpose. Nordin said summits were “occasions for leaders to tell stories about the world, about their country’s place in it … and one of the most important audiences for those stories is at home.”

For the locals watching the skyscraper light show on Monday night, the symbolism was not lost. China’s export might had helped it become increasingly powerful on the world stage, said one local man, who did not give his name. “It’s so great that the summit will take place in Shenzhen,” he said. “I feel very proud.”

items.title: I'm a human doctor with human intelligence. But I sure do like my AI notetaker
paragraphs: Dr. Mara Gordon, a family physician in Camden, N.J., answers reader health questions monthly. Send in your question to: thrive@npr.org.

Question: My doctor has started recording our office visits with an artificial intelligence scribe. She says it helps write notes in my medical record. I said yes when she asked if I was comfortable with it, but in hindsight I feel a little freaked out. Should I be worried about AI listening in on my private medical conversations?
Answer: AI scribes are all the rage in medicine right now. Doctors are using them to take notes everywhere from the gynecologist's office to the emergency room.

I admit I've been an eager adopter in my own primary care practice. I use an app on my phone that records my conversation with a patient and then uses AI to write a preliminary summary for the medical record.

It saves me time. But more importantly, I like using it because it helps me focus more fully on my patient. When I use the AI scribe, I don't have to talk and take notes at the same time – I can actually make eye contact with my patient rather than staring at the computer screen.
But I totally get why people feel uncomfortable with the technology. I share my patients' concerns about privacy and how AI scribes might impact the doctor-patient relationship.
I also worry that corporate health systems will put pressure on doctors to use any time we save with an AI scribe to squeeze in even more patients.
And like many people, I worry that artificial intelligence might one day put me out of a job!

When I use an AI scribe during a primary care visit, I first ask the patient if they're comfortable using the service. If the patient says yes, I start recording using an app on my smartphone. I usually set it down on the desk in the exam room.

The scribe uses a technology called "automatic speech recognition" which records our conversation and automatically distinguishes between the doctor's and patient's voices. (Sometimes, when the patient has a family member accompanying him, the app needs to distinguish between three – or more! – voices.)

When the visit ends, the recording is then transcribed. A large language model – the kind of AI technology that powers ChatGPT, but specifically geared toward medicine – converts the raw transcript into a medical note. These notes follow a standard format that is specific to the speciality and the type of visit. They reflect what the patient told the doctor, physical exam findings, and the doctor's medical decision-making.

There are lots of AI scribes on the market, ranging from products embedded within the electronic medical record to free apps a doctor can download on her phone. Most scribes use a smartphone's recording capabilities to "listen in" on the conversation, although there are some that use a desktop computer or a separate recording device.

I use my personal smartphone for this purpose, as do many physicians I know. I downloaded the AI scribe software as an app on my phone. This causes occasional hiccups. For example, I've gotten notification pings from my book club's group chat while recording a patient visit – which made me make sure to put the phone in "do not disturb" mode whenever I'm using it for patient care.

Even though I use my personal phone for scribing patient visits, our conversations aren't stored on my device. They're uploaded directly to a HIPAA-compliant cloud, where the data is then transcribed into the AI-generated clinical note. Most scribe systems then delete the recording and the note after a set period of time.

HIPAA-compliance is an important feature of all AI scribe services. It means that the computer program was designed in accordance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, a federal law designed to protect patients' privacy.

The software company is responsible for safeguarding the data at every step of the process, from recording to generating notes. AI scribe companies encrypt the data, control who has access to it, and have systems to protect against "data breaches." It also means these companies are liable if the data is leaked.

Recently, I saw a patient who had metastatic cancer. Despite multiple conversations about his diagnosis with me, his oncologist, and his surgeon, he did not believe he had cancer. I had even – with his permission – called his spouse to tell her what was going on. He still did not accept it.

This kind of tricky clinical situation comes up on occasion, and the AI scribe did not get it right. Rather than reflecting the nuances of our conversation, the note that the scribe produced simply said that the patient had been misdiagnosed.

I often catch other errors that the software makes, like mistaking a patient's gender or age. Alarmingly, these scribes are also known for mistaking "I do" statements with "I do not." In medicine, this can be critical: The difference between "I do have chest pain" and "I do not have chest pain" can be a matter of life and death.

To better understand how AI scribes can contribute to errors in the medical record, I talked to Dr. Eileen Kim, an assistant professor of internal medicine at the University of California San Diego. Kim specializes in clinical informatics and thinks a lot about how AI might shape the future of medicine.

"You have a doctor who's overburdened, seeing way too many patients," she said. "They have this AI tool that's offered to them that seems like a great solution, but they don't have time to adequately review everything. It goes into the chart. Then you have another AI tool that's reading through all these notes. But they're wrong. And then it just propagates errors throughout the chart."

In my work caring for patients, I come across erroneous information in the electronic health record all the time. It's hard to know how much is related to AI and how much is caused by human error. But I think Dr. Kim is right to worry that AI scribes might make the problem worse.

As the doctor caring for my patient, I'm ultimately the one responsible for the content of the AI-generated note, so I always read them carefully before clicking "sign" and adding them to the medical record. Most AI scribe software makes doctors sign a user agreement stating doctors are liable for everything they write in the medical record, even if a scribe helps them with it.

When the AI-generated notes are factually accurate, I almost always end up editing them to make my clinical decision-making more clear. I'm happy to have robots help me with my administrative tasks, but I still take pride in being a human doctor with human intelligence!
Many AI scribes can only be used with English-speaking patients. Health equity advocates say they fear this means unequal access to the technology, which could further widen health disparities.

For example, the scribe allows me to look more at my patient and less at my computer, which might make a patient feel more comfortable disclosing a stigmatizing health concern. Or the opposite might be true, too: A patient fearful that an AI company is "listening in" to our conversation might be afraid to share sensitive information, which in turn could affect the quality of their medical care.

As a security feature, most AI scribe companies delete the recorded conversations within a set period of time. This is to protect patient privacy and also protect doctors from lawsuits. There is widespread concern in health care that the transcriptions could be used in medical malpractice lawsuits.

But some researchers call the recordings "digital gold" that could be used to assess the quality of AI-generated medical notes or even to study broader questions about physician-patient communication.

For example, I'd love to know how other doctors handle tricky conversations with patients who are fearful of vaccines. There are theoretical best practices, but analyzing hundreds of thousands of office-visit transcripts could help doctors learn what actually works best in real life.
For now, recordings of regular doctors' appointments — unless you've been enrolled in a research study — are not used for research purposes.

Most of my patients readily agree when I ask if it's OK to use the AI scribe software, but occasionally my patients have concerns. They worry that the data isn't really secure or that it could be used to identify them in the future.
If a patient doesn't want to use the AI scribe, it's no problem. I just take notes on the computer while they talk — it's what I've done for years before the AI scribes became available.
Opting out of AI in medicine more broadly may prove to be tricky.
"It's just everywhere," said Kim, the clinical information specialist. "It would be impossible to separate. We use it throughout the healthcare system."
Software that relies on machine learning is used for billing, for clinical decision-making, and for communication between the doctor's office and patients.

AI is often used in risk calculators, like clinical tools that estimate a patient's risk of, say, heart disease based on variables like cholesterol levels and blood pressure. AI is also common in "early warning" systems that notify clinicians their patients might be vulnerable to high-risk conditions like sepsis, based on vital signs and lab values.
Kim says it's basically impossible for patients to opt out entirely from having AI involved in their medical care, "unless you're so healthy that no risk calculators ever come near you," she said.

I asked Kim — a primary care doctor like me — if she thought AI would replace us in the coming years. If the AI scribe could learn to ask the same questions I do, could it generate a treatment plan as good — or better — as the one I recommend?
Kim thought AI might change how patients experience primary care. (Possibly for the better, she said, if AI scribes allow doctors to focus more on their patients and less on the computer!)
But ultimately, she thinks human intelligence is critical in medicine.
"It looks really good because it's really good at sounding like us, and it's really good at pretending to be us," she said. "But it's still just pretending in a way. There's no real brain."
I agree. I think the AI scribe technology has the potential to do both good and harm for health care. But the core of medicine is the relationship I have with my patients. No robot can replace that.
Dr. Mara Gordon is a family physician in Camden, NJ. Find her newsletter Your Doctor Friend on Substack.

items.title: Construction underway on Jean Nouvel's landmark opera house in China
paragraphs: French architecture studio Ateliers Jean Nouvel has shared photos revealing construction progress on the giant Shenzhen Opera House, due for completion in China in 2028.
Located on the Shekou Peninsula overlooking Shenzhen Bay, the opera house will eventually be defined by an elongated, wavy roofscape, nodding to the site’s connection to the sea.

Pritzker Prize-winning architect Jean Nouvel’s studio has designed it as a new cultural landmark for the city, with a 2,300-seat concert hall, an 1,800-seat theatre and an 800-seat venue among its facilities.
The construction photos help visualise the scale of the 250,000-square-metre opera house, with its various facilities sprawling out across its waterfront site.
They showcase its main concert hall with its horseshoe-shaped plan, alongside the two smaller performance venues.

Ateliers Jean Nouvel’s design for Shenzhen Opera House was the winning entry of an invited international architecture competition, for which other entrants included BIG, Snøhetta, MVRDV and Kengo Kuma.
Alongside the main performance halls, it will contain a multifunctional theatre with 400 seats, cultural spaces, backstage areas, apartments for performers and offices.
To help further connect the building to the surrounding water, the interior is expected to feature iridescent materials such as mother-of-pearl, also known as nacre.
“The sea will be both around you and over you,” explained Nouvel when the project was revealed in 2021.
“This explains more clearly why the main foyer has to be made of a noble, precious and luminous material that spells the meeting of sea and music and light,” Nouvel continued.
“Using the lustrous white reflections of a nacreous material will be a concrete poeticisation of the meeting of the sea and the auditorium and concert halls of the Opera House.”

French architect Nouvel founded his eponymous studio in 1994. We recently reported on the news that the studio’s La Querola housing development in Andorra, designed with Spanish studio Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos, was damaged in a fire. The project won the housing category of this year’s Dezeen Awards, which took place last night.
Another landmark opera house recently featured on Dezeen is the Shanghai Grand Opera House, designed by Snøhetta with a giant spiral staircase.

items.title: More than £160m needed to clean up one of Europe's largest illegal dumps
paragraphs: The contaminated Mobuoy dump is thought to cover more than 100 acres of land
ByMike McBride and Davy WilsonBBC News NI
More than £160m is needed to clean up and maintain one of Europe's largest illegal landfill sites, government officials have said.
The contaminated Mobuoy dump at Campsie in County Londonderry, discovered and shut down in 2013, was used to bury thousands of tonnes of rubbish at a site spanning more than 100 acres.
Last year, two businessmen were jailed for their part in the operation.
Northern Ireland's Environment Minister Andrew Muir said his department had now received an updated cost estimate of £161m for the clean-up over a 30-year period.
Muir described what happened at Mobuoy as "an absolute scandal" and said "the community rightly expects and deserves remediation of the site".
He is now seeking a meeting with the Finance Minister John O'Dowd to discuss how the work will be paid for - with funding from Westminster a possibility.
Once the finances are agreed, they will work towards appointing a contractor.
Andrew Muir says it could take a generation to clean up the Mobuoy dump in County Londonderry
Investigations indicate an estimated 1.6m tonnes of waste was present at the site and 627,000 tonnes of that was believed to have been dumped illegally.
The Mobuoy site is beside the River Faughan, which supplies a significant proportion of Derry's drinking water but officials have not found any contamination to it.
The area of polluted ground stretches to about 100 acres, or the equivalent of about 65-70 football pitches.
"This is a complicated project, as you'll understand, given the complexity of the site," Muir told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme on Tuesday, .
The minister said he took environmental protection very seriously and would continue to push for the establishment of an independent environmental protection agency.
"One of the massive lessons that needs to be learned from the Mobuoy site is the need for stronger environmental protections, so people have confidence that our environment is being looked after."
The site, located on the outskirts of the city, is a former recycling plant
Muir said the next assembly election was fast approaching in May, so he understood there might be some concerns about the potential costs involved.
"I want to finish this mandate with a degree of certainty for the local community, so we have a road map here for remediation," he said.
"I am pushing ahead with real enthusiasm with this."
Muir said the drinking water was tested regularly to ensure it was safe and that he would continue to work with all agencies to provide the local community with greater assurances about the site.
Muir said the Mobuoy site remained in private ownership, but they were "actively" considering ways of transferring it.
One option is vesting, which allows government departments to obtain compulsory and legal ownership of land through a court order.

items.title: Dazzling Leonid meteor shower to peak on Tuesday night
paragraphs: Experts advise finding a safe, dark location away from sources of light pollution such as street lights.
The meteors will be visible with the naked eye, with no binoculars or telescope required.
However, giving your eyes some time to adapt to the dark, perhaps 20 or 30 minutes, will give you the best chance of spotting them.
A wide open space is the best place to be, giving a full view of the night sky.

Meteors could be visible anywhere but the Leonids' radiant, the point from which they seem to appear, will, as the name suggests, be around the head of the constellation Leo, meaning this is the best part of the sky to focus your gaze. Leo does not rise until around midnight, so the best time to look is after midnight and in the hours before dawn.
As with all celestial spectacles, clear skies will be a must.

items.title: Actors in UK to get more rights over their ‘digital replicas’ in deal on AI protections
paragraphs: Actors in the UK are to be given more rights over their “digital replicas” as part of a new agreement on AI protections with TV and film producers, secured after a growing on-set backlash.

Under a wide-ranging new deal secured by Equity, the actors’ union, performers will have the rights to be paid when their digital replicas are used and to consent to whether their digital replica is used or not.
Approval must be secured from an actor if a digital double or digital alteration is used to make “substantive changes” to scenes involving agreed levels of nudity or simulated sexual activity.
The agreement also makes clear that producers may not use a digital replica during a strike “in any circumstance where consent is required for such use”.
Contracts will now make clear that producers only obtain permission for a specific project, rather than obtaining “blanket consent” to an actor’s digital replica.

The deal, signed after years of talks with the production body Producers Alliance for Cinema and Television (Pact), marks an attempt to create some ground rules for the use of an actor’s image, with AI developing rapidly.

The three-year deal will be put to a vote among 8,000 Equity members, with the union’s leadership recommending they approve it. It also includes a 24% increase in pay rates for major films and a 9% increase for TV projects.
It comes after Equity members voted 99% in favour of taking industrial action and refusing to be scanned on set without further AI protections, in an indicative ballot last December.
However, Equity said there were areas that a new agreement simply could not cover, such as digital scanning traditionally undertaken in production for digital effects added later.

There have been mounting concerns on set about the use of AI, which has made many actors more wary of undergoing body scans. Many fear the data could be used to train AI models on their likenesses or poses, paving the way for the technology to take away work.
Last year, the actor Olivia Williams told the Guardian that actors should have as much control over the data harvested from scans of their body as they do over nudity scenes.

The star of Dune: Prophecy and The Crown said she and other actors were regularly pressed to have their bodies scanned by banks of cameras while on set, with few guarantees about how the data would be used or where it would end up.
Equity said that “despite our efforts”, the new agreement did not establish explicit contract protections regarding the use of actors’ performances for training AI systems.
In a note to its members, Equity explained that digital replicas could be made using the same photography captured for the production itself, without the need to scan artists.

However, producers must limit access to digital replicas to people with a legitimate business need and “use commercially reasonable efforts” to protect digital replicas from unauthorised access, use or copying.

The new deal also includes a commitment to safe casting and audition spaces, as well as training and reporting on sexual harassment. Producers also have a new obligation to provide artists of all ethnicities and cultures with adequate hair and makeup provision.
Paul W Fleming, Equity’s general secretary, said: “We set about to radically improve and modernise the terms and conditions for performers across UK TV and film. The result is groundbreaking.
“We’ve achieved the best AI provisions in the business – protecting performers and ensuring that human performance is valued and prioritised across the industry.”

items.title: Black timber elements traverse concrete fragrance store in Tokyo
paragraphs: Mexican design firms Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts divided the interior of this concrete building in Tokyo, designed for perfume brand Xinú, with angular black-timber displays.

Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts designed the timber elements as sculptural interventions that also organise the interior of the three-storey shop, which is located in the city’s Aoyama neighbourhood.
The black-laminated wooden planks span the interior walls at jaunty angles, as if puncturing the building, which was originally designed by Japanese studio Satoshi Hirano.
“We approached the project as an intervention within an existing building, rather than simply designing an interior,” said Esrawe Studio founder Héctor Esrawe, who also co-founded Xinú.

“By introducing a continuous architectural structure that traverses its different levels, appearing and disappearing throughout the volume, we intended to generate a new perception of the original architecture,” he told Dezeen.
“Both structures coexist, establishing a dialogue between what was already there and what has been introduced, creating an unexpected spatial experience.”
Long, overlapping shelves with mirrored accents display products on the ground floor, which is dedicated to body perfume.
Xinú’s room scents are located on the first floor, where hand-painted brass panels on the walls and ceilings add a touch of warmth to the concrete and black-timber surfaces.
Aiming to reveal the processes behind the perfume products, the top floor displays botanical specimens, raw materials, found objects and collages in drawers.

Esrawe Studio also designed cabinet drawers to reference the storage and organisation typically found in natural history museums, intending to give visitors a feeling of discovery when interacting with the furniture.
“For Xinú, architecture has never been conceived simply as a backdrop for products, but as an essential part of how they are experienced,” said Esrawe.
“Our intention is to create spaces that encourage curiosity, discovery and a more intimate relationship with objects, materials and scent,” he continued.
“In Tokyo, the inserted architectural structures move beyond conventional retail display, becoming sculptural elements that enhance the presence of the objects.”

Xinú Tokyo is the latest branch Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts have designed for the perfume brand. Other shops include a radial wooden pavilion in Mexico City and a showroom in Oaxaca informed by basalt rock formations.

items.title: Disney’s radical new animation technique will make Hexed the end of an era
paragraphs: It's clear that some people are getting tired of the contemporary Disney style. That can be seen in the allegations of Disney same-face syndrome, the disappointment that Hexed doesn't look like its concept art and the perennial controversy over the hybrid live-action remakes, with Moana being the latest flop.

The fatigue was evident at D23 this year. The announcements that generated the most excitement were a return of 2D animation, if only in combination with live action for the nostalgia-heavy TV series in Oswald, and the news that Disney's Clay will look like claymation even if uses CG.

A lot of fans will be happy then to learn that Clay won't be a one off but rather the start of a whole new Disney era after Hexed. The studio's developed a new animation pipeline that will allow it to apply different art styles to 3D models, potentially replacing the realism popularised by Pixar with a unique look for each new movie – and it's all starting with Lilo & Scratch.

Set to show in cinemas alongside Hexed, Lilo & Scratch is the first theatrical short from Walt Disney Animation Studios in five years. Written and directed by Fawn Veerasunthorn and Malcon Pierce, it will see the much-loved blue alien Stitch having to contend with the introduction of a mischievous cat called Scratch. Maia Kealoha voices Lilo, reprising her role from the 2025 live-action film Lilo & Stitch, and Chris Sanders with voice Stitch again.

Like all of the studios' feature animations in the last 15 years, the short was made using computer-generated animation with 3D models, but these are blended with hand-drawn elements to create a hybrid style that looks surprisingly faithful to Lilo & Stitch from 2002.

Disney's VFX supervisor Jeremy Sikorski has said that the new pipeline was developed through experimentation on the previous shorts Paperman and Once Upon a Studio. Pixar is also exploring the same direction, as we saw in the Gatto trailer: environments, characters and sets are modeled and animated in 3D to retain spatial depth, lighting and camera movement, but certain characters and other details are hand drawn.

Disney says about 25% of the backgrounds in Lilo & Scratch are watercolour paintings reused from the original Lilo & Stitch, while more than a dozen new background paintings were created by artists including Tia Kratter and Larry Wu. Some of these were digitally painted in Photoshop to look like watercolour, while others were hand-painted on paper.
Combined with digital backgrounds and set extension, this blend of old and new hand-painted watercolours helped the filmmakers remain faithful to the look of the 2002 feature, Disney says.

In an interview at the Governors Awards in LA on Sunday (see the post by Deadline below), Disney Animation Chief Creative Officer Jared Bush confirmed that all original Disney movies from Clay onwards will use this approach. That doesn't mean that they'll all look like Renaissance-era 2D animation, but that each with have its own "wildly different" look.
Zootopia 3 and Frozen 3 will still look like we would expect, but Hexed may be "the last original in the Disney art style as people know it," he says.

Jared Bush shares updates on ‘Zootopia 3,’ ‘Frozen 3’ and ‘Hexed’ and reveals the new, upcoming animated films at Disney will have “wildly different art styles”: “We’re really going to be pushing into some new areas” | #GovernorsAwards https://t.co/nw16Ci8WoDNovember 16, 2026

The new approach looks like a win for Disney. Despite some success with the live-action The Jungle Book and last year's Lilo & Stitch, the poor reception of Moana, Snow White and Mulan suggests waning interest in the remake formula is waning. Meanwhile, the 3D animation style that once looked so modern is starting to feel dated and generic.

Nostalgic audiences miss 2D animation, while younger audiences want something fresh. It sounds like Disney's new animation pipeline could make both things possible without sacrificing the efficiency that comes with 3D-based CG animation, which makes it much quicker and easier to swap and adjust environments, characters and props compared to traditional hand-drawn 2D, where even a relatively small change might mean having to redraw from scratch.The Disney principles of animation will remain in tact, but in a vast realm new possibilities.
I do wonder though. In ten years time, will people start to feel nostalgic about the much-maligned 3D Disney style?
Hexed will be released on 25 November. Lilo & Scratch will screen before it.
